card.question: How many stars hide in the single point of σ Orionis?
card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the left-hand Belt star.
card.whyHere: σ Orionis sits at the heart of its own young cluster below the Belt, and its stars are some of the best-weighed heavy stars known.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; a closer one due east, and many more, need a telescope.
card.understand: The central pair is far too close for any ordinary telescope, but interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, have traced its orbit. Combine the size of that orbit on the sky with spectra that clock the stars’ speeds, and you get masses of about 17 and 13 Suns. The distance comes as a bonus, because the orbit’s true size in kilometers and its apparent size in arcseconds can only match at one distance.
card.wonder: Around the bright star swarm dozens of faint brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen, born from the same cloud.
card.connect: The same young family stretches along the Belt just above.
card.answer: At least three heavy stars are bound together in the central point, with more stars around them, and the central pair’s orbit pins the young cluster’s distance at about 1,260 light-years with rare precision.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split σ Orionis into a sparkling multiple; binoculars show one bright star with one or two companions.
card.deeper: Schaefer et al. (2016) resolved the inner Aa–Ab orbit with CHARA, NPOI and VLTI: 16.99 ± 0.20 and 12.81 ± 0.18 solar masses, B at 11.5 ± 1.2, and an orbital-parallax distance of 387.5 ± 1.3 pc. Simón-Díaz et al. (2015) found the inner pair’s model ages younger than the 3 ± 1 million years usually adopted for the cluster. WDS lists E at 42″ and D at 13.5″.

card.question: How do you weigh a star a thousand light-years away?
card.glance: The left-hand star of Orion’s Belt, brilliant blue-white.
card.whyHere: Alnitak belongs to Orion’s young family of hot, heavy stars, and it is one of the few of its kind weighed directly rather than estimated.
card.see: Fit all three Belt stars in one field, then center Alnitak at the eastern end. Just south of it lies the Horsehead region, but binoculars show only stars there; the dark horse needs a telescope and a filter.
card.understand: Alnitak is a supergiant of the hottest kind, with a close partner that circles it every seven years. Astronomers followed that partner around a full orbit with an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, measuring how far apart the two appear on the sky, while spectra clocked how fast each moves toward and away from us. Put the angle and the speed together and you get both the true size of the orbit and a distance of about 960 light-years, closer than the 1,250 light-years measured for its Belt neighbor Alnilam, a disagreement not yet settled.
card.wonder: Its light set out around the 11th century, when William the Conqueror crossed to England.
card.connect: Its Belt neighbor Alnilam looks just as bright, and it weighs about twice as much.
card.answer: You watch something orbit it, because an orbit’s size and period pin down the mass inside; for Alnitak they give at least about 14 Suns, and more if it lies as far away as the rest of the Belt.
card.photoCaption: Wide photos show the Flame and Horsehead nebulae beside Alnitak; binoculars show the star alone.
card.notSee: The Flame and Horsehead nebulae: telescope and camera targets.
card.deeper: Hummel et al. (2013) followed the Aa–Ab pair with the Navy Precision Optical Interferometer over its full seven-year orbit and combined it with spectroscopy: 14.0 ± 2.2 and 7.4 ± 1.1 solar masses at 294 ± 21 pc. A photometric distance from the B companion gives 387 ± 54 pc, so the distance is still debated. Brown et al. (1994) dated the Belt subgroup, Orion OB1b, to about 1.7 million years, but models of its brightest member, Alnilam, give 4.5 (Zsargó et al. 2020) to 5.7 million years (Voss et al. 2010).

card.question: Which star points the way to a runaway from Orion?
card.glance: The brightest star of Columba, the Dove, a blue-white point south of Lepus.
card.whyHere: Phact is a hot, fast-spinning star and the signpost to the runaway Mu Columbae.
card.see: Phact is easy to the naked eye. Put it near the edge of your binocular view, and Mu Columbae is the fainter bluish star about 2° to the north-east.
card.understand: Phact is a Be star, a hot blue star that spins fast enough to shed a thin disk of gas from its equator. That disk glows, adding bright lines to its spectrum, which is how such stars are recognized. Its distance, from Gaia’s parallax, is about 286 light-years.
card.wonder: Mu Columbae looks much fainter, yet it lies over six times farther away and far outshines Phact.
card.connect: Mu Columbae, a star thrown out of Orion, is a short hop away.
card.answer: Phact, the brightest star of Columba: about 2° north-east of it lies Mu Columbae, flung out of the Orion Nebula’s cluster. Phact is the easy step toward a star with a remarkable past.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a white point; its gas disk is detected only in spectra.

card.question: Can a star be thrown out of the cluster where it was born?
card.glance: A faint bluish star about 2° from Phact in Columba, easy in binoculars and hard to pick out by eye.
card.whyHere: Mu Columbae is a stellar escapee, thrown out of the Orion Nebula’s star cluster and still racing away.
card.see: Find Phact, the brightest star of Columba, the Dove, south of Orion, and nudge about 2° north-east to the faint bluish-white star there. Nothing about it looks special, because its story is in its motion.
card.understand: Astronomers measure a star’s speed across the sky and toward or away from us, and from those they can run its path backward like a film in reverse. Run back Mu Columbae and AE Aurigae, in the northern sky, and both lead to the young cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula about 2.5 million years ago. Computer simulations show how: two pairs of stars came too close, and in the gravitational tangle two were flung out in opposite directions.
card.wonder: It is about 19 times the Sun’s mass and 44,000 times as bright, yet it looks faint because it is about 1,900 light-years away.
card.connect: The cluster that threw them out still shines in Orion’s sword.
card.answer: It can, and a close encounter in the Orion Nebula’s cluster flung Mu Columbae one way and AE Aurigae the other, each at more than 100 km/s, proof that stellar nurseries can be rough places.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an ordinary bluish star; its speed is revealed only by careful position and spectrum measurements.
card.deeper: Hybrid non-LTE spectroscopy gives Teff = 33,400 ± 300 K, 18.9 M☉, 6.3 R☉ and log L/L☉ = 4.64, with a spectroscopic distance of 581 pc matching Gaia (Aschenbrenner et al. 2023). N-body simulations by Gualandris et al. (2004) reproduce μ Col and AE Aur as products of a binary–binary encounter in the Trapezium about 2.5 Myr ago that also left ι Ori as an eccentric binary; both runaways move at over 100 km/s.

card.question: How can the hotter of Orion’s two feet look fainter?
card.glance: Orion’s lower-left foot, a blue-white star a bit fainter than Rigel.
card.whyHere: Saiph is hotter than Rigel yet looks fainter, a lesson in how much of a star’s light our eyes simply miss.
card.see: Compare Saiph with Rigel at Orion’s opposite foot. Rigel looks brighter, both are blue-white, and nothing hints that Saiph is the hotter star.
card.understand: Saiph’s surface is more than twice as hot as Rigel’s. Heat a body and its glow shifts toward shorter wavelengths, the way a poker goes from red to yellow to white; a star this hot pours much of its energy out as invisible ultraviolet. Saiph is even the closer of the two, so distance is no excuse.
card.wonder: Our eyes evolved under sunlight, and they miss most of what a star this hot gives out.
card.connect: Above Saiph, Orion’s Belt holds three more hot stars from Orion’s young family.
card.answer: Much of Saiph’s light is ultraviolet, invisible to us, so it looks fainter than Rigel even though it is closer and hotter.

card.question: What does a planetary system look like while it is still forming?
card.glance: A modest white star in faint Pictor, about 6° west of brilliant Canopus.
card.whyHere: Beta Pictoris is a young star still building its planets, with two giant worlds and a dusty disk around it.
card.see: Start at Canopus and sweep about 6° west to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. Nothing in binoculars hints at its planets, so the wonder lies in knowing what is there.
card.understand: Beta Pictoris is only about 23 million years old, a toddler among stars. In 1984 astronomers blocked its glare with a disk inside the telescope and saw, for the first time around any star, a thin, edge-on disk of dust and rock, a young version of the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune. Two giant planets, each several times Jupiter’s mass, have since been photographed inside it.
card.wonder: Comets seem to plunge toward Beta Pictoris constantly, their evaporating gas showing up as fleeting marks in its spectrum.
card.connect: Kapteyn’s Star, in the same constellation, is the opposite, one of the oldest stars nearby and a visitor from the halo.
card.answer: It looks like Beta Pictoris, a young star wrapped in a flat disk of dust and rock with giant planets already formed inside it, much as our own Solar System must have looked long ago.
card.photoCaption: Telescope images remove the star’s glare to reveal the planet; such pictures take the largest telescopes, not binoculars.
card.notSee: The disk and planets are invisible in any amateur instrument.
card.deeper: Smith & Terrile (1984) imaged the edge-on debris disk with a coronagraph, after IRAS found its infrared excess. Planet b was imaged with VLT/NACO (Lagrange et al. 2009, 2010; ESO eso1024). Planet c, first found by radial velocities, was confirmed with VLTI/GRAVITY: 8.2 ± 0.8 Jupiter masses at 2.7 au, temperature about 1,250 K (Nowak et al. 2020). The parent moving group is 23 ± 3 Myr old (Mamajek & Bell 2014).

card.question: How can two stars eclipse each other without anyone noticing?
card.glance: The second-brightest star of Auriga, white, at the pentagon’s eastern corner.
card.whyHere: Menkalinan is a pair of nearly identical stars that eclipse each other every four days.
card.see: Find the Auriga pentagon, with Capella at its top; Menkalinan is the white star at its eastern corner. Its eclipses are invisible to the eye, so enjoy it as a steady beacon.
card.understand: Menkalinan is a pair of twin white stars orbiting every 3.96 days. Seen almost edge-on, they take turns eclipsing each other. Because they are twins, each eclipse looks much like the other, and the small dips together with the stars’ measured speeds let astronomers weigh and measure both.
card.wonder: Two whole stars orbit each other in under four days, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
card.connect: Auriga holds a far more dramatic eclipse at the Kids.
card.answer: When they are near-twins seen almost edge-on: Menkalinan’s two white stars do eclipse each other, but each eclipse dims it by less than a tenth, too little for the eye.

card.question: How can a star’s light wobble as it spins?
card.glance: A white star on the south-eastern side of the Auriga pentagon.
card.whyHere: θ Aurigae is a white star in the Auriga pentagon whose light rises and falls on a beat of a few days.
card.see: On the Auriga pentagon, θ Aurigae is the white star between Menkalinan and Elnath. Its close companion needs a telescope.
card.understand: θ Aurigae has strong magnetic fields that gather certain elements, such as silicon, into patches on its surface. Those patches absorb and re-emit light differently from the rest of the surface, so the star looks a little brighter from one side than from the other. Measuring how its brightness and spectrum repeat tells astronomers that it turns every 3.6 days.
card.wonder: These patches can last for decades, a kind of weather that never changes.
card.connect: At Taurus’s horn, a fast-spinning star wears a disk of its own gas.
card.answer: Its patches swing into and out of view as it rotates, like a lighthouse with a smudged lens, changing its brightness very slightly.

card.question: Can a star that looks perfectly steady actually be pulsing?
card.glance: The western end of Cassiopeia’s W, a bright white star that looks steady to the eye.
card.whyHere: Caph pulses every two and a half hours, far too gently for your eyes, so even a “steady” star can be breathing.
card.see: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-south-west.
card.understand: Caph is a δ Scuti star, one of a family of pulsating stars a little hotter than the Sun. A layer near its surface works like the valve on a pressure cooker, trapping heat, swelling, venting and sinking back. Light meters catch the rhythm as a change of only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.wonder: Caph swells and shrinks slightly, out and back about every two and a half hours, far too gently for the eye to notice.
card.connect: ρ Cassiopeiae, a short hop away, varies far more and lies roughly 170 times farther off.
card.answer: Caph does exactly that, swelling and shrinking about ten times a day, always too little for the eye, so its steadiness is only a limit of our senses.

card.question: Is every orange-red star a supergiant like Betelgeuse?
card.glance: A clearly orange-red star at Castor’s foot, near the cluster M35.
card.whyHere: μ Geminorum is a cool red giant right beside the cluster M35, a color contrast you can take in with one sweep.
card.see: Find Gemini’s western foot. μ Geminorum is the orange-red star there, and the cluster M35 sits about 2° to its north-west.
card.understand: μ Geminorum is a red giant, an aging star swollen and cooled, about 230 light-years away. Its surface is near 3,600 K, the same as Betelgeuse’s, so the two share a color. But color tells you only temperature; true power needs distance too, and Tejat is less than half as far as Betelgeuse yet looks much fainter.
card.wonder: It also flickers slightly and irregularly in brightness, as many cool giants do.
card.connect: Next door, M35 holds a whole family of stars.
card.answer: Tejat matches Betelgeuse in color but is an ordinary red giant, far less luminous, so the same color can belong to very different stars.

card.question: How can a star sixty times farther than Sirius still be easy to see?
card.glance: A blue-white star just west of Sirius, ‘the announcer’ that rises first.
card.whyHere: Mirzam is the hot star that heralds Sirius, and it is far more powerful than its modest looks suggest.
card.see: Look about 5° west of Sirius for a blue-white star: Mirzam. Compare the two and Sirius looks dazzling, Mirzam modest.
card.understand: Mirzam is about 490 light-years away, nearly sixty times farther than Sirius. A star that far would need thousands of times Sirius’s output to match it, and Mirzam, though fainter, gets a respectable fraction of the way. It is a hot star that also pulses every six hours, far too slightly for the eye to notice.
card.wonder: Its name means ‘the announcer’, because it rises shortly before Sirius.
card.connect: Sirius, beside it, is bright because it is close, not because it is powerful.
card.answer: Mirzam is a hot, powerful star that gives out far more light than Sirius, more than enough to shine brightly from that distance.

card.question: How can a star 310 light-years away outshine almost every other star?
card.glance: The second-brightest star of the night, in Carina, a dazzling white point well south of Sirius.
card.whyHere: Canopus outshines nearly everything in the night sky from about 310 light-years, so its brilliance must come from power rather than closeness.
card.see: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers through colors as our air splits its light, while higher up it is a steady white. Sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer, for perspective.
card.understand: Interferometers combine telescopes to measure the tiny disk of Canopus, about 7 thousandths of an arcsecond across. Knowing the distance, that angle becomes a true width of roughly 73 Suns. A surface that large and that hot must shine fiercely, and its total light, measured across all colors, confirms it: about 16,000 times the Sun’s output.
card.wonder: Spacecraft have long steered by Canopus, because it is bright and sits far from the Sun’s path across the sky.
card.connect: Bright does not mean near: faint Beta Pictoris, 6° away, is five times closer.
card.answer: Canopus simply pours out power, a giant of nine or ten Suns’ mass swollen past its long, steady adult life and probably now burning helium in its core, and few stars in our part of the galaxy match it.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only glare; Canopus’s true disk has been measured only by linking telescopes together.
card.deeper: Domiciano de Souza et al. (2021) measured a limb-darkened diameter of 7.184 mas with VLTI/PIONIER and combined it with the Hipparcos distance (94.8 ± 5.0 pc): R = 73 ± 4 R☉, Teff ≈ 7,660 K, log L/L☉ = 4.22. Geneva tracks give 9–10 M☉ and 24–34 Myr, placing Canopus most likely on the core-helium-burning ‘blue loop’. The ~5% distance error dominates the radius uncertainty.

card.question: Where does the carbon in your body come from?
card.glance: An orange-red star in eastern Auriga.
card.whyHere: UU Aurigae is an old red giant in eastern Auriga, and its color is a chemical signature.
card.see: Look in eastern Auriga, between Capella and the Gemini twins: among white stars, one glows orange-red. Judge its color with short glances rather than a stare.
card.understand: UU Aurigae has fused helium into carbon deep inside, and its churning outer layers have dredged that carbon up to the surface. Carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere, about 2,800 K, absorb blue light and leave a warm red glow. A slow wind carries its outer layers, carbon dust and all, out into space.
card.wonder: Every atom of carbon in you has been through a star at least once.
card.connect: W Orionis, across the sky in Orion, is another carbon star to compare.
card.answer: Partly from stars like UU Aurigae, which make carbon, bring it to the surface and puff it into space, where it ends up in new stars, planets and eventually people.

card.question: What kind of star stands at Gemini’s feet?
card.glance: The bright white star at the feet of Gemini.
card.whyHere: Alhena is a white signpost star at Gemini’s feet, a near neighbor in stellar terms.
card.see: Follow the Gemini twins down from Castor and Pollux to their feet; Alhena is the brightest star there. Use it as a jumping-off point for ζ Geminorum to the north-east.
card.understand: Alhena is a white star with a surface about 9,300 K, roughly one and a half times as hot as the Sun’s, about 110 light-years away. Its spectrum shows it has started to leave the long, steady phase of burning hydrogen in its core, the same change Procyon is going through. Before long, by stellar standards, it will swell into a giant.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time of the First World War.
card.connect: North-east of Alhena, ζ Geminorum pulses like a slow heartbeat.
card.answer: A white star hotter and heavier than the Sun, just beginning the change that will turn it into a giant.

card.question: Why does Mebsuta shine steadily when its cousin ζ Geminorum pulses?
card.glance: A yellow-orange star on Castor’s side of Gemini.
card.whyHere: Mebsuta is a yellow supergiant much like ζ Geminorum, yet it shines steadily.
card.see: Follow Castor’s ‘body’ down Gemini; Mebsuta is the yellow-orange star halfway. Compare its color with ζ Geminorum to the south-east.
card.understand: Mebsuta is a supergiant, one of the most luminous kinds of star, about 870 light-years away and cooler and redder than ζ Geminorum. Cepheids, the stars that rhythmically swell and shrink, pulse only within a narrow range of surface temperatures. In that range a layer of helium inside the star acts like a valve, trapping heat as it is squeezed and releasing it as it expands, which keeps the pulsing going.
card.wonder: Far more luminous than the Sun, it still looks like an ordinary star from 870 light-years away.
card.connect: ζ Geminorum, to the south-east, is the pulsing kind.
card.answer: Mebsuta is too cool to sit inside that narrow band, so its valve never catches and the star shines steadily.

card.question: What kind of star is Tau Puppis?
card.glance: A yellow-orange star in southern Puppis, between Canopus and the Milky Way.
card.whyHere: Tau Puppis is an orange giant with a close companion, a typical aging star near brilliant Canopus.
card.see: In binoculars Tau Puppis is a soft yellow-orange point. Compare it with brilliant white Canopus about 5° to the west-south-west.
card.understand: Tau Puppis is a giant about 25 times the Sun’s width, with a cooler surface near 4,600 K. Its companion is too close to see, revealed only by the shifting lines in its spectrum. Stars like it are in a long, settled phase after their core hydrogen ran out.
card.wonder: Canopus beside it is a far heavier giant, though both have left their steady adult lives behind.
card.connect: Canopus, nearby, is a far more powerful giant.
card.answer: An aging orange giant about 25 times the Sun’s width, quietly orbited by a companion no telescope can split. It is the kind of star the sky is full of once you start looking.

card.question: Which is really the more powerful star, Sirius or Adhara?
card.glance: A bright blue-white star in the hindquarters of Canis Major.
card.whyHere: Adhara is only the second-brightest star in Canis Major, which makes it easy to overlook beside Sirius.
card.see: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius’s white.
card.understand: Adhara is about 400 light-years away, nearly fifty times farther than Sirius, yet it is one of the brightest stars in the sky. Fifty times the distance means some two and a half thousand times less light, so a star out there would need thousands of times Sirius’s output to look as bright. Adhara looks fainter than Sirius, but far less faint than that distance would make it.
card.wonder: Moved out to Adhara’s distance, Sirius would fade below naked-eye visibility.
card.connect: Nearby Wezen and Aludra are even farther and more luminous.
card.answer: Adhara, which must outshine Sirius more than a hundred times over to look this bright from nearly fifty times the distance.

card.question: Why has the middle star of Cassiopeia’s W brightened and faded over the decades?
card.glance: The blue-white center star of Cassiopeia’s W, plain to look at but wrapped in a disk of glowing gas.
card.whyHere: γ Cassiopeiae is the original Be star, a hot young star spinning so fast that it sheds gas from its waist.
card.see: γ Cas is the middle star of the W, a clean blue-white point in binoculars. Swing to orange Schedar, the next bright star west, and back: over the decades γ has sometimes outshone Schedar and sometimes fallen below it, so your comparison tonight joins a long record.
card.understand: γ Cas is about 8 million years old, many times heavier than the Sun, and spinning so fast that its equator barely holds on. Gas leaks off that bulging equator into a flattened disk, like mud flung from a spinning wheel. In 1866 Angelo Secchi spread its light into a spectrum and saw bright lines where dark ones belong, a first for any star, and those lines come from the glowing disk.
card.wonder: Its light set out in the late Middle Ages, so tonight you see the disk it wore more than five centuries ago.
card.connect: Spin shapes stars: Alderamin in Cepheus is flattened by its spin, and γ Cas spins hard enough to shed a disk.
card.answer: The star stays much the same while its disk comes and goes, adding its glow as it builds and taking it away as it thins. That is why the W’s middle star has wandered between about magnitudes 1.6 and 3.0.
card.photoCaption: No photograph is shown: the gas disk is far too small for any ordinary image. Its story is written in its spectrum.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 5.94 ± 0.12 mas (about 550 light-years). Classified B0.5 IVpe. GCVS lists a visual range of 1.6–3.0 as the disk built up and dissipated over the 20th century. Isochrone fitting gives an age of about 8 million years (Tetzlaff et al. 2011). Secchi’s report of bright Hβ in 1866 (published 1867) made it the first emission-line star.

card.question: How can a star’s pulse tell you how far away it is?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Gemini that brightens and fades on a 10-day rhythm.
card.whyHere: ζ Geminorum is a pulsating yardstick, one of the stars that let astronomers stretch distance measurements out to other galaxies.
card.see: Find ζ Geminorum about 7° north-east of Alhena, at the twins’ feet. Over a week or two, compare it with δ and λ Geminorum nearby: at its brightest it matches them, at its faintest it falls clearly behind.
card.understand: ζ Geminorum is a Cepheid, a yellow supergiant that rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every 10.15 days. In 2000 an interferometer actually watched its disk grow and shrink, a star breathing in plain view. Cepheids obey a remarkable rule, first noticed by Henrietta Leavitt: the slower the rhythm, the more light the star truly gives out, and the Hubble Space Telescope measured this star’s parallax to help calibrate that rule.
card.wonder: Stars of this kind, spotted in other galaxies, first showed that the universe extends far beyond the Milky Way.
card.connect: Its neighbor ε Geminorum is a similar yellow supergiant that does not pulse at all.
card.answer: Time the rhythm and you know the star’s true power; compare that with how faint it looks and the distance follows, just as a lamp’s dimness tells you how far away it is once you know its wattage.
card.photoCaption: A photo freezes one moment of its 10-day cycle; it looks like any yellow star.
card.deeper: Benedict et al. (2007) measured its parallax with Hubble’s Fine Guidance Sensor, 2.78 ± 0.18 mas (about 1,170 light-years), as one of ten Cepheids anchoring the Galactic period–luminosity relation. Lane et al. (2000) detected its angular-diameter pulsation with the Palomar Testbed Interferometer. GCVS gives a period of 10.15 days and a range of 3.62–4.18 V.

card.question: How can a star 1,600 light-years away rank among the brightest in the sky?
card.glance: A creamy-yellow star in Canis Major’s hindquarters, south-east of Sirius.
card.whyHere: Wezen is a yellow supergiant more than a thousand light-years away, yet still among the brightest stars of the night.
card.see: In Canis Major’s triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara and Aludra nearby, a temperature ladder in one sweep.
card.understand: Wezen is a supergiant, one of the most luminous kinds of star, swollen and cooled in old age so that it shines yellow-white. Its distance is uncertain, because its parallax is tiny, and so is its power, which grows with the distance squared. Heavy stars like it end as supernovae, exploding when their cores give out.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 1,600 years ago, in the late Roman Empire.
card.connect: Next door, Aludra is a blue supergiant of similar power.
card.answer: It is a yellow supergiant tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun, enough to shine across that gulf.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a yellowish point.

card.question: What will the Sun look like near the very end of its giant life?
card.glance: A reddish variable star in Puppis that can be easy or faint depending on the year.
card.whyHere: L² Puppis is a star of about the Sun’s mass near the very end of its giant life, a preview of the Sun’s distant future.
card.see: Find L² Puppis about 7.5° south of Pi Puppis, where it forms a wide pair with its blue-white neighbor L¹ Puppis. In binoculars L² is clearly redder, so check its brightness against L¹ on different nights.
card.understand: L² Puppis is shedding its outer layers in a slow, dusty wind, and it pulses every 140 days or so while its dust can dim it for years. ALMA, an array of radio dishes, watched the gas swirling close to the star and, from how fast it circles, weighed the star at about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass. The Sun will pass through this stage before leaving a small, hot core behind.
card.wonder: ESO’s VLT has seen a dusty disk and a close companion around it, the first stirrings of a butterfly-shaped planetary nebula.
card.connect: When the dust clears, the exposed core will light up the shed gas as a glowing shell, a planetary nebula.
card.answer: Much like L² Puppis, a dying giant of about the Sun’s mass, pulsing and wrapping itself in dust as it lets its outer layers go, which astronomers call a flash-forward of our own Sun by 5 to 6 billion years.
card.photoCaption: The VLT photo shows a dusty disk seen edge-on; binoculars show only a reddish point.
card.notSee: The disk and companion are invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: ALMA observations resolved the rotating gas close to the star and gave 0.659 ± 0.011 ± 0.041 M☉ for L² Pup A, plus a candidate companion about 2 au away (Kervella et al. 2016). NACO aperture masking showed a dusty torus with an inner radius of about 4.2 au (Lykou et al. 2015). VSX lists a semiregular period of 140.6 d and a range of 2.6–8.0 mag; the faint end reflects dust episodes since the 1990s, so present brightness cannot be predicted offline.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun shine 11,000 times brighter?
card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.whyHere: Pi Puppis is the cool end of the Puppis thermometer, an orange supergiant 10° from blue-white Naos.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange, and at 10× a much fainter star separates just to its south-west, easier still on a tripod, though at 7× it usually drowns in the glare. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with a surface near 3,900 K. Each square meter of a surface that cool gives out only a fraction of the Sun’s light. Its total light, measured across all colors and scaled by distance, still comes to about 11,000 Suns, leaving one way to balance the books.
card.wonder: It is the brightest member of a loose young cluster scattered around it, which binoculars show as a sprinkle of fainter stars.
card.connect: Ten degrees east, Naos burns ten times hotter.
card.answer: It must be vast, and it is, about 230 times the Sun’s width, so its sheer extent makes up for its coolness.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point with faint neighbors; the color is real.

card.question: How can one star outshine its whole cluster?
card.glance: A star sitting inside a tiny, sparkling cluster in Canis Major, south-east of Sirius.
card.whyHere: τ Canis Majoris is a knot of young, heavy stars so luminous that it outshines the entire cluster that bears its name.
card.see: Find τ Canis Majoris about 2½° north-east of Wezen, below and left of Sirius. In 10× binoculars a halo of faint stars surrounds it; at 7× the cluster may look like a soft glow around one bright star.
card.understand: τ CMa is a small group of very hot, very heavy stars, including a pair that eclipses every 1.3 days. Its cluster is only about five to seven million years old, an age astronomers read from its members: the faint ones are still settling down, while none of the heavy ones has yet burned out. Heavy stars are not just a little brighter than light ones but enormously so, which is why a handful can outshine all the rest.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 4,000 years ago, when the first written laws were being carved in Mesopotamia.
card.connect: Close by lies VY CMa, what a star this heavy becomes after a few million more years.
card.answer: By gathering the heaviest stars in one spot: τ CMa gives out so much light that it reaches naked-eye brightness from about 4,000 light-years, and its cluster mates are faint by comparison.
card.photoCaption: Photos resolve dozens of faint cluster stars around τ CMa; binoculars show a handful.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) give 1,228 pc and about 7 (4.3–9.3) million years for NGC 2362 from Gaia DR3; Moitinho et al. (2001) found 5 (+1/−2) million years at 1,480 pc from photometry and called the cluster a template for early stellar evolution. GCVS lists τ CMa as a 1.282-day eclipsing system of small amplitude.

card.question: How do you know two close stars are truly partners?
card.glance: A neat multiple star in the faint constellation Lynx, a bright point with a wider, fainter companion.
card.whyHere: 19 Lyncis is a young, hot multiple star and a fair test of what binoculars can and cannot split.
card.see: In faint Lynx, between the Big Dipper’s bowl and the Gemini twins, look for a fainter star about a tenth of a Moon-width from 19 Lyn; that wide companion is easy. The main pair is much tighter and stays merged in most binoculars.
card.understand: The two main stars are hot blue-white stars about three times the Sun’s mass. Gaia measures nearly the same parallax for both, putting them about 640 light-years away. Two stars this close on the sky and at the same depth are unlikely strangers.
card.wonder: The light you see set out in the late 1300s, while Chaucer was writing The Canterbury Tales.
card.connect: Wider, brighter doubles wait in the Big Dipper and Boötes.
card.answer: They must share a depth as well as a direction on the sky, and the pair of 19 Lyncis passes that test.

card.question: Why is Aludra’s true power so hard to pin down?
card.glance: A blue-white point marking the end of Canis Major’s tail.
card.whyHere: Aludra is one of the most powerful stars in the winter sky, though nothing in its look says so.
card.see: Aludra is the blue-white star at the tip of the Great Dog’s tail, south-east of Sirius. Compare it with yellow Wezen to the west.
card.understand: Aludra is a blue supergiant, a hot star of the most luminous kind. Its power follows from how bright it looks and how far away it is, and at this distance the parallax is under two thousandths of an arcsecond. Since power grows with the square of the distance, a quarter’s error in distance becomes more than half in power.
card.wonder: Its light set out roughly 2,000 years ago, in the first years of the Roman Empire.
card.connect: Nearby, VY Canis Majoris shows where the heaviest stars head next.
card.answer: Its distance lies somewhere between about 1,600 and 2,600 light-years, so its power, tens of thousands of times the Sun’s, comes with a wide margin.

card.question: Why does Gomeisa look fainter than Procyon though it is more powerful?
card.glance: The fainter blue-white partner of Procyon, 4° to its north-west.
card.whyHere: Gomeisa is a fast-spinning hot star with a gas disk, sitting right next to creamy Procyon.
card.see: Put Procyon and Gomeisa, in the little constellation Canis Minor, in one sweep and compare colors: Gomeisa is bluer. It is also about fourteen times farther away.
card.understand: Gomeisa is a hot blue-white star spinning fast enough to throw gas into a disk around its equator, a disk that shows up as bright hydrogen light in its spectrum. It is much more luminous than Procyon. Its distance, measured by the Hipparcos satellite, is why the stronger star looks the weaker.
card.wonder: The light you see from it left about 160 years ago, while Procyon’s left only about 11 years ago.
card.connect: Procyon, right beside it, is bright because it is close.
card.answer: Gomeisa is simply so much farther away that all its extra power cannot make up the difference, and the weaker star wins the contest of looks.

card.question: How many stars are hiding in Castor?
card.glance: The fainter of Gemini’s twin stars: crisp white, beside orange Pollux.
card.whyHere: Castor looks like one crisp white star, and it turns out to be one of the best places to learn how stars are weighed.
card.see: Compare Castor’s white with Pollux’s orange, 4½° away. At 10× Castor looks single, because its two bright stars are only 5 arcseconds apart. With braced binoculars, look about 70 arcseconds south-south-east for a very faint point: Castor C.
card.understand: Castor A and Castor B circle each other over several centuries. Each is a tight pair of its own, revealed by the way the lines in its spectrum split and merge as the stars swing around. Castor C is two small red stars called red dwarfs that eclipse each other every 19½ hours, and timing those eclipses weighed each one to better than 1%.
card.wonder: Castor C’s two red dwarfs each weigh about 0.6 Suns, which makes the faintest pair in the family the best-measured.
card.connect: Its ‘twin’ Pollux is nothing like it: an orange giant with a planet.
card.answer: Six stars in three pairs, all bound by gravity, share the light you see as one white point.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split Castor A and B; binoculars show one white star and, at best, faint Castor C.
card.deeper: Torres & Ribas (2002) measured YY Gem (Castor C): two nearly identical M dwarfs of 0.599 solar masses and 0.62 solar radii in a 0.814-day orbit. Re-reducing the Hipparcos data while allowing for the 467-year A–B orbit, they found a parallax of 66.90 ± 0.63 mas (about 49 light-years) and estimated an age of roughly 370 million years. WDS lists A–B at 5.4″ and A–C at 70″ (2023).

card.question: Can a planet survive its star turning into a giant?
card.glance: The brighter of Gemini’s twins: a warm orange point.
card.whyHere: Pollux is one of the nearest giant stars to us, and it has kept a planet through the swelling of old age.
card.see: Put Pollux and Castor in one field: Pollux is orange, Castor white, and a touch of defocus makes the difference vivid. The ‘twins’ lie at different distances and are at different stages of life.
card.understand: Pollux is an orange giant about 34 light-years away that has finished burning hydrogen in its core, swollen, and cooled to about 4,850 K. Its planet gives itself away by tugging on the star. Pollux’s light shifts slightly toward blue, then toward red, every 590 days as the star swings toward and away from us, and astronomers followed that rhythm for 25 years before they were sure.
card.wonder: The same fate awaits the Sun, and whether Earth will survive it is a question astronomers still argue about.
card.connect: Procyon, to the south, is just about to begin this chapter of a star’s life.
card.answer: This one has survived so far, a planet at least twice Jupiter’s mass still circling at about 1.6 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, well clear of its swollen star.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point; the planet was found only by measuring the star’s tiny wobble.
card.deeper: Hatzes et al. (2006) confirmed with 25 years of radial velocities a 589.6-day, nearly circular orbit and a minimum mass of 2.3 Jupiter masses (for a 1.7-solar-mass star); Reffert et al. (2006) found 589.7 ± 3.5 days and 2.9 ± 0.3 Jupiter masses assuming 1.86 solar masses. The Hipparcos parallax, 96.54 ± 0.27 mas, gives 33.8 light-years.

card.question: Can binoculars split a pair of stars that truly travel together?
card.glance: A matched pair of white stars in Pisces, 30 arcseconds apart, a test for steady binoculars.
card.whyHere: ψ¹ Piscium is a near-twin pair that steady 10× binoculars can just split, and a real one rather than a chance alignment.
card.see: ψ¹ Piscium lies in Pisces, well south of Mirach; brace your binoculars or use a tripod. At 10× the two white stars touch but separate.
card.understand: How do you tell a real pair from two stars that merely line up? You watch them over time. Observers have measured these two since 1755, and their separation has barely changed, whereas unrelated stars would long since have drifted apart.
card.wonder: Each is a hot white star, both far brighter than the Sun.
card.connect: α Capricorni looks like a pair too, but its stars only line up by chance.
card.answer: Just barely, for the two white stars are 30 arcseconds apart, a fine split for steady 10× binoculars, and centuries of measurement show them moving together as a true pair of suns.

card.question: How hot can a star you see with your eyes be?
card.glance: A steely blue-white star in a rich Milky Way field in Puppis.
card.whyHere: Naos sits at the hot end of the stellar thermometer, with a surface about seven times hotter than the Sun’s.
card.see: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Swing about 10° west to Pi Puppis, a deep yellow-orange star, and you have both ends of the temperature scale in neighboring fields.
card.understand: A star’s temperature is written in its spectrum: certain atoms only show their lines when hot enough to lose electrons, and Naos shows lines of helium stripped of an electron, a sign of extreme heat. Naos is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with about 25 times the Sun’s mass. It pours out roughly 450,000 times the Sun’s light, most of it ultraviolet.
card.wonder: It also races through space, probably thrown out of its birth cluster.
card.connect: Gamma Velorum, next door in Vela, shows what such a star becomes once its outer layers are stripped away.
card.answer: About 40,000 K, nearly seven times the Sun’s surface temperature, and most of its enormous output is ultraviolet light your eyes cannot see. What reaches you is only the visible tail of a far greater glare.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a bright blue-white point; its ultraviolet glare is recorded only by space telescopes.
card.deeper: Howarth & van Leeuwen (2019) re-examined the Hipparcos parallax (3.01 ± 0.10 mas; 332 ± 11 pc) and derived Teff ≈ 40 kK, log L/L☉ = 5.65, R ≈ 13.5 R☉ and a spectroscopic mass of 25 ± 5 M☉, below single-star predictions. Its runaway velocity (~56 km/s), rapid rotation (v sin i ≈ 213 km/s) and anomalous parameters suggest past binary interaction; Trumpler 10 is a candidate birthplace.

card.question: Can a star’s brightness change within a few hours?
card.glance: A yellow-white star in northern Puppis that pulses every few hours.
card.whyHere: Tureis is a star you could, in principle, watch breathe in a single night.
card.see: In binoculars Tureis is a plain yellow-white point. Its brightness rises and falls by about a fifth every three and a half hours, too little to judge easily by eye.
card.understand: Tureis is a pulsating star whose outer layers swell and shrink in a steady rhythm. As the star expands and contracts, its surface heats and cools slightly, changing its brightness. Instruments time the beat precisely, and the rhythm is as regular as a clock.
card.wonder: It belongs to the same pulsing family as δ Scuti, stars whose outer layers trap and release heat like a valve.
card.connect: Other stars change far more, through eclipses, dust or wild outbursts.
card.answer: It can, as Tureis swells and shrinks about seven times a day, changing its brightness by about a fifth.

card.question: What is left when a heavy star’s winds strip it to the core?
card.glance: Vela’s brightest star, with a fainter companion 41 arcseconds away that steady 10× binoculars split.
card.whyHere: Gamma Velorum holds a rare Wolf–Rayet star, the stripped-bare core of a heavy star near the end of its life.
card.see: Steady your binoculars and Gamma Velorum splits into a bright white star with a fainter one just beside it. A little farther out, two much fainter stars complete a tiny group.
card.understand: The bright star is itself two stars in a 78-day orbit: a hot giant about 28 times the Sun’s mass and a Wolf–Rayet star of about 9. A Wolf–Rayet star is a heavy star whose fierce winds have blown away its outer hydrogen, exposing hot inner layers rich in carbon. Astronomers weighed both by following the orbit with an interferometer and with the shifting lines of their spectra.
card.wonder: Around it lie hundreds of faint newborn stars, a family only 5–10 million years old, all about 1,100 light-years away.
card.connect: Naos, next door in Puppis, is a heavyweight still wrapped in its hydrogen, the earlier stage of the same life.
card.answer: A Wolf–Rayet star is what remains, and Gamma Velorum’s smaller star, stripped to its hot inner layers, was once far heavier. It will probably end as a supernova.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the bright pair and a scatter of fainter stars; the Wolf–Rayet’s winds are revealed only by spectra.
card.notSee: The two stars inside γ² Vel cannot be separated in any binocular.
card.deeper: North et al. Jeffries et al. (2009) found a few hundred low-mass pre-main-sequence stars clustered around γ Vel, 5–10 Myr old by low-mass models but 3–4 Myr by high-mass models, a tension still discussed. γ² Vel is a member of Vela OB2 (de Zeeuw et al. 1999).

card.question: Why is one corner of the False Cross orange?
card.glance: The orange corner of the False Cross, in Carina.
card.whyHere: Avior is a blend of two stars, an orange giant and a hot blue star, that looks like one orange point.
card.see: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Delta Velorum and Aspidiske.
card.understand: Spread Avior’s light into a spectrum and two sets of fingerprints appear, those of a cool orange giant and those of a hotter blue star. The giant is the more luminous in visible light, so it sets the color. The two are too close to split with any binoculars.
card.wonder: It is roughly seven times farther away than Delta Velorum, its partner in the False Cross.
card.connect: The False Cross is a pattern of stars at very different distances.
card.answer: Avior’s light blends two stars, and the cool orange giant outshines its hot blue companion, so the mixture looks orange, two colors blended into one point.

card.question: Why is Mirach the usual starting point for finding two galaxies?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star in Andromeda, the usual stepping stone to the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies.
card.whyHere: Mirach is a cool red giant and a signpost to two neighboring galaxies.
card.see: Mirach is the middle bright star of Andromeda’s chain, a ruddy orange point in binoculars. Hop north-west through μ Andromedae to the Andromeda Galaxy, or the other way to the Triangulum Galaxy.
card.understand: Mirach is a red giant, cooler than the Sun and so redder, but far larger and brighter. Its parallax puts it about 197 light-years away. The galaxies beside it are far too remote for parallax; their distances come from pulsing stars like δ Cephei.
card.wonder: Seen from Mirach, our Sun would be far too faint to find with the naked eye.
card.connect: The Triangulum Galaxy, on the other side of Mirach, is fainter and a little farther still.
card.answer: It happens to sit between them on the sky, so one binocular sweep runs from a star two centuries of light away to galaxies whose light is millions of years old.

card.question: How could a bright star hide its eclipses for all of history?
card.glance: One corner of the False Cross, a bright white star that dims for some hours every few weeks.
card.whyHere: Delta Velorum was quietly eclipsing for all of history, unnoticed until the year 2000.
card.see: Find the False Cross in Vela and Carina, a larger, fainter look-alike of the Southern Cross, and Delta Velorum is one of its four corners. On most nights it is clearly brighter than Kappa Velorum and Aspidiske, and during an eclipse it drops to about their level.
card.understand: Delta Velorum is two white stars orbiting each other every 45 days, and our view runs almost along their orbit, so once per orbit one passes in front of the other: an eclipsing binary. Each dip lasts only hours and costs less than half a magnitude, so in most years you would have to be watching at just the right time. An amateur caught one by eye in 1997, and the star-tracker of NASA’s Galileo probe, which used the star to steer, had recorded others.
card.wonder: Earth’s slowly wobbling axis is carrying the south celestial pole toward it, and around the year 9000 Delta Velorum will serve as a southern pole star.
card.connect: The False Cross fools navigators, and its stars are not even close together: Avior is roughly seven times farther away.
card.answer: Its eclipses are rare and brief, one short dip per orbit, and they slipped past generations of observers until 2000, when the two records were put together. Even the brightest stars can keep a secret.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a bright white point; eclipses are seen by comparing its brightness with nearby stars.
card.deeper: Otero, Fieseler & Lloyd (2000) reported a ~0.3 mag fading seen visually in 1997 and in Galileo star-scanner engineering data (1989, 2000); Hipparcos had missed the eclipses. Their ephemeris gives P = 45.150 ± 0.001 d with unequal primary and secondary minima (eccentric orbit). The bright pair has a 1″ companion (F8 V), and Hipparcos places the system at 40.5 mas (81 ly).

card.question: What is it like on a planet that circles its star in under a day?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in northern Cancer, easy in binoculars once you know where to look.
card.whyHere: 55 Cancri has five known planets, including a scorching rocky world whose year is shorter than a day.
card.see: 55 Cnc lies about nine degrees north-north-east of the Beehive Cluster in Cancer. In binoculars it is a pale yellowish point, just visible to the naked eye from a very dark site.
card.understand: 55 Cancri is a little cooler and smaller than the Sun, about 41 light-years away. Its planets were found from the tiny wobble they cause in the star’s motion, and the innermost, 55 Cancri e, also passes in front of the star, dimming it slightly, which reveals its size: about twice Earth’s width. Mass from the wobble and size from the shadow together give its density, which is that of rock.
card.wonder: A year on 55 Cancri e lasts under 18 hours.
card.connect: τ Boötis, near Arcturus, is another nearby star with a giant planet in a tight orbit.
card.answer: 55 Cancri e orbits so close that its surface is probably a sea of lava, and in 2024 the Webb telescope found hints of a thick atmosphere rising from it.
card.photoCaption: No photograph shows these planets; every one was found from the star’s motion, and e also by its passages in front of the star.
card.deeper: The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists five planets: b (14.65 days; Butler et al. 1997), c (44.4 days), d (about 4,800 days, minimum mass about 3.9 Jupiters), e (0.737 days, about 8 Earth masses and 1.9 Earth radii) and f (260.6 days; Fischer et al. 2008). A JWST emission spectrum (Hu et al. 2024, reported by Eos) favors a secondary atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide or monoxide over bare rock. Gaia EDR3 parallax 79.45 mas (41.1 light-years); the red dwarf 55 Cnc B lies 85″ away (WDS).

card.question: What turns a dying giant deep red?
card.glance: A vivid red-orange star a few degrees south-east of the Beehive Cluster, easy in binoculars once you know the field.
card.whyHere: X Cancri is a dying giant just off the Beehive, one of the redder stars within binocular reach.
card.see: From the Beehive, the misty patch in Cancer between Regulus and the Gemini twins, move about four and a half degrees south-east. X Cnc stands out by color, a warm red-orange that deepens the longer you look, and its brightness changes over months.
card.understand: Like La Superba, X Cancri is an old giant whose core is spent and now burns helium in thin shells. Churning currents bring freshly made carbon to the surface, and at about 2,600 K carbon molecules in its atmosphere soak up blue and green light. Its color index, a measure of how much brighter it is in yellow light than in blue, is among the largest of any binocular star.
card.wonder: It looks like the Beehive’s neighbor but lies far behind the cluster.
card.connect: La Superba in Canes Venatici is its brighter carbon-star cousin.
card.answer: Its own carbon, dredged up from deep inside, filters X Cancri’s light until mostly red is left.
card.photoCaption: This ALMA image shows a different carbon star in radio light; X Cancri itself appears only as a red point.
card.deeper: Lambert et al. (1986) derived an effective temperature of about 2,625 K. GCVS lists X Cnc as a semiregular SRb variable, V 5.52–7.50, with a period of about 193 days and spectral type C5,4. The DEATHSTAR catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 332 +41/−36 pc, about 1,080 light-years. Its B−V color index of about 3.2 makes it one of the redder stars within binocular reach.

card.question: How can a cool star also be enormously bright?
card.glance: A bright orange star in Vela, glowing like an ember among blue-white neighbors.
card.whyHere: Suhail is a supergiant, cool, orange and enormous, the biggest star in this part of Vela.
card.see: Suhail is the bright orange star about 11° east-north-east of Gamma Velorum. Defocus a little to make its color glow, then swing to blue-white Gamma Velorum to read the temperature difference.
card.understand: Suhail is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with a surface near 3,900 K. A cooler surface gives off less light per square meter, so a cool star can only be this bright by having an enormous number of square meters. Its total light, gathered across all colors and combined with its distance, reveals the size: about 200 times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Put it where the Sun is and its surface would reach almost to Earth’s orbit.
card.connect: Gamma Velorum and Naos, not far away, show hotter chapters in the lives of heavy stars.
card.answer: Each patch of Suhail is dimmer than the Sun’s surface, but there is so much of it that the star gives out nearly 9,000 times the Sun’s light.
card.photoCaption: Photos show an orange point; the color in binoculars is real.
card.deeper: Hipparcos gives 5.99 ± 0.11 mas (≈545 ly). An SED fit (McDonald et al. 2017) gives ~3,900 K and ~8,700 L☉; the JSDC photometric diameter (11.9 ± 1.4 mas) implies about 210 R☉ (≈1 au, so ‘almost to Earth’s orbit’ given the ±12% uncertainty). GCVS classes it as a slow irregular variable (Lc), 2.14–2.30 mag.

card.question: How far apart are a bright star and the star swarm beside it?
card.glance: A bright white star deep in the southern sky, in Carina, south-west of the Southern Pleiades.
card.whyHere: Miaplacidus is a bright white star near the end of its adult life, and a stepping stone to a globular cluster nearby.
card.see: Miaplacidus shines bright white about 5° south of the globular cluster NGC 2808. In binoculars compare the sharp star with the cluster’s soft glow.
card.understand: Miaplacidus is a white star heavier than the Sun, close to the end of its long hydrogen-burning life. Its parallax, the shift as Earth circles the Sun, puts it about 113 light-years away. The cluster beside it is far too remote for that shift to show.
card.wonder: Its light set out before anyone knew that other galaxies existed.
card.connect: From a near star to a distant swarm of ancient ones is a single hop.
card.answer: Enormously far: the globular cluster NGC 2808 sent its light some 33,000 years ago, so it and Miaplacidus share a field of view and almost nothing else.

card.question: Are the corners of the False Cross neighbors in space?
card.glance: A white corner of the False Cross, in Carina.
card.whyHere: Aspidiske is one of the four corners of the False Cross, and the way to test whether those corners are neighbors.
card.see: Aspidiske marks one corner of the False Cross. It looks about as bright as Delta Velorum on most nights.
card.understand: Aspidiske is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, about 47 times the Sun’s width and about 5,000 times its light. Its parallax puts it about 770 light-years away. To look as bright as nearby Delta Velorum from that far, it must be vastly more luminous.
card.wonder: Its light set out around the year 1260, when Marco Polo was still a boy.
card.connect: Kappa Velorum, at the next corner, makes a handy gauge for catching Delta Velorum in eclipse.
card.answer: Aspidiske looks about as bright as Delta Velorum but is a supergiant almost ten times farther away, so the False Cross is drawn with stars at very different depths.

card.question: How can you tell when Delta Velorum is in eclipse?
card.glance: A blue-white corner of the False Cross, in Vela.
card.whyHere: Kappa Velorum is a hot blue-white star and a handy comparison star for Delta Velorum’s eclipses.
card.see: Kappa Velorum is the dimmest corner of the False Cross. Use it as a yardstick for Delta Velorum.
card.understand: Kappa Velorum is a hot young star, much heavier and more luminous than the Sun, about 570 light-years away. Eyes judge brightness poorly on their own but compare two stars well, so a steady neighbor makes a good gauge. Kappa sits close to Delta’s eclipse level.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time Gutenberg was printing his first books.
card.connect: Check Delta Velorum against it tonight.
card.answer: Compare the two, because when Delta Velorum sinks to Kappa’s brightness an eclipse is under way, while on most nights Delta is clearly the brighter.

card.question: How does a yellow giant compare with the Sun?
card.glance: The star at the top of Leo’s Sickle, pale yellow in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Ras Elased Australis is a yellow giant much larger and brighter than the Sun, marking the top of the lion’s head.
card.see: Follow Leo’s Sickle, the backward question mark, up from Regulus to its top. In binoculars this star is a soft pale yellow; compare it with blue-white Regulus at the bottom of the same curve.
card.understand: It has left its long, steady adult life and swollen to about 21 times the Sun’s width, a size measured from its tiny disk with an interferometer. Its surface, near 5,300 K, is a little cooler than the Sun’s. That gives it a slightly deeper yellow tint.
card.wonder: Moved to its distance of about 250 light-years, the Sun would be too faint to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Regulus, at the foot of the Sickle, is the hot contrast.
card.answer: Much bigger and only a little cooler, so it glows a slightly deeper yellow while pouring out far more light than the Sun.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a pale yellow point; the color difference from Regulus is easier to judge by eye.

card.question: How can a star fade to a five-hundredth of its brightness and recover?
card.glance: A red giant near Regulus that brightens and fades enormously over about ten months, so it may be easy, faint or invisible tonight.
card.whyHere: R Leonis is a dying giant whose brightness swings by hundreds of times, and you can follow it through the year.
card.see: R Leo lies about five degrees west of Regulus, the star at the foot of Leo’s Sickle, and an AAVSO finder chart shows the field. Near its peak it is an easy orange-red binocular star; near its low point it drops out of reach.
card.understand: R Leonis is a Mira star, a giant in its last stage of life that swells and shrinks, here every 310 days. Its total output changes far less than its visible light: as the outer layers cool, molecules form and block the visible light while much of the energy slips out as infrared. Each pulse also lifts gas and dust off the surface into space.
card.wonder: Its light takes over three centuries to reach you, so you see it as it was around 1700.
card.connect: Regulus, nearby, is a hot, young, fast-spinning star beside this cool, dying one.
card.answer: The star dims far less than it seems; its cooling atmosphere shifts the light out of the colors our eyes can see, cutting the visible glow more than 500-fold before the next swell brings it back.
card.photoCaption: Any photo shows R Leo at one moment of its cycle; tonight it may look very different.
card.deeper: GCVS lists R Leo as a Mira variable with a range of V 4.4–11.3 and a period of 309.95 days; a 6.9-magnitude swing is a factor of about 575 in visible light, although its total light output changes far less because much of it moves into the infrared. The DEATHSTAR distance catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 100 ± 5 pc (about 330 light-years), from the Mira period–luminosity relation; the Hipparcos parallax is too uncertain to help.

card.question: Why does Algenib look fainter than the other three corners?
card.glance: A blue-white star a shade fainter than the other corners of the Great Square of Pegasus.
card.whyHere: Algenib is a hot, heavy star that pulses every few hours, and its place in the Square shows how distance can hide power.
card.see: Algenib is the south-east corner of the Great Square. Compare it with Alpheratz at the north-east corner, nearly as bright though not quite.
card.understand: Algenib is a blue-white star many times heavier than the Sun. Its parallax, the tiny shift in its position as Earth orbits the Sun, puts it about 469 light-years away. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star five times farther looks twenty-five times dimmer.
card.wonder: Of the four corners, it is the only one whose light set out before the telescope was invented.
card.connect: Scheat, the cool orange giant at the opposite corner of the Square, is its color opposite.
card.answer: Algenib is roughly five times farther away than Alpheratz yet looks almost as bright, so it must be far more powerful, and the faintest corner is really the mightiest.

card.question: Why does Regulus spin so fast that it bulges?
card.glance: A bright blue-white star at the foot of Leo’s ‘Sickle’, with a faint companion that steady binoculars may show.
card.whyHere: Regulus spins so fast that it is visibly flattened, and the reason lies with a companion nobody could see for decades.
card.see: Regulus is the bright dot at the bottom of the backward question mark of Leo’s head, crisp and blue-white in binoculars. Brace them and look about a tenth of a Moon-width to the north-west for faint Regulus B, a small star that travels with it.
card.understand: Regulus is a hot, young star of about three and a half Suns that turns once in roughly 16 hours, so fast that its equator bulges and runs cooler and dimmer than its poles. Interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, measured the squashed shape directly. A tiny wobble then revealed an unseen partner on a 40-day orbit, and in 2020 astronomers finally caught its faint light: the stripped core of a star.
card.wonder: Spin it much faster and Regulus would begin flinging gas off its equator; it already turns at about 86% of that limit.
card.connect: Nearby, a cool orange giant makes a vivid color contrast.
card.answer: That partner was once the bigger star, and when it swelled, Regulus pulled away its outer gas and, with it, the spin, leaving the partner a small, hot core.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single bright point; the flattened shape was measured with linked telescopes (CHARA), not imaged directly.
card.deeper: McAlister et al. (2005) combined CHARA interferometry with spectroscopy: projected rotation 317 ± 3 km/s, an equatorial speed about 86% of break-up, and radii of about 4.2 (equator) and 3.1 (pole) solar radii. Gies et al. (2008) found a 40-day orbit from tiny radial-velocity shifts, and Gies et al. (2020) detected the companion’s own spectrum: a pre-white dwarf of about 0.31 solar masses, as predicted for a star stripped by mass transfer. WDS lists Regulus B (K2 V) 176″ away; it has its own faint partner. Hipparcos parallax 41.13 ± 0.35 mas (79 light-years).

card.question: Are the five stars of Cassiopeia’s W really neighbors in space?
card.glance: The fourth star of Cassiopeia’s W, a white star about 100 light-years away.
card.whyHere: Ruchbah and its neighbor γ Cas are the simplest way to see that a constellation is a flat picture of deep space.
card.see: Ruchbah is the fourth star of the W, counting from Caph. It looks much like γ Cas next door.
card.understand: A constellation shows only directions, not depths, like a photograph of streetlights in which near and far lamps look alike. Parallax adds the missing dimension, and over a year Ruchbah shifts more than five times as much as γ Cas. A star’s shift shrinks in step with its distance, so Ruchbah is much the closer.
card.wonder: Ruchbah’s light left it about a century ago, while γ Cas’s light set out in the late Middle Ages.
card.connect: γ Cas looks similar only because its far greater power makes up for its distance.
card.answer: Ruchbah lies about 100 light-years away and γ Cas several times deeper, so the W is a letter drawn only for observers on Earth.

card.question: Is the faint star beside Algieba its companion?
card.glance: A golden star in Leo’s mane, with a fainter whitish star a third of a degree to the south.
card.whyHere: Algieba is a golden double for telescopes, and in binoculars it seems to come with a ready-made companion.
card.see: Algieba is the brightest star of Leo’s Sickle after Regulus. Binoculars cannot split its two golden giants, so notice instead 40 Leonis, a fainter whitish star about a third of a degree south that looks like a companion.
card.understand: Algieba is really two orange-gold giants orbiting each other far apart, with surfaces around 4,500 K, cooler than the Sun’s. The brighter one also has a giant planet at least about nine times Jupiter’s mass, found from the star’s gentle wobble. 40 Leonis, meanwhile, has a parallax nearly twice as large as Algieba’s, which means it lies almost twice as close.
card.wonder: Through a small telescope the two golden giants appear side by side, one of the finest color pairs in the sky.
card.connect: Blue-white Regulus, at the foot of the Sickle, completes the color contrast.
card.answer: 40 Leonis only lines up by chance, and Algieba’s real partner is a second golden giant, far too close for binoculars.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split the golden pair; binoculars show a single star and its chance neighbor, 40 Leonis.
card.deeper: Hipparcos gives 25.07 ± 0.52 mas for the combined pair (about 130 light-years). WDS lists STF 1424 AB at 4.8″ (magnitudes 2.37 and 3.64). The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists γ¹ Leo b (Han et al. 2010): period 429 days, minimum mass 8.8 Jupiters. 40 Leo (F6 IV-V) has a Gaia EDR3 parallax of 47.13 mas (about 69 light-years), so it is a foreground star.

card.question: Which looks brighter, a nearby cluster star or a distant monster?
card.glance: The brightest star of the Southern Pleiades in Carina, a scatter of blue-white stars that fills a binocular view.
card.whyHere: Theta Carinae is the leading light of a nearby star family, and its neighbor Eta Carinae turns brightness upside down.
card.see: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group spreads over about a degree, with dozens of fainter members, and about 5° north lie the Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae.
card.understand: The Southern Pleiades is an open cluster, a family of stars born together, tens of millions of years old and about 490 light-years away. Theta Carinae is its brightest and hottest member. Eta Carinae looks fainter from here, yet it is more than 15 times farther away, so it must be vastly more powerful.
card.wonder: Seen from a planet near Eta Carinae, this whole cluster would be too faint to notice.
card.connect: Swing north to Eta Carinae and compare: the fainter-looking star is the true giant.
card.answer: The nearby star wins to the eye: Theta Carinae, about 456 light-years away, outshines Eta Carinae, although Eta Carinae is the true giant, because apparent brightness always mixes power with distance.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the cluster as a spray of blue-white stars; binoculars give a very similar view.
card.deeper: θ Car (B0 V, spectroscopic binary) is the brightest star in the field of IC 2602, whose Gaia DR3 members give a distance of about 150 pc (Hunt & Reffert 2024) and whose lithium-depletion age is about 46 Myr (Dobbie et al. 2010). Its Hipparcos parallax (7.16 ± 0.21 mas, ~455 ly) is slightly nearer than the cluster mean; Gaia does not measure stars this bright well. An early-B star in a cluster this old would be unexpected for a normal single star, so its history may involve a companion.

card.question: What does a star on the brink of exploding look like?
card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula, whose brightness changes over the years.
card.whyHere: Eta Carinae is one of the most massive and unstable stars known, and almost certain to end as a supernova one day.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbors, and that is Eta Carinae. It looks ordinary; the drama lies in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years, and the heavier may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived, and that gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus. Measuring how fast the cloud expands and how large it looks gives its distance, like judging a balloon by its growth.
card.wonder: For a few years it was the second-brightest star in the night sky, even though its light travels about 7,500 years to reach us.
card.connect: Stars this heavy shed their outer layers before they die, and Gamma Velorum, in neighboring Vela, holds a star that already has.
card.answer: It looks surprisingly ordinary, a small yellow-orange point dimmed and reddened by the very cloud it blew off in the 1840s, and that quiet look hides a star that once nearly tore itself apart.
card.photoCaption: Hubble’s photos show the Homunculus, two billowing lobes of gas and dust that no binocular can show.
card.notSee: The Homunculus is far too small to see in binoculars.
card.deeper: The expansion of the Homunculus gives a distance of 2.35 ± 0.05 kpc (Smith 2006). A 2,022.7 ± 1.3-day cycle in spectra and X-rays reveals a massive companion on an eccentric orbit (Damineli et al. 2008). Hubble ultraviolet imaging traces gas launched in the Great Eruption, estimated at more than ten solar masses (ESA/Hubble heic1912). Because dust in the Homunculus dims and reddens the star, its apparent brightness says little about its true output; it has brightened markedly since the 1990s.

card.question: Can a giant and a Sun-like star share one orbit?
card.glance: A yellow star in Vela, north of the Carina Nebula region.
card.whyHere: Mu Velorum is a yellow giant with a Sun-like companion, two stages of life side by side.
card.see: Mu Velorum is a plain yellow point in binoculars. Its Sun-like companion lies too close to split without a telescope.
card.understand: The two stars were probably born together, but the giant started out heavier. Heavier stars use up their core hydrogen sooner, so it has already swollen while its partner is still a Sun-like dwarf. One system now holds two chapters of the same story.
card.wonder: Its light left about 112 years ago, around when the First World War began.
card.connect: Giants are a phase every Sun-like star passes through.
card.answer: They can, and Mu Velorum is a yellow giant that has left its steady adult life, circled by a companion still in the Sun’s stage, two siblings moving at different paces.

card.question: How can the North Star help measure the distance to other galaxies?
card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole, sitting on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.whyHere: Polaris is more than the pivot of the northern sky; it is also the nearest of a special breed of pulsing star.
card.see: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl up to Polaris, at the tip of the Little Dipper’s handle. Binoculars show it sitting on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring, like the diamond on top. Its pulsing is far too slight for the eye to catch.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant, a big, bright aging star, and a Cepheid: it rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every four days, at a rate tied to its true brightness. The rule needs calibrating, and Polaris offers a rare chance. A close partner circles it about every 30 years, and an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, followed the orbit and weighed Polaris directly at about five Suns.
card.wonder: Close-up images from the CHARA telescope array show bright and dark patches on its surface that come and go.
card.connect: Polaris has not always been the pole star, and Kochab, nearby, once had the job.
card.answer: Time a Cepheid’s beat and you know its true power; compare that with how faint it looks and you have its distance, and a nearby, weighable Cepheid like Polaris is where astronomers check that the rule is honest.
card.photoCaption: Survey photos show Polaris as a saturated point among its ring of field stars; its spotted surface appears only in interferometer reconstructions.
card.deeper: Evans et al. (2024) followed the roughly 30-year orbit of the close companion with the CHARA Array and found 5.13 ± 0.28 solar masses; the result depends on the high eccentricity (0.63), and the star is brighter than models predict for that mass. The distance is still argued over: Gaia EDR3 measures the wide companion Polaris B at 7.29 mas (about 448 light-years), Hipparcos gave 7.54 mas for Polaris A, and an HST parallax of Polaris B (Bond et al. 2018) gives 6.26 mas (about 521 light-years). GCVS lists a 3.97-day period and a range of only 1.86–2.13 mag.

card.question: Are there planetary systems like our own?
card.glance: A faint Sun-like star in southern Ursa Major, easy in binoculars and just visible to the eye from dark sites.
card.whyHere: 47 Ursae Majoris has a giant planet on a Jupiter-like orbit, one of the first signs that systems like ours exist.
card.see: It lies about 16 degrees south of Merak, the Big Dipper’s lower pointer star, in a sparse field. In binoculars it is a pale yellow point, worth comparing with white Merak if you start there.
card.understand: This is a star very like the Sun, about 46 light-years away. Three giant planets have been found from the wobble they cause in the star; the first, announced in 1996, takes about three years per orbit and weighs a few Jupiters. That was a more familiar arrangement than the scorching ‘hot Jupiters’ found around the same time.
card.wonder: Not one of its planets has ever been seen; only the star’s tiny back-and-forth motion gave them away.
card.connect: Lalande 21185, a red dwarf with planets of its own, lies about four and a half degrees south.
card.answer: 47 Ursae Majoris comes close, a Sun-like star whose giant planet keeps its distance as Jupiter does.

card.question: Which Big Dipper stars belong together?
card.glance: The lower pointer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl, white in binoculars beside yellow-orange Dubhe.
card.whyHere: Merak is the lower pointer of the Big Dipper’s bowl, and one of the first stars caught moving in step with its neighbors.
card.see: Merak and Dubhe are the pointers to Polaris. In binoculars Merak is white and Dubhe yellow-orange, a sibling and a stranger side by side.
card.understand: In 1909 Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that Merak and several other Dipper stars drift across the sky in the same direction at the same rate, like a flock. Modern measurements confirm a family moving through space together about 80 light-years away. The family’s age comes from interferometers that measured the shapes and sizes of its stars, including Merak’s two and a half Suns.
card.wonder: Stars of Merak’s mass are expected to end as white dwarfs inside glowing shells, much like the Owl Nebula two degrees away.
card.connect: Phecda, another sibling, is the next star around the bowl.
card.answer: Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth and Mizar still move as one family, while Dubhe and Alkaid are strangers passing through.

card.question: Is the Big Dipper one family of stars?
card.glance: The bright yellow-orange pointer star at the top of the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.whyHere: Dubhe points the way to Polaris alongside Merak, and the two look like a matched team.
card.see: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl, and Merak, the lower one, is five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is yellow-orange and Merak white, so sweep between them a few times. Dubhe’s true companion is far too close to see.
card.understand: Dubhe is a giant that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 26 times the Sun’s width, cooling to a yellow-orange glow. Astronomers sort family from strangers with two measurements: distance, from parallax, and motion, from both the drift across the sky and the speed along our line of sight. Five of the Dipper’s stars pass both tests together, and Dubhe fails.
card.wonder: The Dipper is slowly changing shape, because its two end stars drift differently from the family in the middle.
card.connect: At the far end of the handle, Alkaid is the other outsider, with the opposite color.
card.answer: Most of it is, but not Dubhe: the two pointers look like partners, but they are strangers, for Merak belongs to the Dipper’s family while Dubhe is a passer-by half again as far away.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only a bright point; the close companion was found by careful measurement, not imaging.
card.deeper: King et al. (2003) re-examined membership of the Ursa Major group using Hipparcos parallaxes and new radial velocities; Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, Mizar and Alcor are members, while Dubhe and Alkaid are not (summarized by Croswell). Hipparcos gives 26.54 ± 0.48 mas (about 123 light-years). A limb-darkened diameter of 6.42 ± 0.04 mas (Baines et al. 2018, via JMDC) implies about 26 solar radii. Dubhe is a G9 III giant with an A-type companion 0.8″ away (WDS BU 1077 AB).

card.question: How much brighter does a star get for a little more mass?
card.glance: The white star on the lion’s back, in the triangle of stars that ends at Denebola.
card.whyHere: Zosma is a nearby white star, hotter and far brighter than the Sun, forming the lion’s hips.
card.see: Zosma and its neighbor Chertan form the lion’s back in Leo, with Denebola at the tail. In binoculars Zosma is white; compare it with golden Algieba in the mane.
card.understand: Zosma is about twice the Sun’s mass with a surface near 8,200 K. A heavier star squeezes its core harder, which heats it more, and fusion speeds up steeply with temperature. The result is that brightness climbs far faster than mass.
card.wonder: Its light left about 58 years ago, around the time astronauts first flew around the Moon.
card.connect: Denebola, the lion’s tail, is the next bright star east.
card.answer: Far more than you might guess: Zosma has about twice the Sun’s mass but gives out about 29 times its light, and it will burn through its fuel correspondingly sooner.
