card.question: Why is there fresh dust around Denebola?
card.glance: The white star at the tip of Leo’s tail, at the opposite end of the lion from Regulus.
card.whyHere: Denebola is a nearby white star at the lion’s tail, surrounded by dust that should not still be there.
card.see: Denebola marks the lion’s tail, east of the Sickle, a clean white point in binoculars. With Arcturus and Spica it forms the large Spring Triangle. Its dust shows only to infrared telescopes.
card.understand: Denebola is a hot white star about twice the Sun’s mass and 16 times as luminous, 36 light-years away. Infrared telescopes, which see warmth rather than light, detect more warmth around it than the star alone should give, the glow of dust. Dust like this cannot last, because starlight blows small grains out and drags others inward, so whatever we see now must be freshly made.
card.wonder: The light reaching you tonight left Denebola about 36 years ago, within many observers’ own lifetimes.
card.connect: The Spring Triangle’s other corners are orange Arcturus and blue-white Spica.
card.answer: Something keeps making it, most likely asteroid- and comet-like bodies colliding and grinding each other down, a busier version of the debris belts in our own solar system.
card.photoCaption: Visible-light photos show only the star; the dust appears in infrared measurements, not in any picture you could take.
card.deeper: Zorec & Royer (2012) give log Teff 3.931 (about 8,530 K), log L 1.21 and 1.93 solar masses. The Hipparcos parallax is 90.91 ± 0.52 mas (35.9 light-years). Near-infrared interferometry (Akeson et al. 2009) found an excess from hot dust close to the star, and Stock et al. (2010) modeled the disk’s structure; later work debates whether one, two or three dust belts are needed.

card.question: Why is Groombridge 1830 racing through our neighborhood?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in a quiet corner of Ursa Major, findable in binoculars with a chart.
card.whyHere: Groombridge 1830 looks like an ordinary faint star, yet it is crossing our neighborhood at about 300 kilometers per second.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about 16 degrees due south of Phecda, the Big Dipper’s bowl star nearest the handle. In binoculars it is a faint yellowish point with no hint of its speed.
card.understand: Most stars near the Sun circle the galaxy with us in its flat disk, like cars in the same lanes. Groombridge 1830 loops through the halo, the old, thin swarm of stars around the disk, so it cuts across our lane at high speed: Gaia sees it creep about 7 arcseconds a year across the sky, enormous for a star 30 light-years away. Its iron, about a twentieth of the Sun’s, shows it formed early, before generations of stars had enriched the galaxy’s gas.
card.wonder: It crosses the width of the full Moon on the sky in about 250 years.
card.connect: Arcturus is another older visitor passing through, from the galaxy’s thicker disk.
card.answer: It is not in our lane at all, but on a steep, looping orbit through the galaxy’s ancient halo that happens to carry it through the Sun’s neighborhood right now.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show an ordinary faint star; its motion is revealed only by comparing images taken years apart.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3: parallax 109.03 ± 0.02 mas (29.9 light-years) and proper motion 7.06″ per year; with SIMBAD’s radial velocity of −98 km/s the heliocentric space velocity is about 320 km/s. Literature metallicities cluster at [Fe/H] ≈ −1.3 to −1.4 (SIMBAD compilation), about one-twentieth of the Sun’s iron. Interferometry (Karovicova et al. 2020, via JMDC) gives 0.597 mas, about 0.59 solar radii: a metal-poor dwarf somewhat smaller than the Sun.

card.question: How do astronomers date the Big Dipper’s family?
card.glance: The bowl star of the Big Dipper nearest the handle on the bottom side, white in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Phecda is another member of the Ursa Major family, sharing a birth and a path through space with Merak and Mizar.
card.see: Phecda is the lower bowl star on the handle side of the Big Dipper, white in binoculars. A faint galaxy, M109, lies just beside it, but that one needs a telescope.
card.understand: Linked telescopes have measured Phecda’s shape, and it spins fast enough to bulge at the equator. Once the bulge is measured, models can allow for the spin and read the star’s age from its size and temperature. Doing this for several family members dated the whole group.
card.wonder: Its light left about 83 years ago, around when the first nuclear reactor was switched on.
card.connect: Megrez, the faintest Dipper star, is the next sibling.
card.answer: By measuring the shapes and sizes of fast-spinning members like Phecda and fitting models to them, which together give the family an age of about 400 million years.

card.question: Can another sun hold a whole family of planets, not just one?
card.glance: A modest yellow-white star in Andromeda, a few binocular fields from the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.whyHere: υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star found with more than one planet, the point where single discoveries turned into whole planetary systems.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, move about eight degrees north-east to a modest yellow-white point. Its planets are invisible, but sweep west and the soft glow of the Andromeda Galaxy drifts into view.
card.understand: Like 51 Pegasi, the star wobbles toward and away from us, but its wobble is a tangle, as if several hands were tugging at once. Untangling it is like picking the separate notes out of a chord: one tug repeats in under five days, another about every eight months, a third about every three and a half years. Each rhythm is a planet, and the strength of each tug gives its mass.
card.wonder: The star is a little hotter and larger than the Sun, so its comfortable zone for liquid water lies farther out than Earth’s orbit.
card.connect: One family of worlds 44 light-years away; a few binocular fields west, the Andromeda Galaxy holds hundreds of billions of suns.
card.answer: It can, and υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star shown to: its wobble resolves into three giant planets on very different orbits. From then on, the Sun was no longer the only Sun-like star known to keep a family.
card.photoCaption: No photo can show its planets; the app shows the star’s color and size instead.

(2021) measured 1.57 solar radii and about 6,600 K interferometrically. Gaia EDR3 parallax 74.19 mas (44.0 light-years).

card.question: Why does Delta Centauri’s brightness drift over months?
card.glance: A blue-white star north-west of the Southern Cross, with two fainter stars nearby in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Delta Centauri is a fast-spinning Be star that sheds disks of gas, set in a pretty binocular triangle.
card.see: In binoculars Delta Centauri forms a wide group with two fainter stars close beside it. Its brightness drifts slightly over months.
card.understand: Delta Centauri is a Be star, a hot blue star spinning so fast that gas leaks from its equator into a thin disk. The disk glows and adds its own light, so as it builds and dissipates, the total shifts. Its spectrum shows bright lines from the disk, the signature of its class.
card.wonder: It probably belongs to the same young star family as Delta Crucis, about 16 million years old.
card.connect: Achernar, far across the sky, is a closer member of the same spinning class.
card.answer: Its disk comes and goes: as the gas spun off its equator gathers and thins, the star’s combined light wanders. You are watching weather on a scale of solar systems.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a blue-white star with two fainter neighbors, relatives from the same young family rather than partners in an orbit.

card.question: Are the stars of Corvus, the crow, neighbors in space?
card.glance: The orange star at the western corner of Corvus, the crow.
card.whyHere: Minkar, the orange corner of the little crow of Corvus, raises a doubt about every constellation you have ever traced.
card.see: Corvus is the small four-star kite south-west of Spica, its main stars fitting in two or three binocular fields. Minkar is the most orange; compare it with blue-white Gienah about five degrees north.
card.understand: Minkar is an orange giant with a surface near 4,300 K. Its parallax puts it at about 320 light-years. That is at least twice as far as the other bright crow stars.
card.wonder: Its light left around the year 1700, not long after Newton showed that one law of gravity rules both apples and planets.
card.connect: Gienah, the crow’s brightest star, is a hot blue-white contrast.
card.answer: Minkar lies twice as far as its crow-mates, so the bird exists only from where we stand.

card.question: Where are the Southern Cross’s brothers and sisters?
card.glance: The faintest of the Southern Cross’s four main stars, on its western arm.
card.whyHere: Delta Crucis is a confirmed member of the scattered young family that the Southern Cross’s blue stars belong to.
card.see: Delta Crucis is the dimmest star of the Cross. Compare its blue-white with orange Gacrux at the top.
card.understand: Delta Crucis was born with thousands of other stars about 16 million years ago in an association, a loose family that has since spread across Crux and Centaurus. The members are recognized by their shared motion, like a flock of birds that has scattered but still flies the same way. Delta Crucis fits that motion well.
card.wonder: It pulses gently every few hours, a trait it shares with several of its hot siblings.
card.connect: Gacrux, at the top of the Cross, is not part of this family.
card.answer: They are scattered across Crux, Centaurus and beyond, still drifting the same way through space though they no longer look like a cluster, so the family is all around the Cross.

card.question: How bright is the faintest-looking Big Dipper star, really?
card.glance: The faintest Big Dipper star, where the handle joins the bowl.
card.whyHere: Megrez is a sibling in the Ursa Major family and the stepping stone to Messier 40, a famous false double.
card.see: Megrez is where the Big Dipper’s handle meets the bowl, white in binoculars. About one and a half degrees north-east lie the two faint stars of Winnecke 4 (M40); brace the binoculars to see them.
card.understand: Megrez is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass, born with Merak, Phecda, Alioth and Mizar about 400 million years ago. Linked telescopes show it spins fast enough to be flattened. It looks faintest of the seven because it is the least powerful, not because it is farther away.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1945, as the Second World War was ending.
card.connect: Beside it, M40 is two stars that only look like a pair.
card.answer: Still about 28 times as bright as the Sun, so even the faintest-looking Dipper star would outshine our own many times over.

card.question: Why does Gienah look blue-white?
card.glance: The brightest star of Corvus, a blue-white point at the crow’s north-western corner.
card.whyHere: Gienah is a hot blue-white star, a color contrast to the orange stars of the crow.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Gienah is crisply blue-white; swing to orange Minkar or pale yellow Kraz to compare.
card.understand: A glowing object’s color tells its temperature, the way metal glows red, then yellow, then white as it heats. Gienah’s surface is about 12,400 K, which tips the balance of its light toward blue. It is a heavier star nearing the end of its long, steady adult life.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1870, while Mendeleev was arranging the elements into his periodic table.
card.connect: Algorab, across the crow, hides a faint companion.
card.answer: Its surface is roughly twice as hot as the Sun’s, and a surface that hot glows blue-white.

card.question: What happens to a star that spins almost fast enough to fly apart?
card.glance: An icy blue-white star shining alone, low in the far south.
card.whyHere: Achernar is one of the fastest-spinning bright stars in the sky, turning so quickly that it is squashed into a flattened ball.
card.see: Look for the lone brilliant blue-white star at the end of the long, faint river of Eridanus. Binoculars show only a sharp point, so enjoy its icy color and compare it with creamy Alpha Hydri about 5° away.
card.understand: Achernar is a hot star about six times the Sun’s mass, spinning near the speed at which it would fling itself apart. As with a spinning pizza dough, the spin pushes its equator outward into a bulge. Interferometers at the VLT combined telescopes to measure its outline and found it longer one way than the other, the flattest star resolved at the time.
card.wonder: It is only about 63 million years old, while the Sun has already lived some 70 times longer.
card.connect: A smaller companion swings around it every seven years, and its orbit is how astronomers weighed Achernar.
card.answer: It flattens and leaks, Achernar’s equator bulging about a third wider than its poles and, from time to time, shedding a thin disk of gas from that waist. Pushed far enough, a star starts to come apart at the seams.
card.photoCaption: No photo shows its shape; the flattening was measured by linking telescopes together (interferometry).
card.notSee: Its flattened shape and its companion are far beyond binoculars.
card.deeper: VLTI interferometry resolved Achernar’s flattened shape; Domiciano de Souza et al. (2014) found an equatorial-to-polar radius ratio near 1.35, the flattest such star then resolved. Kervella et al. (2022) followed the A-type companion through a 7-year, highly eccentric orbit (e = 0.73): 6.0 ± 0.6 M☉ for the Be star, and a critically rotating 6.4 M☉ model at 63 Myr fits best. At 42.8 pc it is the nearest Be star; a comoving low-mass star suggests membership of the Tucana–Horologium moving group.

card.question: Do the stars of the Southern Cross really belong together?
card.glance: The foot of the Southern Cross, a dazzling blue-white point with a fainter star beside it.
card.whyHere: Acrux is the brightest star of the Southern Cross and the place to ask whether the Cross is a family or a coincidence.
card.see: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross, and binoculars show a much fainter star beside it. The two brilliant stars that make up Acrux itself sit too close for binoculars, though a small telescope splits them.
card.understand: Stars born together drift through space together, so astronomers test family ties by measuring each star’s motion across the sky and its distance. Delta Crucis, and probably Mimosa, share the motion of a scattered family of hot young stars called an association. Acrux seems to belong too, though its measured motion fits less neatly, and the debate continues.
card.wonder: The brighter of the two stars inside Acrux is itself a pair that only its spectrum reveals, so this one point of light holds at least three stars.
card.connect: Swing up to Gacrux at the top of the Cross and compare the colors: a blue-white family and an orange stranger.
card.answer: Mostly they do: Acrux probably shares a scattered family born about 16 million years ago with Mimosa and Delta Crucis, while orange Gacrux, at the top, is a nearer stranger that only lines up with them.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the glare of Acrux with its fainter neighbor; the close pair inside it needs a telescope.
card.deeper: WDS lists the A–B pair (DUN 252) at 3.5″ and a 4.8-magnitude star, C, at 89″. The combined Hipparcos parallax is 10.13 ± 0.50 mas (≈ 320 ly). In the Sco-Cen review by Preibisch & Mamajek (2008), α Cru is one of six bright stars whose membership of the Lower Centaurus–Crux group (mean age ~16 Myr, ~118 pc) has been debated because their Hipparcos proper motions do not match well.

card.question: How many stars make up Acrux?
card.glance: The fainter half of Acrux, which binoculars merge with its partner into one star.
card.whyHere: Alpha² Crucis is the second bright star inside Acrux, a hot blue-white star of the same system.
card.see: Center Acrux at the foot of the Southern Cross. Its two bright stars sit a hair’s breadth apart, so binoculars show one point while a small telescope shows two.
card.understand: Like its partner, Alpha² Crucis is a hot, heavy young star whose blue-white color marks a surface far hotter than the Sun’s. The other bright star has a secret of its own. Its spectral lines shift back and forth on a regular rhythm, the signature of an unseen companion.
card.wonder: Each of the two would rank among the brighter stars of the sky on its own.
card.connect: Acrux’s wider family spreads across the whole Southern Cross.
card.answer: There are at least three, two bright blue-white stars a hair’s breadth apart, the brighter of them itself a close pair.

card.question: Is the orange star at the tip of the Coma Cluster one of its members?
card.glance: An orange star at the northern tip of the sprawling Coma Star Cluster.
card.whyHere: γ Comae sits at the tip of the Coma Star Cluster like its leader, the obvious candidate for the family’s brightest member.
card.see: Find the Coma Star Cluster between Denebola and the Big Dipper’s handle, a loose spray of white stars filling the field. γ Com, at its northern tip, stands out as orange, the clue that it does not belong.
card.understand: Gaia’s parallaxes place the cluster’s members about 280 light-years away, but γ Com only about 170. It is a giant about 12 times the Sun’s width. It simply lies in front of the cluster along the same line of sight.
card.wonder: A Gaia census lists about 270 members of the cluster, and this star is not among them.
card.connect: The cluster’s white stars are the true siblings, all of one age.
card.answer: γ Comae stands well in front of the cluster’s white stars and only lines up with them.
card.photoCaption: Wide photos show γ Com as the only obviously orange star in the cluster’s field.

card.question: Can binoculars catch a faint star in a bright star’s glare?
card.glance: A white star at the crow’s north-eastern corner, with a faint companion that steady 10× binoculars can just reveal.
card.whyHere: Algorab is a white star with a much fainter orange companion, a binocular test of separation and contrast.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica; Algorab is its north-eastern corner. With 10× binoculars on a tripod, look very close to it for a far fainter point. In hand-held 7× it usually hides in the glare.
card.understand: Algorab is a hot white star about two and a half times the Sun’s mass. The companion is a cool orange dwarf, and whether the two actually orbit each other is not settled. Seeing it is hard because a faint point beside a bright one drowns in the bright star’s scattered light.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1940, so it has been on its way for about a human lifetime.
card.connect: The Sombrero Galaxy lies about five and a half degrees north-north-east, a faint smudge under dark skies.
card.answer: Steady 10× binoculars can just reveal Algorab’s far fainter companion, while hand-held 7× usually lose it in the glare.
card.photoCaption: Telescope photos split the pair easily; binoculars barely do.

card.question: Why is the top star of the Southern Cross orange when the others are blue-white?
card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross, the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.whyHere: Gacrux looks like part of the Cross’s family, but it is a stranger, a nearby red giant that only lines up with the others.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot; defocus slightly and the color jumps out. A faint white star just to the north-east is a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant, a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. Its parallax is several times larger than those of the other Cross stars, which places it much nearer to us.
card.wonder: Its light set out less than a century ago, while the blue-white stars behind it sent theirs centuries earlier.
card.connect: Giants like this one end by puffing away their outer layers into a glowing shell, a planetary nebula, around a hot dying core.
card.answer: Gacrux is not one of the Cross’s blue-white family at all: it is an old red giant three to five times closer than the others. The Cross is a family photo with a neighbor standing in front.
card.photoCaption: In photos Gacrux looks like a member of the Cross; only distance measurements reveal it is in the foreground.
card.deeper: Hipparcos (van Leeuwen 2007) gives 36.83 ± 0.18 mas (88.6 ly), against roughly 280–460 ly for Mimosa, δ Cru and Acrux. An SED fit (McDonald et al. 2017) gives about 3,700 K and 860 L☉; the JSDC photometric diameter (28 mas) implies about 82 R☉. Its exact evolutionary phase (first-ascent giant or early asymptotic giant) is not settled. The 6.4-mag star 2.2′ away is optical (WDS).

card.question: What would our Sun look like seen from another star?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in Canes Venatici near La Superba, easy in binoculars and barely visible to the eye under dark skies.
card.whyHere: Chara is a near-twin of the Sun 27 light-years away, our own star seen from outside.
card.see: Chara lies about four and a half degrees south-south-west of La Superba, below the Big Dipper’s handle. Put each in the field in turn, pale yellow Chara and then deep red La Superba; Chara looks unremarkable, just as the Sun would from here.
card.understand: Chara has almost the Sun’s surface temperature and size, and slightly less iron. Its width was measured directly by an interferometer and comes out at about one solar diameter. Like the Sun it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, a steady stage lasting billions of years, which makes it a natural target in searches for Earth-like planets.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left Chara just after the first planets around Sun-like stars were found.
card.connect: La Superba, close by, is a star far along a later, very different stage of life.
card.answer: It would look like Chara, a plain, pale yellow point barely visible to the naked eye, with nothing to suggest it might warm a world of its own.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show a plain yellow-white point, which is exactly the lesson: a Sun-like star is unremarkable from afar.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 118.49 ± 0.20 mas (27.5 light-years). Literature effective temperatures span about 5,650–6,010 K and recent metallicities are [Fe/H] ≈ −0.2 (SIMBAD compilation). Interferometry (Baines et al. 2018, via JMDC) gives 1.13 mas, about 1.0 solar radii. At this distance the Sun (absolute magnitude about 4.8) would appear near magnitude 4.5, close to Chara’s own 4.3.

card.question: Can a star the Sun’s color be very different from the Sun?
card.glance: The pale yellow star at the crow’s south-eastern corner.
card.whyHere: Kraz is a bright giant, nearly the Sun’s color but far larger and more luminous.
card.see: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Kraz is pale yellow, about the Sun’s own color; compare it with blue-white Gienah across the crow.
card.understand: Its surface, near 5,100 K, is a little cooler than the Sun’s, so the colors are similar. But Kraz is a swollen giant, and from about 150 light-years it still shines as one of the crow’s brightest stars. The Sun at that distance would need binoculars to see.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1880, while Edison was perfecting the electric light bulb.
card.connect: Gienah, the hot star of the crow, makes the color contrast.
card.answer: Kraz glows nearly the Sun’s pale yellow, but as a giant it is far larger and pours out far more light.

card.question: Does the Southern Cross family reach beyond the Cross?
card.glance: The brightest star of Musca, the Fly, just south of the Southern Cross.
card.whyHere: Alpha Muscae is another sibling of the Southern Cross family, a short hop south of Acrux.
card.see: Alpha Muscae is a blue-white star about 6° south of Acrux. Its color matches Acrux and Mimosa, a hint that they are related.
card.understand: It belongs to the same scattered family of young stars as Delta Crucis, born about 16 million years ago. Its motion through space matches theirs, which is how membership is decided. Like several of its siblings, it is hot and heavy.
card.wonder: It flickers in brightness every two hours or so, by an amount far too small to see.
card.connect: Back north, the Coalsack’s dark cloud lies between the Fly and the Cross.
card.answer: It does, for Alpha Muscae shares the Cross stars’ blue-white color and their motion, a sibling just outside the famous pattern, since constellation lines do not bound families.

card.question: Can one star turn out to be a pair of twins?
card.glance: A white star in Centaurus, north of the Southern Cross.
card.whyHere: Gamma Centauri is a pair of near-identical white stars, too close to split in binoculars.
card.see: Gamma Centauri is a steady white point in binoculars. Its two equal stars sit far too close together for binoculars, or even most telescopes.
card.understand: Two stars of nearly the same mass and temperature orbit each other here. Their combined spectrum shows two matching sets of lines, and only careful measurement separates them. Binaries like this are common; the Sun’s single life is the less usual arrangement.
card.wonder: Its light takes about 130 years to reach you, so it set out around when X-rays were discovered.
card.connect: Most stars have partners, and many are far too close to see.
card.answer: Gamma Centauri is exactly that, two near-identical white stars orbiting far too close together for binoculars to split.

card.question: Can a star and a cluster born at the same time sit side by side?
card.glance: The eastern arm of the Southern Cross, a blue-white star and your signpost to the Jewel Box.
card.whyHere: Mimosa is a hot young star with a star cluster of the same age sitting right beside it in the sky.
card.see: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the Cross’s eastern arm. Place it at the edge of your view and look about 1° south-east, where a tight, glittering knot of stars appears: the Jewel Box, whose brightest stars share Mimosa’s icy color.
card.understand: Mimosa is a heavy, hot star that swells and shrinks very slightly several times a day, too little for your eye to notice. Its motion through space suggests it belongs to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. The Jewel Box is dated separately, from its own brightest stars, and lands at a similar age.
card.wonder: You hold two families of the same age in one binocular view, one spread across the sky around you and one packed into a distant jewel.
card.connect: Gacrux, the orange star at the top of the Cross, is the one star here that does not belong with the others.
card.answer: They can, for Mimosa and the Jewel Box are both about 16 million years old, yet the Jewel Box lies more than twenty times farther away: the same birthday at very different addresses.
card.photoCaption: Photos show Mimosa beside the Jewel Box cluster; the cluster’s colored stars need a telescope to stand out.
card.deeper: Mimosa is a β Cephei pulsator (main period about 0.24 d, amplitude under 0.1 mag, GCVS). Its angular diameter from the Narrabri intensity interferometer (0.722 ± 0.022 mas) and the Hipparcos distance give about 6.6 R☉. Preibisch & Mamajek (2008) note that long-baseline proper motions favor its membership of Lower Centaurus–Crux (mean age ~16 Myr). The Jewel Box (NGC 4755) has a similar age but lies about 6,500 ly away.

card.question: How can a star’s surface be blotched with different elements?
card.glance: The brightest Big Dipper star, first in the handle next to the bowl, plain white and steady in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Alioth looks like an ordinary white star, but its surface is blotched with unusual elements, and it is a sibling in the Dipper’s family.
card.see: Alioth is the handle star touching the Big Dipper’s bowl, white and steady in binoculars; its light changes by only about two percent as it turns. Glide along the handle to Mizar and Alcor to take in three family members in one sweep.
card.understand: Alioth is a hot white star born with the Ursa Major family. Its outer layers are unusually calm, so some elements sink under gravity while others are pushed upward by the light streaming out, and a weak magnetic field herds them into patches. Astronomers mapped those patches by watching how each element’s lines in the spectrum shift and change shape as the star turns every five days.
card.wonder: It belongs to the class of spotted stars named after Cor Caroli, just below the handle.
card.connect: Alioth is family, but Dubhe and Alkaid, at the Dipper’s two ends, are not.
card.answer: In a star calm enough to let its elements sort themselves, even a weak magnetic field can gather them into patches that rotate in and out of view, flickering its light ever so slightly.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single white point; the spots are mapped from changes in its spectrum as it rotates.
card.deeper: GCVS classes ε UMa as an α² CVn (ACV) variable with a period of 5.0887 days and a range of only 1.76–1.78 mag. Shulyak et al. (2010) reproduced most of its light variation from Doppler-imaging maps of several elements; its dipole field is weak, a few hundred gauss at most, among the weakest of the magnetic chemically peculiar stars. King et al. (2003) count it in the nucleus of the Ursa Major group, dated to 414 ± 23 million years by Jones et al. (2015). Hipparcos parallax: 39.51 ± 0.20 mas (about 83 light-years).

card.question: What lies beyond Vindemiatrix?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Virgo’s northern arm, the gateway to the Virgo galaxy cluster.
card.whyHere: Vindemiatrix is a yellow giant in Virgo’s northern arm, and a signpost to something far more distant.
card.see: Vindemiatrix sits in Virgo’s northern arm, about 20 degrees west-south-west of Arcturus, pale yellow in binoculars. Under dark skies, sweep slowly west toward Denebola: the faint smudges along the way are galaxies far beyond our own.
card.understand: Vindemiatrix is a giant about 12 times the Sun’s width with a surface near 5,000 K. It lies roughly 110 light-years away. The galaxies behind it belong to the Virgo cluster, entire star systems so far away that this star is a next-door neighbor by comparison.
card.wonder: The star’s light is about a century old, and the galaxies’ light is tens of millions of years old.
card.connect: M49, among the brightest Virgo galaxies in binoculars, lies about eight degrees west-south-west.
card.answer: Beyond it lie whole galaxies, the faint smudges of the Virgo cluster west of this nearby giant, whose light set out before there were humans.

card.question: What does a giant look like before it starts to pulse?
card.glance: A modest yellow star in Hydra’s long tail, the signpost for the variable R Hydrae.
card.whyHere: γ Hydrae is an ordinary yellow giant and the perfect comparison for its dramatic neighbor, R Hydrae.
card.see: Well below Spica, γ Hya is the brightest star in this stretch of Hydra. R Hya lies about two and a half degrees east, often in the same binocular field, so compare their colors: yellow against orange-red.
card.understand: γ Hya is a giant with a surface around 5,100 K, calm and steady, burning helium in its core. R Hydrae is further along the same road, cooler, larger and pulsing. The change comes once core helium runs out and the star must burn in thin, unstable shells.
card.wonder: Its light left around 1890, about when Van Gogh painted The Starry Night.
card.connect: R Hydrae, in the same field, shows that later stage.
card.answer: Calm and steady, like γ Hydrae, a yellow giant that has not yet reached the restless stage its neighbor is in.

card.question: How do you climb a distance ladder to another galaxy?
card.glance: A white star in northern Centaurus, about 6° from the galaxy Centaurus A.
card.whyHere: Iota Centauri is a nearby white star that makes a perfect first rung on a distance ladder to a galaxy.
card.see: Iota Centauri is a plain white point. About 6° south lies Centaurus A, a faint galaxy smudge, and Omega Centauri’s glow is about 11° away.
card.understand: Each rung of a distance ladder uses a method that works only within a certain range. Parallax handles nearby stars like this one, only about 58 light-years away. Farther rungs rely on stars of known brightness, calibrated with parallax, which in turn reach clusters and galaxies.
card.wonder: From Centaurus A, our entire galaxy would look like a faint smudge, much as that galaxy looks to you.
card.connect: Omega Centauri, a ball of millions of stars, is the next rung, then a whole galaxy.
card.answer: One rung at a time, from Iota Centauri through Omega Centauri to Centaurus A, 6° south and about 200,000 times farther, with every rung resting on the one below.

card.question: What decides whether a star ends quietly or in an explosion?
card.glance: A brilliant blue-white star alone in the low southern sky at the bottom of Virgo.
card.whyHere: Spica is two heavy, very hot stars in a four-day orbit, so close they pull each other out of round, and their weight seals their fate.
card.see: From Arcturus, continue the Dipper-handle curve about as far again to a lone, brilliant blue-white star. It stays one sharp point, since no telescope can split the pair. Compare its icy color with Arcturus’s orange.
card.understand: Spica is a pair of hot stars of about 11 and 7 Suns, weighed by tracking their orbit in 1,731 spectra. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so this pair is only about 12 million years old, while Arcturus is billions of years old. The two orbit so tightly that tides stretch each into an egg shape, and the light wobbles as the eggs turn.
card.wonder: Arcturus looks brighter to your eye, yet Spica’s bigger star is the one that will explode.
card.connect: Back in the Big Dipper, a family of stars has stayed together for about 400 million years.
card.answer: Mass decides, and Spica’s bigger star, about 11 Suns, is heavy enough to end as a supernova, while Sun-weight Arcturus will fade quietly into a white dwarf.
card.photoCaption: No photograph separates the two stars; their shapes are known from spectra and from tiny, regular changes in brightness.
card.deeper: Tkachenko et al. (2016) combined 1,731 high-resolution spectra with space photometry: masses 11.43 ± 1.15 and 7.21 ± 0.75 solar masses, radii 7.47 and 3.74 solar radii, a primary temperature of 25,300 ± 500 K, an orbital period of 4.0145 days and an age of 12.5 ± 1 million years. One of the primary’s β Cephei pulsation modes is an exact multiple of the orbital frequency, a tidally excited oscillation. GCVS lists the light variation (ellipsoidal plus β Cep) at about 0.1 mag. Hipparcos parallax: 13.06 ± 0.70 mas (about 250 light-years).

card.question: What did one of the first planets around a Sun-like star look like?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star in northern Virgo, easy in binoculars, near τ Boötis.
card.whyHere: 70 Virginis hosts one of the first planets found around a Sun-like star, announced in 1996.
card.see: It lies about six degrees west-south-west of τ Boötis, itself west of Arcturus. In binoculars it is a pale yellow point among fainter stars.
card.understand: This Sun-like star is older than the Sun and has begun to swell, now nearly twice the Sun’s width. Its planet, at least seven times Jupiter’s mass, takes about 117 days per orbit. The orbit is stretched rather than round, another surprise for astronomers who had expected copies of our solar system.
card.wonder: Its light left in the late 1960s, a generation before anyone knew the planet was there.
card.connect: τ Boötis, nearby, hosts another planet announced the same year.
card.answer: It looked nothing like Earth, for 70 Virginis’s planet is a heavyweight on a short, lopsided orbit.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only the star; the planet is known from its pull on the star.

card.question: Can a star change its own heartbeat?
card.glance: A red pulsating giant beside γ Hydrae, at its best a naked-eye star and at its faintest beyond binoculars.
card.whyHere: R Hydrae is a dying giant whose pulse has been timed by observers for three centuries.
card.see: Start at γ Hydrae, the brightest star in this part of Hydra, well below Spica. R Hya lies about two and a half degrees east, often in the same field; near maximum it is obviously orange-red, but for part of its cycle it fades out of reach, so check AAVSO first.
card.understand: R Hydrae is a giant in its last stage of life, pulsing slowly and shedding gas. The clue to its change came from patience rather than technology: astronomers gathered three centuries of observations, from the early 1700s on, and found the cycle shrinking from about 495 days to about 385 by the mid-1900s. Its spectrum also shows technetium, an element with no stable form, which must have been made inside the star recently.
card.wonder: Its present period, about 389 days, has stayed nearly constant since the mid-twentieth century.
card.connect: Steady γ Hydrae beside it shows the calmer giant stage that comes before this one.
card.answer: It can, and R Hydrae has: perhaps a brief flare of helium burning deep inside made the star shrink and quicken, a heartbeat altered by an upheaval in its core.
card.photoCaption: A photograph catches R Hya at one moment of its cycle; tonight it may be far brighter or fainter.
card.deeper: Zijlstra, Bedding & Mattei (2002) assembled about three centuries of observations: the period was about 495 days before 1770 and declined to roughly 380–385 days by about 1950, staying near that since. They discuss both a helium-shell flash (thermal pulse) and envelope relaxation; the flash interpretation is common but not settled. GCVS lists V 3.5–10.9, P = 388.87 days and spectral type M6e–M9eS(Tc), the Tc marking technetium. DEATHSTAR (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022): 126 +3/−2 pc, about 410 light-years.

card.question: How much like the Sun is the nearest lone star of the Sun’s kind?
card.glance: A modest pale-yellow star in Cetus that looks like nothing special, yet is one of the Sun’s nearest look-alikes.
card.whyHere: τ Ceti is the nearest lone star of the Sun’s type, only 12 light-years away, and it shows how varied “Sun-like” can be.
card.see: τ Ceti lies about fifteen degrees east of Diphda, the Whale’s brightest star. In binoculars it is a steady pale-yellow point. Swing back to Diphda, which looks brighter and more orange: that one is a far bigger, farther giant, while τ Ceti is a true dwarf like the Sun.
card.understand: τ Ceti is a yellow dwarf, a star in the steady middle of life like the Sun. Its spectrum shows much weaker lines of iron and other heavy elements than the Sun’s, a sign that it formed from gas less enriched by earlier generations of stars, and earlier usually means older. Its gentle oscillations, read the way seismologists read earthquakes, point to an age of roughly 8 to 10 billion years.
card.wonder: In 1960 it was one of the first two stars ever searched for radio signals from another civilization, in Frank Drake’s Project Ozma.
card.connect: Same color as its neighbor Diphda, a completely different star: color tells you temperature, not size or power.
card.answer: Close, but not a twin: τ Ceti has about 80 percent of the Sun’s mass, under a third of its heavy elements and roughly twice its age. It is less a sibling than an older cousin from a poorer branch of the family.
card.photoCaption: No photo is needed: in every image it is a point. The app’s distance bar shows how close it is.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 parallax 273.81 ± 0.17 mas (11.9 light-years). Korolik et al. (2023) give 0.80 solar masses; asteroseismic modeling (Tang & Gai 2011) suggests 8–10 billion years; [Fe/H] ≈ −0.55 (Tuomi et al. 2013). Feng et al. (2017) proposed four small planet candidates with minimum masses of a few Earths; later data have not confirmed all of them, so the app treats them as candidates.

card.question: How much farther is Omega Centauri than the bright star beside it?
card.glance: A bright blue-white star in Centaurus, between Hadar and a great star cluster.
card.whyHere: Epsilon Centauri is a hot young star of the Centaurus family, and a stepping stone toward Omega Centauri.
card.see: Epsilon Centauri is the bright blue-white star between Hadar and the fuzzy ball of Omega Centauri. The cluster lies about 6° away.
card.understand: Epsilon Centauri is a heavy young star that pulses slightly every few hours. Its parallax puts it about 427 light-years away. Omega Centauri is too far for parallax to help much, so its distance comes from its stars’ brightness and motions.
card.wonder: Its whole life will be over long before the oldest stars in Omega Centauri have aged noticeably.
card.connect: The cluster’s soft glow is a short hop away.
card.answer: Omega Centauri is about 40 times farther, a swarm of ancient stars far beyond this young one, so two neighbors on the sky are separated by most of the galaxy’s history.

card.question: Can a giant planet orbit closer to its star than Mercury does?
card.glance: A pale yellow-white star about seven degrees west of Arcturus, easy in binoculars.
card.whyHere: τ Boötis hosts one of the first planets found around a Sun-like star, a giant racing around it in three days.
card.see: From Arcturus in Boötes, sweep about seven degrees west to a modest yellow-white star, clearly whiter than orange Arcturus. Its red-dwarf companion is far too close and faint for binoculars.
card.understand: τ Boötis is a little heavier and hotter than the Sun. Its planet was found in 1996 from the regular shift of the star’s spectral lines, back and forth every 3.3 days as the planet swings the star around. That rhythm, together with the star’s mass, puts the planet far closer than Mercury is to the Sun, and the pull between the two may be strong enough to make the star’s outer layers turn in step with it.
card.wonder: Its magnetic field flips north and south again and again, far faster than the Sun’s.
card.connect: Not far away, 70 Virginis hosts a giant planet announced the same year.
card.answer: τ Boötis’s planet does, weighing about six Jupiters yet racing around its star faster than any planet of ours, one of the first discoveries to show that other planetary systems can be very unlike ours.
card.photoCaption: The planet has never been photographed; its presence is read from the star’s regular wobble.
card.deeper: The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists τ Boo b with a period of 3.312 days and a minimum mass of about 5.95 Jupiters, discovered by radial velocities (Butler et al. 1997, announced 1996). Spectropolarimetry (Fares et al. 2009) caught a second reversal of the star’s large-scale magnetic polarity within a short span. Gaia EDR3 parallax: 64.05 mas (50.9 light-years). WDS lists τ Boo B, an M2 dwarf, 1.5″ away.

card.question: Why is the star at the end of the Dipper’s handle blue-white?
card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.whyHere: Alkaid is the hottest Dipper star and, like Dubhe, an outsider to the family.
card.see: Alkaid ends the Big Dipper’s handle, crisply blue-white against yellow-orange Dubhe at the far end. About three and a half degrees south-west, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 K, three times hotter than the Sun’s. That temperature was read from a telltale step in its spectrum, a sharp drop in the ultraviolet whose size and position depend on how hot the gas is. Hot stars are heavy and burn their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go, and it travels a different way from the five family stars in the middle.
card.wonder: The Dipper’s two ends are a hot youngster and a cool elder, with a true family between them.
card.connect: From hot and blue here to the cool, red end of the scale: La Superba.
card.answer: At three times the Sun’s surface temperature Alkaid glows blue-white, a young, heavy star that shares the Dipper’s outline but not its family.
card.photoCaption: Photographs record Alkaid as a white point; its blue tint is easier to sense when you compare it with Dubhe in binoculars.
card.deeper: Zorec et al. (2009) give an effective temperature of 17,870 ± 1,060 K and an angular diameter of 0.83 mas from the Balmer-discontinuity (BCD) method; at the Hipparcos distance (31.38 ± 0.24 mas, about 104 light-years) that is roughly 2.9 solar radii. Rapid rotation makes single-number temperatures approximate. King et al. (2003) list Alkaid as a non-member of the Ursa Major group.

card.question: What separates a young star from the ancient swarm beside it?
card.glance: A blue-white star about 5° from Omega Centauri.
card.whyHere: Zeta Centauri is a young star beside an ancient star swarm, and a handy signpost to Omega Centauri.
card.see: Zeta Centauri sits about 5° east of Omega Centauri. Put both in turn in your view: a sharp young star, then a soft ball of ancient ones.
card.understand: Zeta Centauri is a hot young binary whose two stars circle every eight days. Its age shows in its color and power, since only young stars can be this hot and heavy. Omega Centauri’s stars are the opposite, small and old, the heavy ones long gone.
card.wonder: Its light left about 380 years ago, while Omega Centauri’s set out before anyone on Earth had planted a crop.
card.connect: The swarm itself is next door.
card.answer: Both age and distance separate them, for Omega Centauri is a ball of ancient stars over 45 times farther away than this hot young binary.

card.question: What does a star look like as it starts turning into a giant?
card.glance: A pale yellow-white star five degrees west of Arcturus.
card.whyHere: Muphrid is Arcturus’s neighbor in space, caught early in the change that Arcturus has already completed.
card.see: Sweep from Arcturus in Boötes about five degrees west to Muphrid. A wide field holds both: orange-gold beside pale yellow-white.
card.understand: Muphrid is just starting to swell as the hydrogen in its core runs low, and it is already about two and a half times the Sun’s width. Arcturus has gone much further down the same road, to a full giant about ten times wider than Muphrid. Side by side they are two frames of the same film.
card.wonder: The two are only about three light-years apart in space, closer to each other than the Sun is to any other star.
card.connect: Arcturus, beside it, shows where Muphrid is heading.
card.answer: Much like Muphrid, a little swollen and a little cooler, setting out on the road Arcturus has already traveled.

card.question: Is the Pointer that looks like Alpha Centauri’s twin really nearby too?
card.glance: The Pointer nearer the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.whyHere: Hadar stands beside Alpha Centauri as if the two were a matched pair, and the truth behind that pairing is a lesson in power.
card.see: Swing between the two Pointers: Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point, because its three stars sit far too close together to split.
card.understand: Hadar is a hot, young triple, and its two main stars, about 12 and 11 times the Sun’s mass, circle each other almost exactly once a year. Watching that orbit both on the sky and in the shifting colors of their light gives its true size in kilometers and its size in angle, and comparing the two yields a distance. That orbital parallax puts Hadar about 361 light-years away, far more precisely than the Hipparcos satellite managed.
card.wonder: The light now reaching you from Hadar left around 1665, when Isaac Newton was a student.
card.connect: Stars this heavy do not live long, and their young relatives crowd the Southern Cross next door.
card.answer: Hadar lies far beyond its partner Pointer and rivals Alpha Centauri only because its heavy, hot stars pour out enormous power, so the Pointers are a pair only from where we stand.
card.photoCaption: Photos show only glare; the pair inside Hadar was separated by linking telescopes together (interferometry).
card.notSee: Its companions are invisible in binoculars.

(2016) combined BRITE nanosatellite photometry with interferometric and spectroscopic orbits: masses 12.02 ± 0.13 and 10.58 ± 0.18 M☉, period 356.9 d, and an orbital parallax of 9.04 ± 0.04 mas (110.6 ± 0.5 pc), against 8.32 ± 0.50 mas from Hipparcos. Both components fit a 10–15 Myr isochrone and pulsate in β Cephei and slowly-pulsating-B modes. Its membership in the Lower Centaurus–Crux group of Sco-Cen is debated (Preibisch & Mamajek 2008).

card.question: What will Sun-like stars look like as giants?
card.glance: A pale orange star in northern Centaurus.
card.whyHere: Menkent is a fairly close orange giant, a preview of a later stage in the life of Sun-like stars.
card.see: Menkent is a pale orange point in binoculars. Compare it with the blue-white stars of southern Centaurus.
card.understand: Menkent has run through its core hydrogen and swollen to about 11 times the Sun’s width. Its surface cooled as it grew, shifting its color toward orange. Iota Centauri lies at almost the same distance, so the two make a fair comparison of a giant and a star still in its prime.
card.wonder: Its light left about 59 years ago, around when surgeons in Cape Town performed the first heart transplant.
card.connect: Further south, far hotter and younger stars wait.
card.answer: Much like Menkent, a pale orange giant, a stage the Sun itself will reach in billions of years.

card.question: Why does Eta Centauri’s brightness wander?
card.glance: A blue-white star in eastern Centaurus.
card.whyHere: Eta Centauri is a spinning Be star whose brightness wanders as it sheds gas.
card.see: Eta Centauri is a blue-white point in binoculars. Its brightness varies a little over weeks to months.
card.understand: Like Achernar and Delta Centauri, it is a Be star, a hot blue star spinning fast enough to fling gas into a disk around its equator. The disk adds its own glow, so the star’s total light depends on how much gas is there. Its spectrum shows bright lines from that disk.
card.wonder: Its light left about 300 years ago, while Edmond Halley was still waiting for his comet to come back.
card.connect: Spinning stars come in many sizes, and Achernar is among the most flattened we know.
card.answer: Its gas disk keeps changing, and the star’s light changes with it over weeks to months. The star is steady; its skirt is not.

card.question: What is the nearest star system you can see with the naked eye?
card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, a single dazzling yellow-white point.
card.whyHere: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system your eyes can reach, and the yardstick for every other distance in the southern sky.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show one brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars sit too close to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Its distance was among the first ever measured, by parallax: as Earth swings around the Sun, a near star shifts slightly against the far ones, and the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Alpha Centauri’s shift is the largest of any naked-eye star, under a second of arc, about the width of a coin seen from several kilometers. Behind that one point are two stars circling every 80 years, one nearly a twin of our Sun and one a smaller orange star.
card.wonder: If the Sun were a 1 cm marble, Earth would be a grain of sand a meter away, and Alpha Centauri another marble about 300 km away.
card.connect: Hadar, the other Pointer, looks almost as bright yet belongs to a completely different league of stars.
card.answer: Alpha Centauri, whose light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. Its faint third member, the red dwarf Proxima, is closer still, the nearest single star of all.
card.photoCaption: Photos show one overexposed glare; only a telescope splits the two stars, and Proxima lies well outside the frame.
card.notSee: You will not see the two stars separately, nor Proxima or its planet.
card.deeper: VLTI/PIONIER interferometry measured the stars’ disks (8.50 and 6.00 mas); with a parallax of 747.17 ± 0.61 mas this gives radii of 1.223 and 0.863 R☉ (Kervella et al. 2017). Ten years of HARPS velocities plus the visual orbit yield masses of about 1.13 and 0.97 M☉ and a 79.91-year period (Pourbaix & Boffin 2016). Spectroscopy puts A near 5,820 K and the pair at 4.5–5.3 billion years, close to the Sun’s age (Porto de Mello et al. 2008). The pair moves 3.7″ per year across the sky.

card.question: What is the second star hiding inside Alpha Centauri?
card.glance: Hidden inside the same point of light as Alpha Centauri A, too close for binoculars to separate.
card.whyHere: Alpha Centauri B is the orange half of our nearest naked-eye star system, a slightly smaller, cooler cousin of the Sun.
card.see: Aim at Alpha Centauri: B is inside that single bright point, adding a touch of orange. Only a telescope at high power shows two stars.
card.understand: The orbit of A and B weighs them, because the size and period of an orbit fix the total mass and each star’s swing sets its share. B has about 97 percent of the Sun’s mass. Its surface is near 5,200 K, cooler than the Sun’s, so it shines orange.
card.wonder: From a planet around B, Alpha Centauri A would blaze far brighter than our full Moon.
card.connect: Same birth, same age, different mass: mass sets a star’s color and brightness.
card.answer: Alpha Centauri B, an orange star almost as massive as the Sun, too close to its partner for binoculars to split, and that small shortfall in mass is enough to change its color.
card.photoCaption: Photos merge A and B into one glare; a telescope shows the orange B beside yellow-white A.

card.question: How far does the Scorpius family of young stars spread?
card.glance: The brightest star of Lupus, a blue-white point low in the south for northern observers.
card.whyHere: The Scorpius stars are only the northern edge of a much larger family, and α Lupi belongs to one of its older branches.
card.see: Look low in the south, about thirty degrees south-west of Scorpius' head. Binoculars show a clean blue-white star in a rich, scattered field, and from mid-northern latitudes a clear southern horizon helps.
card.understand: α Lupi is a hot giant of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, siblings of the Scorpius stars born about 16 million years ago. Like many hot, heavy stars it gently pulses, about every six hours. The change is only a few hundredths of a magnitude, far too little for the eye.
card.wonder: This is the nearest family of hot young stars to the Sun.
card.connect: β and γ Lupi, its siblings, are scattered a few degrees away.
card.answer: Across a quarter of the southern sky: α Lupi belongs to an older branch of the same family.
card.photoCaption: No photo resolves it; the swatch shows its blue-white color.

card.question: Is Izar just a fainter Arcturus?
card.glance: An orange star in Boötes, single in binoculars, though telescopes reveal a lovely color pair.
card.whyHere: Izar looks like a fainter copy of nearby Arcturus, the same orange in a smaller dose.
card.see: In binoculars Izar is orange, like a dimmer copy of Arcturus ten degrees away in the kite of Boötes. Its blue-white companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Izar lies about 200 light-years away, five or six times farther than Arcturus, though the parallax measurements disagree a little. Light spreads out as it travels, over an area that grows with the square of the distance, so from that far it would need around thirty times Arcturus’s output just to look as bright. It looks dimmer, but not by nearly that much.
card.wonder: Through a telescope its tiny companion looks blue against the orange primary, one reason it is nicknamed ‘the most beautiful’.
card.connect: δ and μ Boötis, nearby, are wide doubles your binoculars can split.
card.answer: Izar is no lesser copy, since it must pour out roughly three times as much light as Arcturus to look even this bright from so far away.

card.question: Why does Sheratan look white beside orange Hamal?
card.glance: The second star of the short line of Aries, a white star near orange Hamal.
card.whyHere: Sheratan and Hamal make an easy two-star lesson in color as temperature.
card.see: Sheratan sits in the short line of Aries, and binoculars show a white point. Swing to Hamal, about four degrees north-east, and compare: white against orange.
card.understand: For a fair color comparison, two stars should be at similar distances behind similar amounts of dust, which reddens starlight. Parallax puts Sheratan about 59 light-years away and Hamal only a little farther. That leaves surface temperature, the physics that makes hot iron glow white and cooler iron orange.
card.wonder: Sheratan is still in its steady adult life, while Hamal has already moved on to its giant years.
card.connect: Hamal, the orange half of this pair, offers a glimpse of the Sun’s possible future.
card.answer: Sheratan’s surface is hotter than Hamal’s, and because the two are near neighbors in depth, the difference is real. You are seeing two temperatures side by side.

card.question: Has Polaris always been the North Star?
card.glance: A bright orange star at the outer end of the Little Dipper’s bowl, beside a fainter white star, Pherkad.
card.whyHere: Kochab is an aging orange giant guarding the pole, and its place in the sky holds a clue to how the sky itself moves.
card.see: Between Polaris and the Big Dipper’s handle shine the two ‘guardians of the pole’. In binoculars Kochab is clearly orange and Pherkad, a few degrees away, white, and a touch of defocus makes the colors easier to judge.
card.understand: Kochab has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant about 45 times the Sun’s width, with a cool orange surface near 4,100 K. The pole itself is not fixed: Earth spins like a top, and like a top its axis slowly wobbles, tracing a big circle on the sky over thousands of years. Wherever the axis happens to point, that star becomes the pole star.
card.wonder: Astronomers have found a giant planet, several times Jupiter’s mass, circling this giant star.
card.connect: Polaris, the current pole star, is a very different star holding the same job.
card.answer: Polaris is a recent holder of the title, for the slow wobble of Earth’s axis carries the pole among the stars, and in ancient times it lay much nearer Kochab.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show only an orange point; the planet is known from the star’s regular wobble, not from images.
card.deeper: Hipparcos (2007) gives a parallax of 24.91 ± 0.12 mas, about 131 light-years. A limb-darkened diameter of 10.30 mas (Mozurkewich et al. 2003, via JMDC) at that distance means about 45 solar radii. The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists β UMi b (Lee et al. 2014): a radial-velocity planet with a 522-day period and a minimum mass of about 6 Jupiters. Literature temperatures cluster near 4,000–4,350 K.

card.question: What happens to a family of stars after 16 million years?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Lupus, low in the south from mid-northern sites.
card.whyHere: Star families do not stay together forever, and β Lupi is a sibling already drifting away from its kin.
card.see: About five degrees north-east of α Lupi sits a steady blue-white point, the same color as α. Put both in one sweep and you have two family members side by side.
card.understand: β Lupi belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, stars born together about 16 million years ago. Their birth cloud has long since dispersed, so nothing holds them together any more, and each drifts slowly along its own path. Astronomers still recognize the family by its shared motion and similar ages.
card.wonder: Its light left around the time Galileo died.
card.connect: γ Lupi, farther east, is a third sibling.
card.answer: It spreads out, and β Lupi and its siblings, no longer held by their birth cloud, are scattering across the southern sky.

card.question: How can you watch one star pass in front of another?
card.glance: A modest white star in Libra that loses more than half its light for part of a night every 2.3 days.
card.whyHere: Most eclipsing stars dip too little to notice, but δ Librae loses more than half its light, a wink you can actually catch.
card.see: δ Lib sits about eight degrees north-north-east of Zubenelgenubi. Compare it with neighboring stars of similar brightness, ideally on two nights: usually it holds steady, but during an eclipse it looks clearly fainter, and the app's eclipse list tells you whether tonight is a good night.
card.understand: δ Lib is an eclipsing binary, two stars orbiting every 2 days and 8 hours, far too close for any telescope to split. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per lap the dimmer star slides in front of the brighter one and blocks much of its light. Gas also streams from one star onto the other, slowly reshaping both.
card.wonder: Each eclipse lasts hours, so on a good night you can watch the star fade and recover before bedtime.
card.connect: μ¹ Scorpii, in the tail of Scorpius, plays the same game with a smaller dip.
card.answer: Watch δ Librae at the right hour: every 2.3 days its fainter star slides across the brighter one and the light drops by more than half, a shadow play staged about 300 light-years away on a schedule predictable to within minutes.
card.photoCaption: The light-curve sketch shows a flat line with a sharp dip each orbit: the classic eclipsing pattern.
card.notSee: The two stars are never seen separately; only their combined light changes.
card.deeper: GCVS: EA/SD (Algol type, semi-detached), V 4.91–5.90, P = 2.3273543 d, epoch JD 2442960.6994, spectral type A0 IV-V. Hipparcos 2007 gives 11.11 ± 0.60 mas (≈290 ly) and Gaia DR3 9.28 ± 0.47 mas (≈350 ly); the difference may reflect the binary's orbital motion. Predicted minima drift if the period changes, so a recent ephemeris is better than the GCVS epoch for timing.

card.question: Are the three stars of the Southern Triangle alike?
card.glance: A white corner of the Southern Triangle, Triangulum Australe.
card.whyHere: Gamma Trianguli Australis is the white corner of a triangle whose three stars all differ in color and distance.
card.see: Compare the three corners of the Southern Triangle: orange Atria, creamy Beta and white Gamma. Gamma is the one at the triangle’s western tip.
card.understand: Gamma Trianguli Australis is a hot white star, hotter than either of its partners. Its parallax puts it about 190 light-years away. The three corners have different temperatures and lie at different depths.
card.wonder: If you could fly around the triangle, its shape would collapse and rearrange itself.
card.connect: Orange Atria makes the color contrast.
card.answer: The corners differ in color and lie at about 40, 190 and 390 light-years, with white Gamma in the middle, so a neat triangle in the sky is a scattered trio in space.

card.question: What would our Sun look like from δ Boötis’s distance?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Boötes with a faint companion that binoculars split cleanly.
card.whyHere: δ Boötis is a wide, genuine double, a yellow giant and a faint Sun-like star traveling together.
card.see: δ Boo sits on the eastern side of the kite of Boötes, north-east of Arcturus. In 10× binoculars look just beside it for a much fainter point, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away; it splits cleanly when you hold steady.
card.understand: The bright star is a giant about 11 times the Sun’s width, and its companion is a Sun-like dwarf. Gaia measures the same distance for both, about 120 light-years, so they belong together and orbit very slowly. The faint companion shows how dim a star like ours looks from here.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left δ Boötis around 1905, the year Einstein published special relativity.
card.connect: μ Boötis, a few degrees north-east, is another wide pair, and its faint star is double too.
card.answer: Almost exactly like δ Boötis’s faint companion, a modest point that binoculars split from the bright giant it travels with.

card.question: Can a star really look green?
card.glance: Libra's northern claw, a blue-white star that some observers insist looks green; defocus it and decide.
card.whyHere: Here is a star that lets your own eyes join an old argument: it is often called the only green star, though physics says it should not be.
card.see: Center Zubeneschamali and defocus slightly so it becomes a small disk. Compare it with white Zubenelgenubi nine degrees south-west and, if it is up, orange Antares low in the south-east, and decide before reading on: green tinge, pale blue, or plain white?
card.understand: Its surface is about 12,000 degrees, twice as hot as the Sun's, so its light leans blue and it should look blue-white. A glowing body never emits just one color; it pours out a broad spread of them, and even a star whose output peaked in green would send plenty of red and blue too. Our eyes blend that mixture into white, which is why the Sun, whose light peaks near green, looks white from space.
card.wonder: Observers have argued about this star's color for generations, and tonight your eyes cast a vote.
card.connect: δ Librae, nearby, is a star that winks.
card.answer: No star truly does, because a star's light is always a broad mix, and a mix centered on green looks white. Zubeneschamali is blue-white, and any green you see comes from contrast with nearby colors and the way our eyes handle color in dim light.
card.photoCaption: The swatch shows its computed color, blue-white; compare that with what your eye reported.
card.deeper: BBC Sky at Night summarizes the case: a B8 V star of about 12,300 K and roughly 80 Myr, often described in older literature as greenish, while most modern observers report blue-white; there is no accepted physical explanation for a green appearance. The 'n' in B8Vn marks broad lines from fast rotation. Hipparcos 2007 parallax 17.62 ± 0.16 mas (≈185 ly).

card.question: How many stars hide in μ Boötis?
card.glance: A white star in northern Boötes with a faint partner, itself a double.
card.whyHere: μ Boötis is a bright white star with a faint companion that binoculars can split.
card.see: μ Boo lies near the top of Boötes, a few degrees north-east of δ Boo. In 10× binoculars a much fainter star sits just south of it, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away; hold steady to separate it from the glare.
card.understand: The bright star is white, about twice the Sun’s mass. The companion is a pair of Sun-like stars orbiting each other closely, too close for binoculars. All three share the same distance and motion through space, the two tests of a real family.
card.wonder: The light you see left these stars a little over a century ago, around the time Einstein was rethinking what light is.
card.connect: ν Boötis, a few degrees north, looks like another pair but is not.
card.answer: There are three: binoculars split a bright white star from a faint companion, and a telescope splits that companion into two Sun-like stars.

card.question: Can planets survive when their star swells into a giant?
card.glance: An orange 3rd-magnitude star in the dragon's tail, between the Little Dipper's bowl and Boötes.
card.whyHere: The Sun will one day swell into a giant, and Edasich offers an early hint of what that means for the planets around it.
card.see: Edasich is a clear orange point in the tail of Draco, between the Little Dipper's bowl and Boötes. Compare it with white stars nearby to see the tint.
card.understand: Edasich has used up its core hydrogen and swollen to about 12 times the Sun's width. Even so, at least two massive planets still orbit it, both found from the star's wobble. One takes over a year per orbit on a strongly stretched path, swinging in close and far out again.
card.wonder: When the Sun swells this way, its own inner planets will face the same test.
card.connect: 16 Cygni B shows planets around a Sun-like star still in its prime.
card.answer: Some can, if they orbit far enough out: Edasich has become a giant and still keeps at least two massive planets.

card.question: Is the matched pair of ν Boötis a real couple?
card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes, one orange and one white.
card.whyHere: ν Boötis looks like the best-matched pair in Boötes, two stars of equal brightness side by side.
card.see: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
card.understand: Whether the two belong together is something Gaia can settle by parallax, the tiny shift of each star as Earth circles the Sun. Those shifts put ν¹, an orange giant, nearly 1,000 light-years away, and ν², a white star, about 440. Light fades with the square of distance, so to look equally bright from more than twice as far, the orange star must give out roughly five times as much light.
card.wonder: The orange star’s light set out around the year 1050, about when Chinese astronomers recorded the supernova that left us the Crab Nebula.
card.connect: μ Boötis, nearby, is a pair that really does belong together.
card.answer: It is a match made only by perspective: a distant giant and a nearer white star that happen to line up.

card.question: Can one point of light be two young stars?
card.glance: A blue-white star at the eastern edge of Lupus; one point in binoculars.
card.whyHere: The third Lupus sibling adds a twist of its own: what binoculars show as one star is really two.
card.see: Look about ten degrees north-east of α Lupi. Binoculars show a single blue-white star, and its companion is far too close to split.
card.understand: γ Lupi is a close double of two hot young stars, both members of the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group. Heavy stars are usually born in pairs or small groups, so a double like this is the rule rather than the exception. Only telescopes reveal the second star.
card.wonder: Its light set out about four centuries ago, around when Kepler was working out how the planets move.
card.connect: Scorpius' head lies about twenty degrees to the north.
card.answer: γ Lupi is exactly that, two hot young stars too close for any binoculars to split, born together with the rest of the Lupus family.

card.question: Is the Northern Crown's brightest jewel really a single star?
card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.whyHere: Alphecca anchors the hops to the Crown's two strange variables, and it hides a small surprise of its own.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star in the arc of Corona Borealis, and binoculars fit the whole crown into one or two fields. Start every hop to T CrB and R CrB here.
card.understand: Watched with sensitive instruments, its light dips slightly every 17 days. The dips come from two stars, a hot white one and a smaller Sun-like one, taking turns to pass in front of each other. We notice only because our line of sight lies almost in the plane of their orbit.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 75 years ago, roughly a human lifetime.
card.connect: From this steady jewel, the crown's unpredictable stars are a short hop away.
card.answer: Alphecca is an eclipsing pair whose dips are far too small for the eye, so its steady look hides a rhythm only instruments can catch.

card.question: What does a heavier Sun look like after its prime?
card.glance: The brightest star of Serpens, a pale orange point in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Unukalhai, the brightest star of Serpens, is a preview of later life for stars a little heavier than the Sun.
card.see: Center Unukalhai and defocus slightly to bring out its pale orange color. The globular cluster M5 lies about eight degrees to the south-west, an easy next hop.
card.understand: Unukalhai has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant. Its surface has cooled and reddened, but there is far more of it, so it shines much more brightly than it did in its prime. At 74 light-years it is a close neighbor as giants go.
card.wonder: Its light left about 74 years ago; M5's left long before there were people to see it.
card.connect: M5, south-west, is a far-off city of ancient stars.
card.answer: It swells, for once the core runs dry the outer layers balloon and cool, and the star becomes a pale orange giant like Unukalhai, far brighter than in its prime.

card.question: How can a star vanish from view for months and then come back?
card.glance: At normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the Northern Crown's bowl; at other times, missing altogether.
card.whyHere: Most variable stars pulse, eclipse or explode; R Coronae Borealis has a stranger habit, disappearing now and then inside its own soot.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a little fainter than the Crown's faintest stars; if the spot is empty, the star is in a fade, and that is a real observation too.
card.understand: R CrB is a supergiant, a star swollen to enormous size, and an oddly built one, almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Now and then a puff of gas leaving its surface cools enough for that carbon to condense into soot, much as a candle flame blackens a cold spoon. When such a cloud forms on our side, the star sinks from 6th magnitude to as faint as 15th.
card.wonder: At its deepest it is thousands of times fainter than normal, as if someone had drawn a curtain across a lamp.
card.connect: Three degrees away, T CrB waits to do the opposite: brighten without warning.
card.answer: It hides behind soot of its own making and stays hidden until the cloud drifts off and thins, which can take months or years. Its strange chemistry hints at an equally strange birth, perhaps two white dwarfs that merged into one swollen star.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows the sudden drop and slow recovery typical of its fades.
card.deeper: R CrB stars are hydrogen-deficient, carbon-rich supergiants that undergo deep, irregular declines when carbon dust condenses in their outflows (Clayton 2012). Two origins are debated: a merger of two white dwarfs, or a final helium-shell flash in a dying star; large amounts of oxygen-18 favor the merger picture, making them low-mass cousins of Type Ia supernova progenitors. About 65 were known in 2012 against thousands predicted. VSX gives V = 5.61 at maximum and 15.1 in deep minimum.

card.question: Why does nearby Beta look about as bright as distant Atria?
card.glance: A creamy white corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.whyHere: Beta Trianguli Australis looks nearly as bright as Atria, though it is about ten times closer.
card.see: Swing between Beta and Atria. Atria looks a little brighter and orange, Beta creamy white.
card.understand: Beta Trianguli Australis is a modest star only a little hotter than the Sun, about 40 light-years away. Atria lies about ten times farther. Light fades with the square of distance, so from ten times as far, Atria must be about a hundred times more powerful just to keep up.
card.wonder: Moved this close, Atria would outshine every star in the sky.
card.connect: Atria, the triangle’s orange corner, is a giant many times wider than the Sun.
card.answer: Atria is simply far more powerful: from ten times farther away it still looks a little brighter, so it must shine hundreds of times brighter than Beta.

card.question: Why does Achernar look brighter than nearer Alpha Hydri?
card.glance: A creamy white star 5° from Achernar.
card.whyHere: Alpha Hydri is a nearby white star and a handy comparison for blue-white Achernar.
card.see: Put Achernar and Alpha Hydri in the same sweep, about 5° apart. Achernar looks icy blue-white, Alpha Hydri slightly warmer and creamier.

card.answer: Achernar is simply far more powerful, so although it lies more than twice as far away, its hot, heavy bulk easily outshines creamy Alpha Hydri.

card.question: Which star anchors the bottom of the Scorpion's head?
card.glance: The lowest of the three stars in Scorpius' head; a blue-white point.
card.whyHere: π Scorpii is another hot sibling of the Upper Scorpius family, and the yardstick for δ's wandering brightness.
card.see: π is the bottom star of the short arc formed with δ and β. Use it, with β, as a brightness yardstick for δ, whose light wanders.
card.understand: π Sco is a close pair of hot young stars, too tight for any telescope to split, revealed only by the way their spectral lines shift back and forth. Both belong to the Upper Scorpius group, about 11 million years old. Its own light barely flickers, which makes it a steady reference.
card.wonder: Its light has been traveling for about six centuries.
card.connect: δ, just above, may now be the brighter of the two.
card.answer: Fang, the lowest star of the head: a hot young pair that holds steady, the perfect yardstick for wandering δ.

card.question: How can a star suddenly grow a disk of gas and brighten?
card.glance: The middle star of the arc at Scorpius' head; a bright white point whose brightness has wandered since 2000.
card.whyHere: Stars change over millions of years, so it is rare to watch one transform within a human lifetime, and δ Scorpii did exactly that in the year 2000.
card.see: δ is the middle star of the short upright arc forming Scorpius' head, north-west of Antares. Compare it with β above and π below: is δ clearly the brightest, or about equal? Your answer is a real measurement, since its disk has made it vary for two decades.
card.understand: δ Sco is a hot, heavy star spinning so fast that gas at its equator is barely held on. When a companion on a stretched 11-year orbit swung in close in 2000, the star began shedding a flat disk of gas around its waist. Hot stars with such disks are called Be stars, the e for the glow of the disk gas, which adds light of its own.
card.wonder: At closest approach its companion dives to within about 15 times δ's own radius.
card.connect: Acrab, just above it, hides a whole family in one point.
card.answer: Spinning near its limit, it was tipped over by a close pass of its companion: since 2000 δ Scorpii has worn a glowing ring of gas that changes how bright it looks, and the familiar shape of the Scorpion's head changed within living memory.
card.photoCaption: No image resolves the disk; the light-curve sketch shows the shape of its slow, irregular changes, not a forecast.
card.notSee: The disk itself is far too small to see; only its effect on the star's brightness reaches your eye.
card.deeper: Miroshnichenko et al. (2001) followed the onset of strong Hα emission and enhanced mass loss just before the 2000 periastron, when the stars come within ~15 primary radii. Their study of the 2011 periastron (2011 July 3) refined the orbit to 10.8092 ± 0.0005 yr, adopted a distance of 136 pc and estimated a disk radius of ~150 R☉ (Miroshnichenko et al. 2013). The GCVS range (V 1.86–2.32) predates the outburst; treat any printed magnitude as historical and compare with β and π Sco on the night.
