card.question: What hides in the quiet far-southern sky of Corona Australis?
card.glance: A small, bright, concentrated glow in Corona Australis.
card.whyHere: Corona Australis looks empty, but it hides a compact, ancient globular, about 12.5 billion years old.
card.see: From α Telescopii go about four degrees north-west. Look for a small, round glow with a bright core.
card.understand: Its stars formed early in the Galaxy's history. They hold less than 2% of the Sun's share of heavy elements, which are forged inside stars and spread when they die. So little enrichment means these stars formed before many generations had lived.
card.wonder: Its light left about 25,000 years ago, when ice sheets still covered much of the northern world.
card.connect: NGC 6397, larger and nearer, lies about eleven degrees south-south-west.
card.answer: It hides NGC 6541, a compact globular about 12.5 billion years old whose stars are almost free of heavy elements.

card.question: Which is the richest of Cassiopeia’s young star clusters?
card.glance: A grainy little cloud of stars with a few brighter points, south-west of Segin in Cassiopeia.
card.whyHere: NGC 663 is the richest of the young clusters along Cassiopeia’s stretch of the Perseus arm.
card.see: From Segin, the eastern end of the W, drop about two and a half degrees south-south-west to a small grainy patch, larger and richer than M103 nearby. Put both in one field and compare.
card.understand: NGC 663 is a young family, roughly 25 to 30 million years old, still rich in hot blue-white stars that will not last much longer. Gaia separates its members from the crowded Milky Way background by their shared motion and distance. That census finds over a thousand of them.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 8,700 years ago, when the first farming towns were growing in Anatolia.
card.connect: M103 is its smaller neighbor, probably born in the same stretch of the arm.
card.answer: NGC 663, with nearly 8,000 Suns’ worth of stars, only 25 to 30 million years old. It is the heart of a whole association of young clusters.
card.photoCaption: Photos resolve hundreds of blue-white members; binoculars show a grainy glow with a few stars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 2.67 kpc, about 1,080 members, 7,800 solar masses and 27 Myr (18–42 Myr). NGC 663 is the largest confirmed cluster of the Cassiopeia OB8 association (arXiv:2507.14125).

card.question: How can you read a star cluster's age from its brightest stars?
card.glance: A long, loose spray of stars in a rich Milky Way field in Ophiuchus, easy in any binoculars.
card.whyHere: IC 4665 and NGC 6633 sit at almost the same distance, so comparing them shows age alone at work, and this family is about ten times older.
card.see: From IC 4665, sweep about 10° due east to an elongated scatter about the width of the full Moon against a dense star background. Pick out its brightest members, then swing back to IC 4665: similar size, similar distance, different age.
card.understand: Heavy, hot, blue stars burn their fuel fastest, so a cluster's brightest surviving stars are a clock. In NGC 6633 the hottest stars are long gone, and its brightest members are white stars and a few yellow-orange giants that have begun to swell. The CoRoT satellite caught three of those giants ringing like bells, and their tones pinned down their masses and the cluster's age.
card.wonder: These stars were born around the time the first animals with hard shells appeared in Earth's oceans.
card.connect: Star families drift apart as they age; the oldest surviving ones are the globular clusters of the halo.
card.answer: Find the heaviest stars still in their steady phase and you know how long the cluster has been burning. In NGC 6633 that clock reads about 550 million years.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo records hundreds of faint members; binoculars show a few dozen.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 390 pc, about 500 Gaia DR3 members and about 650 solar masses. Brogaard et al. (2025) combined CoRoT oscillation measurements of three red-giant members with Gaia photometry for 0.55 (+0.05/−0.10) Gyr; Hunt & Reffert’s neural-network age is 0.47 Gyr (0.30–0.80). Jeffries et al. (2002) found its lithium pattern almost identical to the Hyades and Praesepe despite slightly lower metallicity, which makes it a useful twin of those clusters.

card.question: How young is a star family that still has blue-white stars?
card.glance: A small, faint scatter of stars in a rich Aquila field.
card.whyHere: Not every cluster is famous, and NGC 6709 is a good example of an ordinary young family going quietly about its life in the Milky Way's disk.
card.see: From ζ Aquilae, at the eagle's tail, sweep about 5° south-west. Look for a small, slightly grainy patch with a few resolved stars, easy to miss against the rich background.
card.understand: Its brightest stars are still blue-white, and such hot stars burn out fast, so the family can be no more than a few hundred million years old. Gaia picked out about 450 members sharing one distance and motion. Fitting their colors and brightness to stellar models gives the age.
card.wonder: The light you see left it about 3,400 years ago, when Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs ruled.
card.connect: The older and younger families of Ophiuchus lie to the west.
card.answer: Young enough to keep its hot stars: NGC 6709 is about 160 million years old, a toddler by the standards of the Sun.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves dozens of members; binoculars show a handful plus haze.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 1.05 kpc, about 450 Gaia DR3 members, neural-network age 161 Myr (109–286). No literature age override was applied.

card.question: Is this faint sprinkle near M25 a real cluster?
card.glance: A small, loose grouping of faint stars east of M25.
card.whyHere: NGC 6716 is a modest family of similar age to nearby M25, sparser and harder to pick out.
card.see: From ξ² Sagittarii, go about one and a half degrees north-west. Look for a small cluster of faint stars against the Milky Way.
card.understand: Gaia measures the distance and motion of every star in the field. About 930 of them share the same values, at roughly 2,300 light-years. That shared motion is what makes it a real cluster, about 80 million years old.
card.wonder: It formed in the age of the late dinosaurs.
card.connect: M25 is a richer family of similar age.
card.answer: It is real, and most of the family is invisible to you: of the hundreds Gaia found, binoculars catch only a sprinkle.

card.question: Why does this ancient cluster have such a starlike center?
card.glance: A bright, round glow with a starlike center in Pavo, far from the band of the Milky Way.
card.whyHere: The Great Peacock Globular is one of the oldest things you can see, a globular cluster formed when our galaxy was young.
card.see: Binoculars show an obvious round glow with a bright, concentrated core, almost like an out-of-focus star, and a fainter halo that spreads with averted vision under a dark sky. If Omega Centauri or 47 Tucanae is up, compare how tightly each gathers its light toward the middle.
card.understand: This globular cluster formed about 12.5 billion years ago, and its stars are poor in heavy elements because few earlier stars had enriched the gas. Over billions of years its stars have traded energy in close passes: the heavier ones sink toward the middle while lighter ones are flung outward, like a crowd sorting itself out. Its core has collapsed into a tiny, dense center.
card.wonder: Its light left about 13,000 years ago, as the last Ice Age was ending, and its stars are nearly three times older than Earth.
card.connect: The Jewel Box’s stars, about 16 million years old, make this cluster look truly ancient.
card.answer: Over its long life the cluster’s heart has packed ever tighter, concentrating its light into a near-point core, a center made by time rather than by birth.
card.photoCaption: Telescope images resolve thousands of stars to the core; binoculars show a bright, smooth glow with a sharp center.
card.notSee: No individual stars; the core does not resolve in binoculars.
card.deeper: Distance 4.12 ± 0.04 kpc (Baumgardt & Vasiliev 2021); relative age 12.50 ± 0.25 Gyr (VandenBerg et al. 2013); [Fe/H] = −1.54 and a core-collapsed density profile (Harris catalog). Mass about 2.6 × 10⁵ M☉ from N-body fits (Baumgardt catalog).

card.question: How does a family of stars survive for billions of years?
card.glance: A small, faint, grainy smudge in a rich Cygnus star field: easy to overlook.
card.whyHere: Most star families dissolve within a few hundred million years, so a cluster that has held together for billions is a puzzle worth a look.
card.see: Start at δ Cygni, the western end of the Northern Cross's crossbar, and move about 5° south. Brace the binoculars and look for a tiny haze, much smaller than the full Moon, that grows slightly with averted vision and hints at graininess.
card.understand: Open clusters are loosely bound, and passing clouds and the Galaxy's own tides keep tugging at them, so most drift apart. NGC 6819 is rich, with thousands of members whose combined gravity has held it together, and its brightest stars are now yellow and orange giants, the blue heavyweights long gone. The Kepler spacecraft recorded eclipses among its stars, which weighed them and pinned down the age.
card.wonder: Its stars were born at roughly the time oxygen first began building up in Earth's air.
card.connect: M71 in Sagitta, a globular cluster, is older still.
card.answer: NGC 6819 survives by being big, with enough members and enough gravity to hold together for about 2.4 billion years while smaller families scatter. It sits inside the patch of sky Kepler stared at for years, which is why we know it so well.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves a dense swarm; binoculars show a faint, slightly grainy glow.
card.notSee: Individual stars: only the brightest few pop out at 10×.
card.deeper: Brewer et al. (2016) used masses and radii of eclipsing binaries found by Kepler: 2.38 ± 0.05 Gyr (±0.22 systematic); the color–magnitude diagram gives 2.21 ± 0.10 Gyr. Hunt & Reffert (2024) find 2.51 kpc, about 2,300 Gaia members and about 7,500 solar masses; their neural-network age (1.7 Gyr) is lower, a known weakness of such ages for old clusters.

card.question: Can you see a cluster still sitting in the cloud it formed from?
card.glance: A small, faint knot of stars in Vulpecula; the glowing gas around it shows only in photographs.
card.whyHere: One of the youngest clusters on the binocular list, NGC 6823 is still wrapped in the gas it formed from.
card.see: About 3.5° east of α Vulpeculae, look for a tiny group of faint stars. Binoculars show only the brightest members; the gas and dark pillars around them need a camera.
card.understand: At about 4 million years old, its hot young stars are still blasting the surrounding hydrogen with ultraviolet light. That light makes the cloud glow and slowly erodes it, carving pillars where denser knots shield the gas behind them. The same process sculpts the famous pillars in the Eagle Nebula.
card.wonder: It formed after the first human ancestors began walking on two legs.
card.connect: The North America Nebula, to the north, is a bigger nursery in the same Milky Way band.
card.answer: Its stars, yes; its cloud, no. The glowing gas around NGC 6823 shows only in photographs, but the cluster you see is still sitting in it.
card.photoCaption: Photographs show red gas and dark pillars around the cluster; binoculars show a few faint stars.
card.notSee: The nebula NGC 6820 and its pillars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 2.04 kpc, about 175 Gaia members, neural-network age 3.8 Myr (2.8–4.6). It is often assigned to the Vulpecula OB1 association.

card.question: Can a black hole still have living siblings?
card.glance: A loose, bright knot of white stars set in the dense Cygnus Milky Way.
card.whyHere: Black holes are born from the heaviest stars, and heavy stars are born in families, so somewhere a black hole should still be traveling with its kin.
card.see: From η Cygni, in the swan's neck below Sadr, move about 2° east-north-east. A compact scatter of fairly bright white stars stands out from the dense background; frame it at low power, then sweep around to sense how many bright stars belong to the wider family.
card.understand: NGC 6871 is the densest part of Cygnus OB3, a loose group of hot, heavy stars born within the last several million years. Stars this heavy burn through their fuel in a few million years, and one former member already has. In 2003 astronomers measured the motion of Cygnus X-1 through space and found it moving along with this group, so its black hole, now weighed at about 21 Suns, very likely began as one of the family’s heaviest stars.
card.wonder: The black hole's parent star seems to have collapsed without a big explosion, since a supernova kick would have stopped it keeping pace with its siblings.
card.connect: Cygnus X-1's companion is a faint star a little to the west, near η Cygni.
card.answer: Cygnus X-1 seems to, for this black hole of about twenty Suns and its blue supergiant still travel with the stars of NGC 6871, probably the family its parent was born in, where some siblings may end the same way.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows the cluster’s bright stars against countless background stars, as binoculars do.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 1.84 kpc, about 350 Gaia members and a neural-network age of 7.8 Myr (5–11); older photometric ages range from about 2 to 20 Myr. Massey et al. (1995) studied the massive-star content of Cyg OB3. Mirabel & Rodrigues (2003) found that Cygnus X-1 moves with Cyg OB3 to within about 9 km/s and argued that its black hole formed from a progenitor of more than 40 solar masses that ejected at most about one solar mass; they used the then-accepted black-hole mass of about 10 solar masses, which Miller-Jones et al. (2021) revised to about 21 solar masses.

card.question: What does a heavy star do in the last stretch before it explodes?
card.glance: In binoculars you see the star that blew this bubble, not the bubble itself.
card.whyHere: Before exploding, a heavy star spends a long time tearing itself apart, and the Crescent is the bubble one such star has blown around itself.
card.see: The Crescent lies nearly 3° south-west of Sadr, at the center of the Northern Cross. Use the chart to find the faint star WR 136; the shell itself is a large-telescope target even with a filter, so in binoculars you are visiting the star that made it.
card.understand: WR 136 is a Wolf-Rayet star, a very heavy star that has lost its outer hydrogen and now drives a fierce wind. Earlier, as a swollen giant, it shed slower gas, and the fast wind is ramming into that older material and piling it into a glowing shell, like a snowplow pushing snow. The chemistry gives it away: the shell is rich in nitrogen made in the star's core, so the gas came from the star, not from space.
card.wonder: The gas you would see in a photo began leaving the star roughly a quarter of a million years ago.
card.connect: The Veil, a few fields south-east, shows what follows when such a star explodes.
card.answer: It strips itself bare, and WR 136's wind now plows the old gas into the Crescent's glowing shell, the portrait of a star in its final chapter before a supernova.
card.photoCaption: Telescope images show a glowing crescent shell around WR 136; binoculars show only the star.
card.notSee: The shell itself: it needs a telescope and a nebula filter.
card.deeper: Gaia EDR3 measures WR 136’s parallax as 0.577 ± 0.016 mas, about 1.73 kpc (via SIMBAD); older studies used 1.26 kpc, and ESA/Hubble quotes about 4,500 light-years. ESA/Hubble describes the shell as material shed about 250,000 years ago and now being torn apart by the wind. Suzaku X-ray data (Zhekov & Park 2011) show hot gas filling the bubble; adopting a WN6 wind of about 1,600 km/s, they estimated a dynamical age near 30,000 years at their distance.

card.glance: A small, tight group of faint stars just north of Sadr, in the same binocular field.

card.wonder: The cluster was born long after the dinosaurs died out.
card.connect: M29, two degrees south of Sadr, is another young family at almost the same distance.
card.answer: Sadr is about 1,800 light-years away and the cluster three times farther, so the bright star is a foreground passer-by.

card.question: How small does a globular cluster look from 50,000 light-years away?
card.glance: A tiny, faint, almost starlike glow in Delphinus: a real challenge for 10×50.
card.whyHere: The Great Hercules Cluster is a globular next door by comparison, and NGC 6934 is the same kind of ancient star ball twice as far away, a real test of your sky and your eyes.
card.see: From ε Delphini, south-west of the dolphin's diamond, drop about 4° south. Look for a tiny fuzzy star that won't focus, and confirm it against the chart.
card.understand: NGC 6934 holds about 150,000 Suns' worth of stars, almost 12 billion years old. Double a cluster's distance and it shrinks to half the size and a quarter of the brightness. At twice the Great Hercules Cluster's distance and with a third of its mass, this one is reduced to a pinpoint glow.
card.wonder: Its light left about 51,000 years ago, while Neanderthals still lived in Europe.
card.connect: Job's Coffin, just north, is only a couple of hundred light-years away.
card.answer: From that far, NGC 6934's ancient stars shrink to a fuzzy star that won't focus.

card.question: What does a real crowd of star siblings look like?
card.glance: A large, rich, even scatter of faint stars in southern Vulpecula, about the size of the full Moon.
card.whyHere: A real family of stars rarely looks dramatic, and NGC 6940 is the proof: a plain patch that turns out to hold hundreds of siblings.
card.see: From ε Cygni, sweep about 6° south-west. Look for a soft, grainy patch the size of the full Moon, sprinkled with faint resolved stars; a dark sky brings out dozens.
card.understand: Its hottest stars are long gone, and the white and yellow stars that remain date the family to the better part of a billion years. Gaia measured the distance and motion of every star in the field, and more than 800 move together. That shared motion is what makes a cluster real, whatever it looks like.
card.wonder: The whole family weighs about 2,200 Suns, spread across a patch of sky the size of the full Moon.
card.connect: The Coathanger looks more like a cluster but is a false one.
card.answer: It can look like NGC 6940, an unremarkable grainy patch that holds hundreds of stars traveling together.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo resolves hundreds of members; binoculars show a grainy glow with a few dozen stars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 1.01 kpc, about 860 Gaia members and about 2,200 solar masses; neural-network age 0.77 Gyr (0.53–1.2). No literature age override was applied.

card.question: What is left of a star thousands of years after it explodes?
card.glance: A thin, very faint streak through the star 52 Cygni; most observers need a dark sky and a nebula filter.
card.whyHere: Heavy stars end with a bang rather than a sigh, and the Veil is the expanding wreck of one such explosion, still spreading across Cygnus.
card.see: Find 52 Cygni, a modest star about 3° south of ε Cygni at the eastern end of the Northern Cross's crossbar; the West Veil runs north–south right through it. Without a filter it is usually invisible in 10×50, but a nebula filter held to one eyepiece may bring out a pale thread.
card.understand: Ten to twenty thousand years ago a star many times heavier than the Sun ran out of fuel, its core collapsed, and the rest exploded as a supernova. The blast wave is still plowing into thin surrounding gas and heating it until it glows. This thread and its eastern partner are opposite edges of one bubble spanning about seven full Moons on the sky.
card.wonder: Its distance comes from a clever fence: stars whose light shows the remnant's fast gas must lie inside or behind it, so their distances pin it down.
card.connect: The East Veil, across the bubble, is the brighter arc and the easier catch.
card.answer: A blast wave still on the move, outlining a bubble about 120 light-years across. The atoms glowing in it include elements forged in that star and its explosion, and they will join future clouds, stars and planets, just as debris like this once joined ours.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures with narrow filters show braided red and blue filaments; binoculars show a ghostly line at best.
card.notSee: No color and no fine braiding; without a filter often nothing at all.
card.deeper: Fesen et al. (2021) used Gaia EDR3 parallaxes of stars whose spectra show high-velocity gas from the remnant, so they sit inside or behind it: 725 ± 15 pc, about 2,400 light-years, giving a radius of about 18 pc. Ritchey et al. (2024) found that one of those stars is a binary unsuitable for the test and placed another star near 870 pc, so the distance may grow. Ages of 10,000–20,000 years are quoted. In BAA reports the eastern arc shows in 10×50 with averted vision; the western one rarely shows without a filter.

card.question: Why does a supernova remnant look like scattered threads instead of a bubble?
card.glance: On a dark night, a faint, curved sliver of light: easier than the western arc, still a stretch for 10×50.
card.whyHere: The East Veil is the brightest stretch of a supernova's blast wave in binocular reach, and its broken, threadlike look is itself a clue.
card.see: From ε Cygni, the eastern end of the Northern Cross's crossbar, move about 3° south-east. Under a dark, transparent sky, sweep slowly with averted vision for a faint, slightly curved arc about two full Moons long; a nebula filter helps enormously.
card.understand: This arc and the West Veil are opposite edges of one expanding shell, and the empty-looking space between them is its inside. Space is not evenly filled, so the blast runs into lumpy clouds, and only where it hits denser patches does it heat gas until it glows. We also see the shell best at its rim, where our line of sight runs through the most glowing gas, the way a soap bubble's edge stands out more than its face.
card.wonder: If your eyes could see all of it, the full loop would span about seven full Moons.
card.connect: The Dumbbell in Vulpecula shows the gentle end of a lighter star.
card.answer: The blast wave only shines where it strikes denser gas and where we look along its edge, so a smooth bubble shows up as scattered, braided arcs. Only stars more than about eight times the Sun's mass end this way.
card.photoCaption: Filtered long exposures show twisted ribbons of glowing gas; binoculars show a faint gray arc.
card.notSee: No color, no ribbons; expect a faint arc only under dark, transparent skies.
card.deeper: Fesen et al. (2021) used Gaia EDR3 parallaxes of stars whose spectra show high-velocity gas from the remnant, so they sit inside or behind it: 725 ± 15 pc, about 2,400 light-years, giving a radius of about 18 pc. Ritchey et al. (2024) found that one of those stars is a binary unsuitable for the test and placed another star near 870 pc, so the distance may grow. Ages of 10,000–20,000 years are quoted. In BAA reports the eastern arc shows in 10×50 with averted vision; the western one rarely shows without a filter.

card.question: Can you see a star nursery whose light source is hidden from view?
card.glance: A large, faint brightening of the Milky Way east of Deneb with a darker notch: subtle, not a bright cloud.
card.whyHere: Stars are born in clouds of gas, and the North America Nebula is a nursery big enough to frame in binoculars, lit by a star nobody found until 2005.
card.see: Put Deneb at the edge of a wide field and look about 3° east. On a dark, transparent night the area looks slightly brighter than the surrounding Milky Way, with a sharper dark edge on its southern side, the Gulf of Mexico; low power and a nebula filter help, but don't mistake rich star fields for the glow.
card.understand: This is a cloud of hydrogen lit by ultraviolet light from very hot young stars, glowing the way a neon sign does when electricity excites its atoms. For a long time nearby Deneb got the credit, but it is not the main lamp. Infrared light passes through dust, and infrared images finally revealed the real source: a hot star hidden behind the dark lane that forms the gulf.
card.wonder: Most of the young stars here are only about a million years old: when they formed, our ancestors already walked on two legs.
card.connect: The dark gulf is one small piece of the dust lane that splits the whole summer Milky Way.
card.answer: The North America Nebula is one, lit by a star hidden behind the dust of its gulf, its continent shape a chance meeting of glowing gas and dark dust.
card.photoCaption: Long exposures record red hydrogen glow and the continent outline; binoculars show a faint gray brightening.
card.notSee: No red color and no sharp continent: just a subtle glow with a darker edge.
card.deeper: Zucker et al. (2020) put the dust cloud at about 810 pc; Kuhn & Hillenbrand (2020) find about 785 pc for the young star groups with Gaia EDR3. Comerón & Pasquali (2005) found the ionizing star in infrared data behind the dark cloud L935; the GOSSS survey later showed it to be a close pair, O3.5 III(f*) + O8 (Maíz Apellániz et al. 2020). Fang et al. (2020) identified about 580 young members with a median age near 1 Myr. Deneb, often credited, is not the main power source.

card.question: How many members can a modest little cluster hide?
card.glance: A small, sparse group of faint stars in eastern Cygnus: pleasant but modest.
card.whyHere: Some clusters reveal their true size only when you measure motions, and NGC 7063 grew from a dozen stars to about two hundred once Gaia looked.
card.see: From υ Cygni, move about 2° north-east, near the star 69 Cygni, to a small group of a dozen faint stars. It is pleasant rather than spectacular, so take a moment to let fainter members appear.
card.understand: Older catalogs counted only the dozen stars you see. Gaia measured the distance and motion of every faint star in the area and found about 200 sharing the same values, most too faint for binoculars. At about 2,140 light-years, this is a nearby family by cluster standards.
card.wonder: Its stars are roughly 150 million years old, a little older than the Pleiades.
card.connect: M39, to the north, is a bigger, brighter family.
card.answer: Many more than it shows: binoculars catch about a dozen stars, but Gaia finds about 200 moving together.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows a loose knot of stars; binoculars show its brightest dozen.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 657 pc, about 200 Gaia members, neural-network age 148 Myr (89–268). No literature age override was applied.

card.question: What does a star nursery look like ten million years on?
card.glance: A small, sparse group of several stars, a couple of them fairly bright, north of ν Cephei.
card.whyHere: NGC 7160 is the older sibling of the IC 1396 nursery, born a few million years earlier.
card.see: From ν Cephei, look about two degrees north-north-east for a little knot of a few brightish stars with fainter ones nearby. It is sparse, with little central concentration.
card.understand: At about 10 million years old, NGC 7160 has lost its birth cloud entirely. Young stars are born with dusty disks, the raw material of planets, which fade as the stars age. Far fewer stars carry them here than in younger IC 1396, so the disks act as a clock.
card.wonder: Next to IC 1396, it is like a toddler standing beside a newborn sibling.
card.connect: IC 1396, to the south, shows a younger generation of the same star-forming region.
card.answer: It looks like NGC 7160, a small, clean group of stars with its nursery blown away and most of its planet-making disks gone, the stage cleared in ten million years.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows a compact group of bright stars and no nebula.
card.deeper: Sicilia-Aguilar et al. (2005) studied disks and accretion across Cepheus OB2 and confirmed ages of about 10 Myr for NGC 7160 versus 1–5 Myr for Tr 37; disk fractions drop with age. Hunt & Reffert (2024) give 895 pc, a little closer than Tr 37 (925 pc, Pelayo-Baldárrago+2023).

card.question: Why do binoculars show only a few stars of a rich cluster?
card.glance: A faint, loose haze with a few stars at the threshold, a dark-sky challenge in Lacerta.
card.whyHere: NGC 7209 is an older family, around 400 million years old, whose members are mostly too faint for binoculars.
card.see: About four degrees south-east of π² Cygni, look with steady, supported binoculars for a faint patch with a few stars on its surface. Most members are fainter than binoculars show.
card.understand: Gaia counts about 500 members, so you see only the brightest end of the family. Age has removed the blue stars that would have stood out, leaving mostly stars like the Sun and smaller. At nearly 3,900 light-years those are far too faint to see one by one.
card.wonder: Its light left about 3,900 years ago, when the first Babylonian dynasty was rising.
card.connect: NGC 7243, a younger and easier Lacerta cluster, is a few degrees away.
card.answer: Distance and age conspire, for the stars that remain are modest, and at that distance most fall below binocular reach, so what you see is only the tip of the family.
card.photoCaption: Photos resolve hundreds of faint members that binoculars cannot.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 1.19 kpc, about 500 members and 397 Myr (243–600 Myr).

card.question: What lies far behind the bright star ε Cephei?
card.glance: A tiny faint knot right beside ε Cephei, a challenge.
card.whyHere: NGC 7235 is a young cluster about 11,000 light-years away, far beyond the bright star beside it.
card.see: Center ε Cephei and look about half a degree north-west for a tiny faint grouping. It needs steady binoculars and a dark sky.
card.understand: NGC 7235 is only about 15 million years old, so it still holds hot, luminous stars. At this distance even those are faint, and its 140 or so members crowd into a few arcminutes. ε Cephei beside it is a nearby star, so the pair is perspective, not partnership.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 11,000 years ago, near the end of the last ice age.
card.connect: IC 1396, a few degrees away, is a younger family barely a quarter as far.
card.answer: A young star family about 11,000 light-years away, so remote that even its brightest stars look faint. The bright star in front is a neighbor; the family behind is a stranger.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows a compact group of faint stars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 3.37 kpc, about 140 members and 15 Myr (10–22 Myr).

card.question: Why does a cluster full of young blue stars look so faint?
card.glance: A loose, irregular group of faint stars, about the Moon’s size, west of α Lacertae.
card.whyHere: NGC 7243 is a family about the Pleiades’ age, six times farther away, in little Lacerta.
card.see: Find α Lacertae, between Cygnus and Cassiopeia, and move about two and a half degrees west. A loose group of a few dozen faint stars appears, best seen in a wide field against the surrounding stars.
card.understand: About 100 million years old, NGC 7243 still has blue-white stars, but at 2,800 light-years they look faint. Gaia counts about 500 members, most of them far below binocular reach. The few you see are the family’s brightest, hottest members.
card.wonder: Its light left around 800 BCE, when Homer’s epics were taking shape.
card.connect: Older NGC 7209, nearby, shows what four hundred million years do to a family.
card.answer: Distance steals the glitter: NGC 7243 has the same young sparkle as the Pleiades, but at six times the distance it fades to a loose scatter of faint points.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows a loose group of bright and faint stars.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 864 pc, about 500 members and 106 Myr (64–168 Myr).

card.question: What will the Sun leave behind when it dies?
card.glance: A large, very faint, round gray glow in Aquarius, half the Moon’s width, a challenge that needs a dark, moonless sky.
card.whyHere: The Helix Nebula is the shed outer layers of a dying Sun-like star, a preview of our own Sun’s far future.
card.see: Low in the south in autumn, go from δ Aquarii about 7° south-west to the faint star υ Aquarii; the Helix lies just over a degree west, a pale disk half the Moon’s size. Use averted vision, and an OIII filter, passing only oxygen’s green glow, helps greatly.
card.understand: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel, it puffs its outer layers into space, and the exposed core, a tiny, very hot ember called a white dwarf, makes that gas glow. Astronomers date the shell by measuring how fast it expands and how far it has gone, like timing a ripple on a pond. The answer is surprisingly young: the inner parts left about 6,600 years ago and the outer ring about 12,000.
card.wonder: At about 650 light-years, the Helix is one of the nearest planetary nebulae, which is why it looks so large.
card.connect: Stars of the Sun’s size die gently like this, while much heavier stars end violently as supernovae.
card.answer: A glowing shell like the Helix, a planetary nebula, an old name with nothing to do with planets. The Sun’s outer layers will drift outward like this, lit for a few tens of thousands of years by the white dwarf left behind.
card.photoCaption: Photos show blue and red rings and thousands of comet-like knots; your eye sees a faint gray disk at best.
card.notSee: Color, the helix shape and the knots.
card.deeper: Gaia measures a parallax of about 5.0 mas for the central star, about 200 pc (650 light-years), which makes the Helix one of the nearest planetary nebulae. O'Dell, McCullough & Meixner (2004) found that the inner disk and the outer ring expand at different speeds, giving ages of about 6,600 and 12,100 years. The central star is a white dwarf (spectral type DAO). Many small dense knots line the inner edge of the ring.

card.question: What is left of a star family after more than a billion years?
card.glance: A broad, even scatter of faint stars larger than the full Moon, next to the orange pair 56 Andromedae.
card.whyHere: NGC 752 is an old star family, over a billion years old, in the middle of falling apart.
card.see: Start at the wide orange double 56 Andromedae in southern Andromeda and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. There is no bright center and no standout blue-white star, so let your eye relax over the whole field.
card.understand: In a young cluster the brightest stars are hot blue-white heavyweights, but here only stars a little heavier than the Sun remain in their steady adult life. That dividing line works as a clock, because the heavier a star, the sooner it leaves its adult phase, and here it reads about 1.34 billion years. Gaia counts about 440 members but only about 320 Suns’ worth of mass still bound together.
card.wonder: This family is already about a tenth as old as the universe, and most clusters dissolve long before reaching such an age.
card.connect: Caroline’s Rose in Cassiopeia is a family of similar age, several times farther away and far richer.
card.answer: Only the lighter members, a few new giants and a family coming loose at the seams. The galaxy’s tides have been pulling NGC 752 apart for over a billion years, and its stars are slowly mixing into the Milky Way.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows the same thin scatter; no photo makes this cluster look rich.
card.deeper: Agüeros et al. (2018) fitted isochrones to Gaia-selected members and found 1.34 ± 0.06 Gyr; an eclipsing-binary study gives 1.45 ± 0.05 Gyr. Gaia DR3 counts about 440 members at 434 pc, with only about 320 solar masses still bound inside the tidal radius (Hunt & Reffert 2024): a sparse remnant of a once larger family.

card.question: What does a star family look like after 1.6 billion years?
card.glance: A round, even, misty glow about half the Moon’s width, midway between ρ and σ Cassiopeiae.
card.whyHere: Caroline’s Rose is an old and very rich family, in which over a billion years of aging have turned the brightest stars into giants.
card.see: From Caph, the end of Cassiopeia’s W, move about three degrees south-west to the faint pair ρ and σ Cassiopeiae; the cluster sits midway between them. In binoculars it is a soft, uniform patch, grainy under a dark sky, and the rose-petal pattern needs a telescope.
card.understand: Caroline’s Rose is roughly 1.6 billion years old, so its hot blue stars burned out long ago, and its brightest members now are stars a bit heavier than the Sun that have swollen into giants. It is also unusually massive: Gaia counts more than 4,000 members, the heaviest open cluster within about 7,000 light-years. Most families dissolve long before this age, and sheer mass is what has held this one together.
card.wonder: Caroline Herschel found it in 1783 while sweeping the sky for comets with a small telescope.
card.connect: M52, a few degrees away, is the young, sparkling version.
card.answer: It looks misty and even, a soft glow of yellow and orange giants among thousands of fainter stars. Time has dimmed its sparkle but not yet scattered the family.
card.photoCaption: Color photos show many yellowish red giants and dark "petal" lanes; binoculars show a gray mist.
card.notSee: Individual stars and the petal pattern.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) list NGC 7789 at 1.97 kpc with about 4,100 Gaia DR3 members and nearly 18,000 solar masses within its tidal radius, the most massive cluster in their census within about 2.15 kpc of the Sun (queried 2026-11-01). Ages in the literature cluster around 1.4–1.7 Gyr; APOD quotes 1.6 Gyr and HR24's neural net gives 1.57 Gyr.

card.question: Why do a few orange stars shine among the Double Cluster’s blue-white crowd?
card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view between Cassiopeia and Perseus, a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.whyHere: The Double Cluster is a pair of star families born together about 14 million years ago: young, hot, far away and beautiful.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, the western one, h Persei, a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so all their stars share a birthday. Most are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun, and the orange points are the heaviest of all. Weight is destiny for a star: the more massive it is, the faster it burns, so those few have already raced to their last chapter.
card.wonder: They lie about 7,400 light-years away, more than ten times farther than the Pleiades, yet are still bright enough to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Its twin, χ Persei, sits half a degree east, born of the same cloud at the same time.
card.answer: The orange stars were born with the rest, but being the heaviest they aged fastest and have swollen into red supergiants, cool on the surface and orange in color. Their ages, read from the supergiants alone, match the cluster’s, a neat cross-check.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the same stars with stronger color; the orange supergiants are the reddest points.
card.notSee: The full halo of fainter members spreading around both clusters.
card.deeper: Currie et al. (2010) found that h Persei, χ Persei and a surrounding halo of stars all have ages near 14 Myr, with the red supergiants giving 13–14 Myr independently. Gaia DR3 places the pair at about 2.3 kpc in the Perseus spiral arm (Hunt & Reffert 2024). Together they hold several thousand solar masses of stars, part of the Perseus OB1 association.

card.question: Are the two halves of the Double Cluster true twins, or a chance pairing?
card.glance: The eastern twin of the Double Cluster, a little looser, with several orange stars.
card.whyHere: Two clusters side by side on the sky are often strangers at very different depths, so the Double Cluster’s eastern half deserves a careful look.
card.see: Keep both clusters in the field and compare: χ Persei is slightly looser and less concentrated than h. Pick out its orange-tinted stars, and defocus a touch to judge their color against the blue-white majority.
card.understand: Twins should pass two tests, the same distance and the same age. Gaia measures the parallax of hundreds of members in each cluster, and the averages land at the same distance within the uncertainties, about 7,500 light-years. For the age, astronomers read three separate clocks: the heaviest stars still burning hydrogen, the small stars still contracting toward adulthood, and the orange supergiants. In both clusters all three agree.
card.wonder: Together the two clusters hold thousands of Suns’ worth of stars, part of a wider family of young stars spread across Perseus.
card.connect: In older families such as M34 or NGC 752, all giants of this size are long gone.
card.answer: They are true twins, born about 14 million years ago from one cloud and still traveling side by side, a rarity among the many chance pairings the sky offers.
card.photoCaption: Color photos make the orange supergiants obvious; in binoculars they are subtle but real.
card.deeper: Currie et al. (2010) derived 13.5 ± 1.5 Myr for χ Persei from its M-type supergiants, matching the turn-off and pre-main-sequence ages. The cluster's Gaia DR3 distance is about 2.29 kpc, the same as h Persei within the uncertainties.

sizeLy.note: 316′ observing extent at 62.44 kpc; projected width only, the galaxy is also deep along the line of sight

card.question: Where did astronomers learn to measure distances to other galaxies?
card.glance: A faint, comma-shaped cloud of light in Tucana, with the bright knot of 47 Tucanae at its edge.
card.whyHere: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a second neighbor galaxy, and the place where the first yardstick beyond our galaxy was found.
card.see: Under a dark sky it looks like a small torn-off cloud, and binoculars show a soft, uneven glow, brighter along one side. Beside it sit two fuzzy stars, bright 47 Tucanae and fainter NGC 362, globular clusters of our own galaxy far in front of the Cloud.
card.understand: In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied pulsing stars called Cepheids in this Cloud. Because all of them lie at nearly the same distance, any difference in brightness had to be real, and she found that the slower a Cepheid beats, the brighter it truly is. Time a Cepheid anywhere and you know its true power; compare that with how faint it looks and you have its distance.
card.wonder: The Cloud is stretched out along your line of sight, tens of thousands of light-years deep, like a cigar seen nearly end-on.
card.connect: 47 Tucanae, the bright globular at its edge, is more than ten times nearer.
card.answer: Here, in the Small Magellanic Cloud, where a careful look at pulsing stars turned them into lamps of known wattage. That rule carried distance measurements out to other galaxies for the first time.
card.photoCaption: Photos show pink nurseries and blue clusters; binoculars show a gray, uneven cloud.
card.notSee: No color; its nurseries are telescope or photo targets.
card.deeper: Graczyk et al. (2020) analyzed 15 detached eclipsing binaries of giant stars: 62.44 ± 0.47 (stat) ± 0.81 (syst) kpc. The binaries span about 10 kpc in distance with a line-of-sight depth of up to 7 kpc, so the SMC is elongated and strongly inclined. Leavitt & Pickering (1912) reported periods for 25 SMC variables whose brightness rises with period: the Cepheid period–luminosity relation.

card.question: Does Aldebaran really belong to the V-shaped cluster it seems to lead?
card.glance: A bright orange star at one tip of the V-shaped Hyades, the face of Taurus the Bull.
card.whyHere: Every family photo has someone who wandered into the frame, and in the Hyades that someone is the brightest star of all.
card.see: Aldebaran is the orange eye of Taurus, at one tip of the V of the Hyades. Frame the whole V and its warm orange stands apart from the white and pale-yellow cluster stars; then glance south-east to Betelgeuse and ask yourself which of the two is redder.
card.understand: Aldebaran is an orange giant, a star that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width. We know its size because the Moon sometimes passes in front of it, and the light fades out over a fraction of a second instead of switching off at once. Its distance comes from parallax, the small yearly shift the Hipparcos satellite measured against faraway stars, and the Hyades, measured the same way, turn out to lie more than twice as far.
card.wonder: Aldebaran’s light left around 1960 and the cluster’s in the 1870s, so a single binocular field holds two different eras.
card.connect: Betelgeuse, just to the south-east, shows how differently a much heavier star grows old.
card.answer: So Aldebaran is a passer-by in the family portrait: at about 67 light-years it stands less than halfway to the cluster and simply lines up in front of it from where we stand.
card.photoCaption: Photos make it look embedded in the cluster; only distance measurements reveal the gap.
card.deeper: Heiter et al. (2015) adopted 3,927 ± 40 K from its angular diameter and total flux. A lunar-occultation diameter of 20.58 milliarcseconds (Richichi & Roccatagliata 2005) combined with the Hipparcos distance gives about 45 solar radii. Gaia-era studies put the Hyades center about 154 light-years away (Hunt & Reffert 2024), so Aldebaran stands roughly 87 light-years in front of the cluster.

card.question: Why does Algol, the Demon Star, lose two-thirds of its light every few days?
card.glance: A white star in Perseus that looks perfectly ordinary until, every few days, it slips to a third of its usual brightness for a few hours.
card.whyHere: Algol is the easiest star in the sky to catch in the act of changing, and the cause has nothing to do with the star itself.
card.see: Algol sits in Perseus, about halfway between Cassiopeia’s W and the Pleiades, and your eyes alone can follow it. At full light it matches Almach, the golden star at the end of Andromeda; deep in eclipse it sinks to the level of ε Persei.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars, with a third circling farther out, and we see the pair’s orbit almost edge-on: an eclipsing binary. Every 2.87 days the dim orange companion slides across the hot blue-white star. The shape of the change gives it away: a pulsing star brightens and fades all the time, while Algol holds steady for most of its cycle and then drops sharply for a few hours, just as a passing body would make it.
card.wonder: Algol's dimmer partner is the lighter star yet the more aged one, because it swelled first and poured much of its gas onto its partner, turning the former heavyweight into the lightweight.
card.connect: Mira and δ Cephei change for the opposite reason: the star itself swells and shrinks.
card.answer: Neither star changes; the fainter one simply passes in front of the brighter and blocks most of its light until it moves on. The Demon’s wink is a shadow play, staged nearly 90 light-years away.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo freezes Algol at one moment, so it cannot show the eclipse. Interferometers have imaged the pair, but only as a few pixels.
card.deeper: Kolbas et al. (2015) separated the three spectra: Algol A is a B8 dwarf of 3.39 solar masses at about 12,550 K; Algol B is a cool subgiant of 0.77 solar masses; Algol C (1.58 solar masses) orbits the pair every 680 days. The “Algol paradox” — the less massive star is the more evolved — is explained by mass transfer: B was once the heavier star, aged first and handed much of its gas to A. CHARA interferometry resolved the inner pair (Baron et al. 2012). Hipparcos parallax: 36.3 ± 1.4 mas.

card.question: How big is the lonely orange star at Hydra’s heart?
card.glance: A lone orange star in an empty stretch of sky south-west of Regulus, the heart of Hydra.
card.whyHere: Alphard is a lone orange giant in a dark patch of sky, an uncluttered lesson in color and size.
card.see: Look about 20 degrees south-west of Regulus for the only bright star in a wide, empty region; its Arabic name means ‘the solitary one’. In binoculars it is a rich orange, so swing to blue-white Regulus and back.
card.understand: Alphard has used up the hydrogen in its core, swollen, and cooled to about 4,200 K, so its light leans red. Its size was measured with an interferometer: the disk spans less than a hundredth of an arcsecond, and at its distance of about 180 light-years that works out to more than 50 times the Sun’s width. Glowing from all that surface, it gives out several hundred times the Sun’s light.
card.wonder: Alphard’s light left it about 180 years ago, around the time of the first photographs.
card.connect: Regulus, up in Leo, is a hot young star to set beside this cool giant.
card.answer: Big enough that, in the Sun’s place, Alphard’s surface would reach about two-thirds of the way to Mercury’s orbit.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows how empty Alphard’s surroundings are; the star itself is a saturated blob.
card.deeper: Hipparcos parallax 18.09 ± 0.18 mas (about 180 light-years). A limb-darkened diameter of 9.36 mas (Cruzalèbes et al. 2013, via JMDC) at that distance gives about 56 solar radii, roughly 0.26 au, compared with Mercury’s 0.39 au. Literature temperatures span about 4,030–4,400 K (SIMBAD compilation); with 4,190 K the luminosity is near 860 Suns.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine it tens of thousands of times?
card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster beside it.
card.whyHere: Scorpius is one big family of stars born about 11 million years ago, and Antares is the sibling that has raced ahead to old age.
card.see: Antares glows low in the south as the red heart of Scorpius. Put it near the edge of the field and its orange deepens, especially if you defocus slightly; about two and a half Moon-widths to the west sits M4, a soft round gray glow.
card.understand: Antares was born perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, and heavy stars burn their fuel recklessly fast, so it has already used up its core hydrogen and swollen into a supergiant. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 degrees against the Sun's 5,800, which is why it glows orange-red. In 2017 astronomers mapped gas rising and sinking across that vast surface.
card.wonder: Antares is heavy enough to end as a supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.
card.connect: τ Scorpii, two degrees away, is a sibling still hot and blue.
card.answer: Antares wins by sheer size: about 680 times wider than the Sun, so although each patch of its surface is dimmer than the Sun's, the total comes to tens of thousands of Suns. Swap it for the Sun and its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
card.photoCaption: ESO's interferometer turned Antares into a lumpy disk of hot and cool patches; the survey photo shows only a saturated point beside M4.
card.notSee: The surface detail and the blue companion about 3 arcseconds away are far beyond binoculars.
card.deeper: Ohnaka et al. (2013) measured a limb-darkened diameter of 37.4 milliarcseconds with ESO's VLTI and derived 3,660 ± 120 K and log L/L☉ = 4.88 ± 0.23. At the Hipparcos 2007 distance (≈170 pc, ±17%) that angle means a radius near 680 R☉; the radius scales with the still-uncertain distance. Pecaut et al. (2012) included Antares when revising the Upper Scorpius age to 11 ± 1 ± 2 Myr. Mass estimates of 12–15 M☉ put it well above the ~8 M☉ needed to end as a core-collapse supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.

card.question: What will the Sun look like in old age?
card.glance: The brightest star of spring, a strong orange-gold light in Boötes at the end of the curve you follow from the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.whyHere: Arcturus is an old orange giant racing through our neighborhood, and it offers a preview of the Sun’s own old age.
card.see: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle away from the bowl to the first bright star, Arcturus, the brightest in Boötes. Its orange-gold is obvious in binoculars. Carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare.
card.understand: Arcturus weighs about the same as the Sun but is billions of years older, and it has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 25 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 4,300 K, yet all that glowing surface makes it shine about 200 times as brightly as the Sun. It is also poor in heavy elements and crosses our sky fast, at about 122 kilometers per second, the mark of a visitor from the galaxy’s older, thicker disk.
card.wonder: In 1933 its starlight switched on the lights of the Chicago World’s Fair.
card.connect: A star ten times heavier, Spica, will end far more violently.
card.answer: In billions of years the Sun will look much like Arcturus does tonight, an orange-gold giant with a cooler surface but far more light.
card.photoCaption: Survey photos saturate on Arcturus and lose its color; the binocular view shows the orange tint better than these plates.
card.deeper: Ramírez & Allende Prieto (2011) found Teff 4286 ± 30 K, log g 1.66, [Fe/H] −0.52, mass 1.08 ± 0.06 solar masses, radius 25.4 solar radii and an age of about 7.1 billion years. Its Hipparcos parallax is 88.83 ± 0.54 mas (36.7 light-years). The proper motion, about 2.3″ per year, shifts it by a full Moon-width in roughly 800 years. Arcturus and other stars sharing its motion (the ‘Arcturus group’) were proposed as debris of a disrupted satellite galaxy (Navarro et al. 2004); that origin remains debated.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine almost everything around it?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star on Orion’s shoulder, whose color blooms when you nudge the focus slightly off.
card.whyHere: Betelgeuse is what a heavy star looks like near the end of its life, a cool, swollen giant on Orion’s shoulder.
card.see: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s eastern shoulder, the bright orange star opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red suddenly becomes obvious; swing to Rigel to feel the contrast. Its brightness drifts over months, so judge it fresh each time.
card.understand: A star’s color is a thermometer, and Betelgeuse’s says its surface is only about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so each square meter of it shines more feebly than the Sun’s. The surprise is how many square meters there are. Astronomers timed its slow pulsations and fed them into models of how heavy stars age, and out came about 18 Suns’ worth of matter swollen to some 760 times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
card.connect: Heavy stars like this do not fade quietly, and the wreckage of one that already exploded lies next door in Taurus.
card.answer: That is the whole trick: a dim glow spread over an almost absurd amount of surface still adds up to far more light than the Sun will ever give.
card.photoCaption: ESO’s VLT pictures show its blotchy surface and the 2019–20 dimming; binoculars and ordinary photos show only a point.
card.notSee: Its disk and surface spots: these need the largest telescopes and interferometers.
card.deeper: Joyce et al. (2020) combined its pulsation periods with evolution models: 16.5–19 solar masses, about 764 solar radii and 168 (+27/−15) parsecs, early in core-helium burning, so the supernova is most likely about 100,000 years away. During the 2020 Great Dimming, Levesque & Massey measured 3,600 ± 25 K, far too small a cooling to explain the fade; VLT imaging then showed a dust veil over its southern half (Montargès et al. 2021).

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.whyHere: Capella looks like one golden star, yet it is two giants in a tight embrace, and the way they were weighed is a small masterpiece.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows one bright point; only interferometers have resolved the two giants.
card.deeper: Torres et al. (2015) combined spectroscopy and interferometry: 2.57 and 2.48 solar masses, radii of 12.0 and 8.8 solar radii, and temperatures of about 4,970 and 5,730 K. Models fit only if the cooler, heavier star is already in its helium-burning (red clump) phase while its companion is still crossing toward the giant branch.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.whyHere: A star's brightness in the sky mixes two things, how much light it makes and how far away it is, and Deneb is where the two come apart most dramatically.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.photoCaption: Survey photographs show Deneb buried in Milky Way stars and glowing gas that binoculars render as a rich grainy field.
card.notSee: Its size, light output and distance are all inferred; the point of light looks no bigger than any other star.
card.deeper: Schiller & Przybilla (2008) analyzed a high-resolution spectrum and found Teff 8,525 ± 75 K, log g 1.10, a radius of 203 ± 17 solar radii, about 196,000 solar luminosities and a current mass of 19 ± 3 suns, adopting 802 ± 66 pc from membership of the Cyg OB7 association. Hipparcos (2.31 ± 0.32 mas) points to a much smaller distance, so treat every derived number as uncertain by tens of percent. Its surface is enriched in nitrogen from the core, and the authors favor a star of about 23 solar masses evolving toward the red supergiant stage.

card.question: What does a planetary system look like while it is still being built?
card.glance: A lone bright white star low in the south on autumn evenings, with nothing as bright for a long way around.
card.whyHere: Fomalhaut is a young, nearby star circled by a wide ring of icy debris, a planetary system still settling down.
card.see: Follow the western side of the Great Square of Pegasus, from Scheat through Markab, and keep going about 45 degrees south. Fomalhaut, in Piscis Austrinus, is the only bright star in that part of the sky, and its ring is far beyond any backyard instrument.
card.understand: Fomalhaut has about twice the Sun’s mass, shines about 16 times brighter and is only about 440 million years old, a tenth of the Sun’s age. Hubble photographed a ring of dust and ice around it roughly 140 times farther out than Earth is from the Sun, with a sharp inner edge. Loose rubble left alone would spread into a fuzzy edge, so a sharp one suggests something is herding it.
card.wonder: Two faint companions, an orange dwarf and a red dwarf, travel with it so far out that one appears several degrees away from it in our sky.
card.connect: The Helix Nebula in Aquarius shows the other end of a star’s life, when it sheds its own ring of material.
card.answer: It looks much like Fomalhaut, a young star wrapped in rings of icy rubble, their edges probably sculpted by the gravity of planets we cannot yet see. The Webb telescope has since found more belts closer in, a system still under construction.
card.photoCaption: Webb’s infrared image shows the dust belts; binoculars show only the bright point at the center.
card.deeper: Mamajek (2012) derived 440 ± 40 million years, 1.92 solar masses and 8,590 K, and Mamajek et al. (2013) showed it forms a very wide triple with the orange dwarf TW PsA and the red dwarf LP 876-10. Hubble imaged the main belt at about 133–158 AU (Kalas et al. 2005). Gáspár & Rieke (2020) reinterpreted “Fomalhaut b” as an expanding dust cloud, and Webb resolved inner belts (Gáspár et al. 2023). Hipparcos parallax 129.8 ± 0.5 mas.

card.question: Why is La Superba one of the reddest stars in the sky?
card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.whyHere: La Superba is a dying giant in Canes Venatici, faint to the eye but glowing like an ember in binoculars.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper’s handle, head about a third of the way toward Megrez. Faint to the eye, La Superba is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember, and red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
card.understand: Late in life a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its spent core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. In its cool atmosphere, about 2,700 K, carbon-rich molecules and soot absorb blue light. The star is also shedding gas and dust, and infrared satellites found a vast shell of it piling up where the star’s wind runs into the surrounding gas.
card.wonder: The carbon in your body was forged in stars like this long before the Sun was born.
card.connect: Cor Caroli, a few degrees away, is hot and white: the other end of the stellar thermometer.
card.answer: It is a carbon star: soot-like molecules at its surface block blue light and let only deep red escape, which is why Angelo Secchi, a pioneer of sorting stars by their spectra, named it ‘the superb one’.
card.photoCaption: Survey plates wash out its color; binoculars show the red better than this photo.
card.deeper: Lambert et al. (1986) derived an effective temperature of about 2,720 K. GCVS classes Y CVn as a semiregular (SRb) variable with V 4.86–7.32; Universe Today describes a cycle of roughly 160 days on top of a longer one of several years. The DEATHSTAR distance catalog (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022) gives 249 +25/−22 pc (about 810 light-years), while the Gaia EDR3 parallax suggests nearer 1,000. IRAS and ISO found a detached dust shell about 0.9 pc across; Libert et al. (2007) model it as wind material piling up where it meets the surrounding gas.

card.question: How can one star be easy to see one season and invisible months later?
card.glance: A red star in the neck of Cetus, the Whale, which is either an obvious naked-eye star or lost even to binoculars, depending on the month.
card.whyHere: Mira is an old red giant caught in the act of pulsing, the clearest preview in the sky of the Sun’s own old age.
card.see: Check a current brightness estimate first, because Mira may be out of reach tonight. Near its peak it is an obvious orange-red point in the Whale’s neck, well south of Aries; judge it quickly, since red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
card.understand: Mira is a red giant, a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to hundreds of times the Sun’s width, and every 332 days it swells and shrinks. That alone would change its light only modestly. The trick is its cool surface, around 3,000 K, where molecules form and break apart with each pulse, and when they form they soak up visible light like a curtain drawn across a window.
card.wonder: Mira races through space trailing a wake of shed gas about 13 light-years long, recorded in ultraviolet by NASA’s GALEX satellite: some 30,000 years of its history written across the sky.
card.connect: The gas it sheds will drift off to seed new stars, and once a star like Mira has lost everything, it ends as a glowing shell like the Helix Nebula.
card.answer: The pulse draws that curtain open and shut, so at its best Mira sends us more than a thousand times the light of its faintest. David Fabricius watched it vanish in 1596, yet it has kept coming back ever since.
card.photoCaption: Hubble’s ultraviolet image shows Mira and its hot companion as two smudges; to the eye it is one red point whose brightness depends on the date.
card.deeper: Near-infrared interferometry (Woodruff et al. 2004) gives a diameter of about 330–400 solar radii and 2,900–3,200 K, both varying with phase; the size also depends on wavelength because of molecular layers. The companion, Mira B, about half an arcsecond away, is a white dwarf feeding on Mira’s wind (Sokoloski & Bildsten 2010). The GALEX tail was reported by Martin et al. (2007). Hipparcos parallax 10.9 ± 1.2 mas (about 270–340 light-years). Period 332 days (GCVS).

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.whyHere: William Herschel likened its color to a garnet, and it is the clearest proof in the sky that color is a star’s thermometer.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows a saturated point in a rich Milky Way field beside the faint glow of IC 1396; its disk is far too small to see in any ordinary image.
card.deeper: The distance is the weak link: published values span roughly 390–870 pc, and Wiesemeyer et al. (2026) adopt 421 (+57/−42) pc. The radius scales with distance. Perrin et al. (2005) measured a photospheric diameter of 14.1 mas inside a larger molecular shell, which gives about 600–1,300 solar radii across that range; Levesque et al. (2005) found about 3,700 K and 1,420 solar radii for their adopted distance. B−V of 2.35 (SIMBAD) makes it one of the reddest naked-eye stars.

card.question: What is a star like Procyon about to become?
card.glance: A bright, creamy-white star, the third corner of the triangle it makes with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
card.whyHere: Procyon is a neighbor at a turning point: its long, steady adult life is ending, and the dead star circling it shows where that road leads.
card.see: Procyon is the eastern corner of the Winter Triangle, with Sirius and Betelgeuse. Compare it with Sirius to the south and it looks a touch warmer, creamy rather than icy white. Then sweep 4° north-west to fainter, blue-white Gomeisa for contrast.
card.understand: Procyon has about one and a half times the Sun’s mass and lies only 11 light-years away. Its faint companion, Procyon B, circles it every 41 years, and Hubble’s patient tracking of that orbit weighed both stars. Procyon’s diameter, measured directly with an interferometer, came out at about twice the Sun’s, a little too large for a star still comfortably burning hydrogen, and its gentle oscillations agree that the core is nearly spent.
card.wonder: Procyon B packs six-tenths of the Sun’s mass into a ball about the size of Earth.
card.connect: An orange giant in Gemini shows the next chapter: a star that has already finished swelling.
card.answer: Procyon is about to swell into a giant and, much later, shrink into a white dwarf, and since its companion has already made that whole trip, the bright star’s future is orbiting right beside it.
card.photoCaption: Photos show a single bright point; Procyon B needs Hubble.
card.deeper: Bond et al. (2015) used two decades of Hubble images to measure 1.478 ± 0.012 (Procyon A) and 0.592 ± 0.006 (Procyon B) solar masses in a 40.84-year orbit, and models then give Procyon A an age of about 2.7 billion years. VLTI interferometry measured its diameter as 2.05 solar diameters (Kervella et al. 2004); together with its oscillations this marks a star finishing its hydrogen-burning life.

card.question: What becomes of a middle-weight star when its core runs out of hydrogen?
card.glance: An orange-red star marking the head of Hercules, 5° west of white Rasalhague: two heads side by side.
card.whyHere: Stars change most dramatically near the end, and Rasalgethi shows that stage up close, a giant so swollen and cool that its surface heaves like a slow sea.
card.see: Rasalgethi and Rasalhague, the heads of Hercules and Ophiuchus, sit about 5° apart and fit in one low-power sweep, one orange-red and one white. Over weeks Rasalgethi's brightness wanders, sometimes drawing much closer to its neighbor's, and its 5th-magnitude companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Once the hydrogen in a star's core runs out, the core shrinks and heats while the outer layers balloon outward and cool. Interferometers measure Rasalgethi's disk at 36 thousandths of an arcsecond across, and at its distance that means a star hundreds of times wider than the Sun. Its loose outer layers heave irregularly, so its light drifts, while a slow wind carries them away.
card.wonder: If Rasalgethi replaced the Sun, Earth would be orbiting inside the star.
card.connect: Rasalhague, 5° away, is a hot white star at the other end of the color scale.
card.answer: A red giant like Rasalgethi: hundreds of times wider than the Sun, cool enough to glow orange-red, and slowly giving its outer layers back to space.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows only a saturated star; the color is best judged by eye.
card.notSee: The bluish-green-looking companion α² Her, 4.9″ away, needs a small telescope.
card.deeper: VSX classifies α Her A as a semiregular variable (SRB) ranging V 2.73–3.60 with a characteristic timescale of about 126 days; GCVS lists it as SRC with 2.74–4.0. Hipparcos 2007 gives 9.07 ± 1.32 mas (about 360 ly, ±15%). The WDS lists the AB pair (STF 2140) at 4.9″. Mark III interferometry measured a limb-darkened diameter of 36.0 ± 0.4 mas (Mozurkewich et al. 2003); at the Hipparcos distance that is roughly 370–500 solar radii, so the uncertainty is mostly the distance.

card.question: Why is Sirius the brightest star in the night sky?
card.glance: A blazing white point below and left of Orion’s Belt, flashing color when low.
card.whyHere: Sirius is the most dazzling star of the night, and the reason is so ordinary it is almost a letdown, until you meet its tiny companion.
card.see: Orion’s Belt, followed down and to the left, points straight at Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers red, green and blue, but that is our turbulent air, not the star. Park it near the edge of the binocular field to tame the glare, which also hides its faint companion.
card.understand: Sirius has about twice the Sun’s mass and a surface near 9,900 K, so it burns pure white, but plenty of stars are hotter and heavier. What sets it apart is its parallax: it shifts against the background more than almost any other bright star, which puts it only 8.6 light-years away. Every 50 years it is circled by Sirius B, a white dwarf, the bare cooling core a star leaves when it dies, and two decades of Hubble images of that orbit weighed both stars.
card.wonder: Sirius B holds about a Sun’s worth of matter in a ball the size of Earth, so a teaspoon of it would weigh tons.
card.connect: Another winter star lets you see a white dwarf for yourself, with nothing more than steady binoculars.
card.answer: Sirius is a fairly ordinary star that simply lives next door, so close that its light reaches you in under nine years.
card.photoCaption: Hubble had to overexpose Sirius A to show Sirius B at all; no binocular or small telescope can.
card.notSee: Sirius B. Only Hubble-class images or large telescopes in perfect seeing show it.
card.deeper: Bond et al. (2017) combined two decades of Hubble images with about 2,300 historical measurements: Sirius A has 2.063 ± 0.023 and Sirius B 1.018 ± 0.011 solar masses in a 50.13-year orbit, and models give Sirius A an age of about 240 million years. VLTI interferometry measured Sirius A’s diameter as 1.711 times the Sun’s (Kervella et al. 2003). The Hipparcos parallax, 379.21 ± 1.58 mas, puts the system 8.6 light-years away.

card.question: What does an ordinary star look like in the long, calm prime of its life?
card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings, the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle.
card.whyHere: Before a star can look strange, you need a normal one to measure it against, and Vega, bright and close, is the sky's classic yardstick.
card.see: Vega is the jewel of the small constellation Lyra and the first star to appear overhead as the summer sky darkens. In binoculars it becomes a hard white spark ringed by faint stars your eyes alone would miss, with the Double-Double a short hop to the north-east and Lyra's little parallelogram hanging just below.
card.understand: Like the Sun, Vega is a main-sequence star, which simply means it is in the long, steady middle of life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. It carries a little over twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight squeezes the core harder, so the fire runs hotter and faster. You can read the result in its color: a surface near 9,500 K glows blue-white.
card.wonder: A disk of dust about a thousand times the Earth–Sun distance across surrounds Vega, and Webb and Hubble found it so smooth that any planets hiding there must be small.
card.connect: Deneb, the Triangle's faintest corner, looks humbler than Vega but lies about a hundred times farther away.
card.answer: It looks like Vega, steady, white and unremarkable in the best sense, though as a heavier star it spends its fuel lavishly and, at about 700 million years, is already well into a life far shorter than the Sun's.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows only a saturated star; the dust disk needs space telescopes and infrared light.
card.notSee: The debris disk, the squashed shape and the temperature difference between pole and equator are all invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: Hipparcos measured a parallax of 130.23 ± 0.36 mas (25.0 light-years). Vega spins quickly, and we happen to look almost straight down on one pole, which is why its rotation stayed hidden for so long. CHARA interferometry (Monnier et al. 2012) modeled the rotation and found a mass of 2.15 (+0.10/−0.15) solar masses and an age of about 700 (+150/−75) million years, older than earlier estimates. The 2024 Hubble and Webb images (Wolff et al.; Su et al.) show a disk roughly 100 billion miles across with only a subtle gap, ruling out planets larger than Neptune on wide orbits.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in the sky really neighbors?
card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars in Cassiopeia, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.whyHere: Stock 2 sits beside the Double Cluster on the sky, and pairing the two shows how much depth a single sweep can hide.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north, and a large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the “Muscleman”. Use the widest field you have, because a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Gaia measures each member’s parallax and averages them, which pins down a cluster’s distance far better than any single star could. For Stock 2 it gives about 1,200 light-years, and for the Double Cluster over 7,000. The ages differ too: Stock 2 has lost its hottest blue stars, a sign of a few hundred million years, while the Double Cluster’s still blaze.
card.wonder: Gaia found about 3,000 members here, a big family hiding in plain sight because it is so spread out.
card.connect: Swing back to the Double Cluster: the nearer family looks bigger and looser, the farther one smaller and denser.
card.answer: These two are not: Stock 2 is about six times nearer and far older than the glittering pair beside it, proof that clusters touching on the sky can live in completely different parts of the galaxy.
card.photoCaption: Photos show the same scattered stars; the cluster is defined by its numbers, not a bright core.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024) list Stock 2 at 370 pc with about 3,000 Gaia DR3 members and some 3,300 solar masses. Their neural-net age is 290 Myr with a wide 160–460 Myr range. Pre-Gaia sources such as Sky & Telescope (2018) quoted about 990 light-years.
