card.question: What makes a small group of stars a real cluster?
card.glance: A small, sparse group of a few stars on the Cassiopeia–Camelopardalis border.
card.whyHere: Stock 23 is a real, small star family, a good contrast with chance patterns like Kemble’s Cascade.
card.see: From η Persei (Miram), at the top of Perseus, move about five degrees north-east. A small group of half a dozen brighter stars sits in a sparse field.
card.understand: Gaia picked out about a hundred stars here that share a distance, about 1,950 light-years, and drift across the sky together. Stars born from one cloud carry its motion with them, like passengers on the same train. Their colors fit a single age of about 72 million years.
card.wonder: It is roughly half the Pleiades’ age.
card.connect: Kemble’s Cascade, nearby, is the chance pattern to compare.
card.answer: Shared birth is the test, and Stock 23’s members pass it, moving together and sharing one age, unlike the chance stars of Kemble’s Cascade.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows the same few stars and a scatter of fainter members.

card.question: How far away is the little group east of the Double Cluster?
card.glance: A loose group of a dozen stars about two degrees west of Miram, east of the Double Cluster.
card.whyHere: Trumpler 2 is a small, nearby family that sits on the sky close to the far-off Double Cluster.
card.see: Center Miram, η Persei, and look about two degrees west. Pick out the brighter stars first, then let the fainter scatter fill in around them.
card.understand: Trumpler 2 is roughly 90 million years old. Gaia picks out about 450 members by their shared motion and averages their parallaxes into one distance. That distance turns out to be far smaller than the Double Cluster’s.
card.wonder: When this family was born, dinosaurs still ruled the Earth.
card.connect: Swing west to the Double Cluster to compare a near family with a far one.
card.answer: About 2,200 light-years, less than a third as far as the Double Cluster, which only looks like its neighbor. One sweep of the binoculars spans thousands of light-years of depth.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows a loose scatter of bright and faint members.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 675 pc, about 450 members and 90 Myr (54–150 Myr).

card.question: Does every star cluster stand out from the sky around it?
card.glance: A modest gathering of faint stars in a wide field of northern Cassiopeia.
card.whyHere: Trumpler 3 is a young, loose family about 40 million years old, spread over a large patch.
card.see: Sweep about eight degrees north of Miram, into Cassiopeia, and look for a slight concentration of faint stars. The surrounding Milky Way stars stay part of the view.
card.understand: Not every cluster is a showpiece, and many young families are loose enough to show only as a gentle rise in star numbers. Gaia finds about 690 members here by their common motion. To the eye, though, they mingle with the field stars of the Milky Way.
card.wonder: Its light left about 2,200 years ago, around when Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth with a stick and a shadow.
card.connect: Rich, compact NGC 663 shows how varied star families can be.
card.answer: Many do not, and Trumpler 3 shows only as a gentle thickening of faint stars, a family you have to go looking for, like many of the galaxy’s quiet clusters.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows a loose group with no strong center.
card.deeper: Hunt & Reffert (2024): 662 pc, about 690 members and 38 Myr (21–59 Myr).

contexts.name: Carina Nebula complex
contexts.text: A giant cloud complex in the Carina arm where several young clusters, including the one around Eta Carinae, formed over the last few million years.

contexts.name: Cassiopeia OB6 association (W3/W4/W5)
contexts.text: A massive star-forming complex in the Perseus arm; IC 1805 (Mel 15) is a core cluster inside the giant H II region W4, the Heart Nebula.

contexts.name: Cassiopeia OB8 association
contexts.text: A group of young clusters (NGC 663 is the largest; M103, NGC 654 and NGC 659 are traditionally included) at about 2.5–2.7 kpc in the Perseus arm. Modern Gaia work confirms NGC 663 as the core; the membership of the others rests on similar distances and ages.

contexts.name: Cepheus OB2 association
contexts.text: A nearby association with an older subgroup around NGC 7160 (~10 Myr) and a younger one in IC 1396 / Trumpler 37 (~4 Myr), where star formation continues at the cloud edges. The red supergiant μ Cephei lies in the same direction; its membership is debated.

contexts.name: Cygnus OB3
contexts.text: A loose group of young, heavy stars in Cygnus whose densest part is NGC 6871. The black-hole binary Cygnus X-1 moves through space with it.

contexts.name: Milky Way halo (globular cluster system)
contexts.text: The roughly spherical swarm of ancient globular clusters around the Milky Way. Their crowding toward Sagittarius and Ophiuchus let Shapley (1918) locate the Galactic center far from the Sun.

contexts.name: Lower Centaurus–Crux (Sco-Cen)

ageMyr.note: mean age of LCC (and UCL) ≈ 16 Myr

contexts.text: The southernmost subgroup of the Sco-Cen family: hot young stars scattered across Crux, Musca and Centaurus, born about 16 million years ago. δ Cru and α Mus are secure members; Mimosa and δ Cen probable; Acrux, Hadar and ε Cen debated.

contexts.name: λ Orionis ring
contexts.text: A young cluster around Meissa (λ Ori) sitting inside a ring of gas pushed out by its stars.

contexts.name: Leo Triplet
contexts.text: Three interacting spirals (M65, M66 and NGC 3628) about 35 million light-years away.

contexts.name: Andromeda subgroup of the Local Group
contexts.text: Andromeda, the largest Local Group galaxy, with its satellites (M32 among them) and the Triangulum Galaxy M33, the group's third-largest spiral.

contexts.name: M51 Group
contexts.text: A loose group dominated by the Whirlpool Galaxy; the Sunflower Galaxy appears to belong to it.

contexts.name: M81 Group
contexts.text: A small group of galaxies about 12 million light-years away; M81, M82 and NGC 3077 are linked by streams of hydrogen gas from a close encounter.

contexts.name: Magellanic Clouds
contexts.text: Two dwarf galaxies orbiting the Milky Way together; the smaller lies about 40,000 light-years beyond the larger.

contexts.name: Monoceros OB1

distanceLy.note: dist50 700.4 pc (Gaia DR3 cluster parallax, 16–84%: 699.2–701.6 pc)

contexts.text: The young stars of the Christmas Tree Cluster and the Cone Nebula region, still embedded in their cloud.

contexts.name: Monoceros OB2

distanceLy.note: dist50 1415.2 pc (Gaia DR3 cluster parallax, 16–84%: 1411.0–1419.5 pc)

contexts.text: The Rosette Nebula and its central cluster NGC 2244, part of a larger cloud still forming stars.

contexts.name: North America / Pelican complex
contexts.text: One cloud complex, about 2,600 light-years away, split by the dark lane L935 into the North America and Pelican nebulae and ionized by the hidden Bajamar star.

contexts.name: Orion OB1 association
contexts.text: A family of young star groups spread across Orion, born in successive waves over about ten million years: the Belt, the stars of the Sword, and the newborns of the Orion Nebula.

contexts.name: Orion A molecular cloud
contexts.text: The southern of Orion’s two giant dark clouds, still forming stars; the Orion Nebula is a bright blister on its near side.

contexts.name: Orion B molecular cloud
contexts.text: The northern of Orion’s two giant dark clouds, east of the Belt; it holds M78 and many very young stars.

contexts.name: Perseus OB1 association (h and χ Persei)

distanceLy.note: h and χ Per dist50 2280–2293 pc

ageMyr.note: h, χ Per and halo converge on ~14 Myr

contexts.text: A large young association in the Perseus spiral arm whose core is the Double Cluster; a halo of young stars and red supergiants surrounds both clusters.

contexts.name: Scorpius–Centaurus association (Sco OB2)
contexts.text: The nearest family of hot young stars to the Sun, spread over a quarter of the southern sky in three subgroups of slightly different ages.

contexts.name: Scorpius OB1
contexts.text: A young association of hot, massive stars whose core is the cluster NGC 6231; the blue hypergiant ζ¹ Scorpii is a member.

contexts.name: Serpens OB1 (Eagle region)
contexts.text: The young association around the Eagle Nebula’s cluster NGC 6611.

contexts.name: Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy
contexts.text: A dwarf galaxy discovered in 1994 behind the Galactic center, being stretched and absorbed by the Milky Way; M54 marks its nucleus.

contexts.name: Sagittarius OB1 (Lagoon region)
contexts.text: A spread of young, massive stars and clusters around the Lagoon Nebula on the Sagittarius spiral arm, born in the same star-forming episode.

contexts.name: Upper Centaurus–Lupus
contexts.text: The middle, slightly older subgroup of Sco-Cen, strung through Lupus and the tail of Scorpius; ζ Oph was probably flung out of it by a supernova.

contexts.name: Ursa Major moving group

ageMyr.note: 414 ± 23 Myr from CHARA interferometry of A-type members

contexts.text: A loose family of stars born together about 400 million years ago. Its core forms five of the Big Dipper’s seven stars; Dubhe and Alkaid are not members.

contexts.name: Upper Scorpius
contexts.text: The youngest part of Sco-Cen: the head of Scorpius and Antares, next to the ρ Ophiuchi clouds where stars are still forming.

contexts.name: Virgo Cluster
contexts.text: The nearest large cluster of galaxies; M49 was the first of its members to be discovered.
